RCWM: Concepts, Mathematics, and the 90-Day Build Plan

A complete technical reference for the team. Every concept defined, every equation explained, every deliverable scheduled week-by-week for the next 12 weeks.

Contents
01 The Core Idea 02 Fundamental Objects 03 The Core Equation 04 World Fragment Algebra 05 Belief Fields 06 Constraint Surfaces 07 Construction Operators 08 Reflexive Fixed Points 09 Prior Art: Performativity 10 The Evaluation Problem 11 Derived Signals 12 State Estimation (L1) 13 Ergodic Training 14 Path Signatures 15 Convergence Theory 16 12-Week Plan 17 Paper 1 Strategy 18 Tech Stack 19 Citation Strategy 20 Evaluation & Baselines 21 Identifiability 22 Competitive Baselines 23 Multi-Timescale Architecture 24 Must-Cite List (50 Papers) 25 EWS AUROC Audit 26 Data Stack & Signal Landscape
Section 01

The Core Idea — What RCWM Actually Is

Every existing model in economics and finance answers the question: "Given the current state, what will happen next?"

RCWM asks a fundamentally different question: "Given the current state, what can be constructed, by whom, under what constraints, and how will the act of construction change the space of future possibilities?"

This is not a semantic difference. It changes the mathematical object you operate on, the loss function you optimize, and the outputs you produce.

Traditional Model

f: St → St+1

A function from states to states. The state space is fixed. The function is fixed after training. The model is external to the system.

RCWM

W(t+1) = C( W(t), A(B(t)), Φ(t) )

A constructive operator that takes world fragments, belief-driven actions, and constraint fields — and produces new world fragments. The state space itself evolves. The model knows it is inside the system. The output is not a prediction but a possibility landscape.

Why this matters for the team

When you write code for RCWM, you are never writing a predictor. You are writing a system that:

  1. Decomposes reality into composable fragments
  2. Tracks what agents believe and how beliefs propagate
  3. Enumerates what transformations are feasible under current constraints
  4. Simulates how construction attempts by agents change the fragments
  5. Detects when the system is becoming reflexive (beliefs creating the reality they describe)

The five fields this unifies — control theory, game theory, causal modeling, reinforcement learning, and market microstructure — each contribute a specific capability:

FieldWhat It ContributesWhere in RCWM
Control TheorySteering systems toward target statesStrategy Generator (L3)
Game TheoryAnticipating rational reactions under incomplete infoMulti-Agent Simulator (L4)
Causal ModelingReasoning about interventions, not just correlationsConstraint Fields + Construction Operators
Reinforcement LearningSequential decision optimizationLearning Loop (L6), ergodic objective
Market MicrostructureHow actions actually propagate through marketsWorld Fragment dynamics, reflexive belief fields
Section 02

The Five Fundamental Objects

RCWM introduces a new ontology. These are not metaphors — they are data structures you will implement. Every piece of data in the system is one of these five types.

Object 1: Constructive Units (CU)

Definition

A Constructive Unit is an agent that can transform the world, not merely observe it. Unlike standard agents, a CU has persistent internal state that evolves across time steps and explicitly models its own uncertainty about the world.

Formal Specification CUi = (si, bi, Ai, κi) where: si ∈ Si // internal state (balance sheet, positions, capacity) bi ∈ Δ(W) // belief distribution over world fragments Ai ⊆ Op(W) // action space: set of construction operators available κi : W → [0,1] // construction capability: probability of successful execution
@dataclass class ConstructiveUnit: uid: str unit_type: Literal["central_bank", "fund", "corporate", "retail", "government"] state: torch.Tensor # internal state vector, dim varies by type belief: Distribution # posterior over world fragments action_space: List[Operator] # available construction operators capability: Callable # W -> probability of execution success history: List[ConstructionEvent]

Key distinction from standard agents: A CU's action space is not fixed. It depends on the current constraint field and on the CU's own state. A central bank with depleted reserves has a smaller action space than one with ample reserves. This is computed, not assumed.

Object 2: World Fragments (WF)

Definition

A World Fragment is a partial, composable description of economic reality at a specific scale. The full world state is not a single vector — it is a collection of fragments that can be composed, decomposed, and recombined.

Formal Specification W = ⨁j WFj Each WFj = (vj, σj, τj, ρj) where: vj ∈ ℝdj // state vector (dimensionality varies by fragment type) σj ∈ {micro, meso, macro} // scale level τj ∈ ℝ+ // characteristic timescale ρj : WF × WF → ℝ // composition compatibility score
@dataclass class WorldFragment: fid: str fragment_type: Literal["liquidity", "volatility", "narrative", "credit", "flow", "policy", "sentiment"] scale: Literal["micro", "meso", "macro"] state: torch.Tensor # latent state vector timescale: float # characteristic frequency (days) timestamp: datetime provenance: List[str] # which data sources contributed uncertainty: torch.Tensor # variance of state estimate

The critical insight: Different fragment types have different dimensionalities. A liquidity fragment might be 16-dimensional; a narrative fragment might be 64-dimensional. They do not share a feature space. This is why the copresheaf structure from the research compendium matters — each fragment type is a different stalk with learned transport maps between them.

Object 3: Constraint Fields (Φ)

Definition

A Constraint Field is a dynamic surface over the space of world fragment transformations that classifies each transformation as feasible or infeasible. It encodes regulatory limits, liquidity bounds, physical constraints, and accounting identities.

Formal Specification Φ(t) : Op(W) × W(t) → {feasible, infeasible} × [0,1] The constraint field is a function that takes: - a proposed construction operator - the current world state And returns: - binary feasibility - a continuous "tightness" score (how close to the constraint boundary) Decomposition: Φ(t) = Φreg(t) ∩ Φliq(t) ∩ Φphys(t) ∩ Φacct(t) Φreg = regulatory constraints (position limits, capital ratios) Φliq = liquidity constraints (market depth, funding availability) Φphys = physical constraints (delivery, settlement, time) Φacct = accounting identities (assets = liabilities + equity, flow conservation)

Why it's a field, not a set of rules: Constraints interact. A regulatory limit that is non-binding in normal conditions becomes binding when liquidity dries up. The constraint field captures these interactions — it is evaluated jointly, not rule-by-rule.

Object 4: Reflexive Loops (RL)

Definition

A Reflexive Loop is a first-class object representing a cycle where beliefs cause actions that cause world changes that validate (or invalidate) the beliefs. In standard models, reflexivity is emergent (if it appears at all). In RCWM, it is an explicit, tracked, measurable object.

Formal Specification RL = (B → A → ΔW → ΔB) A reflexive loop is a 4-tuple cycle: Bt → A(Bt) → W(t+1) = C(W(t), A(Bt), Φ) → Bt+1 = U(Bt, W(t+1)) Measuring reflexivity: ε = dB/dW · dW/dA · dA/dB // the reflexivity coefficient ε < 1 ⇒ stable (beliefs and world converge) ε = 1 ⇒ critical (phase transition) ε > 1 ⇒ unstable (self-amplifying spiral) // This is the formal version of Soros's reflexivity. // The convergence condition ε·C < 1 from the compendium.

Implementation note: You compute ε at every timestep. It is both a diagnostic (is the system reflexive right now?) and a control signal (attenuate model influence when ε approaches 1).

Object 5: Composition Operators (⊗)

Definition

Composition Operators combine world fragments into larger structures with guarantees about consistency and constraint preservation. This is where category theory enters — composition must be associative and respect the constraint field.

Formal Specification ⊗ : WFi × WFj → WFij Requirements: 1. Associativity: (WFi ⊗ WFj) ⊗ WFk = WFi ⊗ (WFj ⊗ WFk) 2. Constraint preservation: Φ(WFi) ∧ Φ(WFj) ⇒ Φ(WFi ⊗ WFj) 3. Scale consistency: σ(WFi ⊗ WFj) ≥ max(σi, σj) // Composition can fail. Two individually-stable fragments // can produce an infeasible composition. This is exactly // what happens in systemic crises — the Composition Fragility signal.
Section 03

The Core Equation — Unpacked

The RCWM Evolution Equation W(t+1) = C( W(t), A(B(t)), Φ(t) ) Expanding each term: W(t) = ⨁j WFj(t) The world at time t: a direct sum of world fragments across all types and scales. B(t) = { bi(t) }i ∈ CUs The belief field: the collection of all constructive units' belief distributions. This is a field over the agent graph, not a collection of independent beliefs. Beliefs interact via contagion: bi(t+1) depends on bi(t) and {bj(t) : j ∈ N(i)} A(B(t)) = { ai(t) = πi(bi(t), si(t)) }i ∈ CUs Actions derived from beliefs: each CU has a policy πi mapping beliefs + state to actions. Actions are construction operators, not simple "buy/sell" signals. Φ(t) = Φreg(t) ∩ Φliq(t) ∩ Φphys(t) ∩ Φacct(t) The current constraint field: what transformations are feasible right now. This evolves over time — constraints tighten in crises, loosen in booms. C(.) = The constructive operator itself: 1. Filter A(B(t)) through Φ(t) to get feasible actions 2. Apply feasible actions to W(t) 3. Resolve conflicts (multiple CUs acting on same fragment) 4. Compose resulting fragments 5. Check composition consistency 6. Return new world state + side effects (failed constructions, constraint violations)

The evolution step-by-step

def evolve(W_t, beliefs, constraint_field, constructive_units): # Step 1: Each CU selects an action based on beliefs + state actions = {} for cu in constructive_units: actions[cu.uid] = cu.policy(cu.belief, cu.state) # Step 2: Filter through constraint field feasible = {} for uid, action in actions.items(): is_feasible, tightness = constraint_field.evaluate(action, W_t) if is_feasible: feasible[uid] = (action, tightness) # Step 3: Apply feasible actions to world fragments new_fragments = [] for uid, (action, _) in feasible.items(): cu = get_unit(uid) success_prob = cu.capability(W_t) if random() < success_prob: delta_wf = action.apply(W_t) new_fragments.append(delta_wf) # Step 4: Compose new fragments with existing world W_t1 = compose(W_t, new_fragments) # Step 5: Update beliefs based on new world for cu in constructive_units: observation = cu.observe(W_t1) cu.belief = cu.update_belief(cu.belief, observation) # Step 6: Compute reflexivity coefficient epsilon = compute_reflexivity(beliefs, actions, W_t, W_t1) return W_t1, epsilon
Section 04

World Fragment Algebra

The world is not a single state vector. It is an algebra of composable fragments. This section defines the algebraic structure precisely.

Fragment types and their state spaces

Fragment TypeWhat It CapturesTypical DimTimescaleData Source
LiquidityMarket depth, funding availability, collateral haircuts16Hours–DaysOrder book data, repo rates
VolatilityRealized + implied vol surface, vol-of-vol, term structure32Days–WeeksOptions data, VIX term
NarrativeDominant market narratives, sentiment clusters64Days–MonthsNews, social, CB speeches
CreditSpread levels, default correlations, credit cycle position24Weeks–MonthsCDS, corporate bonds
FlowCapital flows across borders, sectors, asset classes32Weeks–QuartersBIS, 13F filings, fund flows
PolicyRate expectations, QE/QT state, fiscal stance16Months–YearsFed funds futures, CB statements
SentimentRisk appetite, fear/greed, positioning extremes16Days–WeeksSurvey data, put/call ratios

Composition rules

Composition Algebra Given WFi ∈ ℝdi and WFj ∈ ℝdj: Same-type composition (merging two liquidity fragments): WFi ⊗ WFj = φ(WFi, WFj) where φ is a learned merger, output ∈ ℝd Cross-type composition (liquidity + volatility): WFliq ⊗ WFvol = ρliq→vol(WFliq) ⊕ WFvol where ρliq→vol : ℝdliq → ℝdvol is a learned transport map // This is the copresheaf structure: each type has its own space, // with learned maps between spaces. Scale composition (micro + macro): WFmicro ⊗↑ WFmacro = coarse_grain(WFmicro) ⊕ WFmacro
Choosing the coarse-graining method — corrected. An earlier draft specified NIS+ (Neural Information Squeezer) to learn this map by maximizing effective information. NIS+ is the wrong tool for our data. Its authors state plainly that it needs a large amount of training data, and that in their own fMRI work a hand-built atlas did the 140,000→100 dimensional reduction before NIS+ ran. We have hundreds of quarters of macro data, not millions of samples. It also assumes Markovian dynamics, which is exactly what our path-signature machinery exists to avoid.

Use instead: Liu, Yuan & Zhang, "An Exact Theory of Causal Emergence for Linear Stochastic Iteration Systems" (Entropy 26(8):618, 2024). It gives a closed-form effective information and the optimal linear coarse-graining directly from the principal eigenvectors of the system's parameter matrix. Cost is O(n³) in the number of variables — not in the number of states, which is the trap that makes every other method in this family intractable. And "linear stochastic iteration system with Gaussian noise" is a VAR, which is the native language of empirical macro. No combinatorial search, no neural network, no arbitrary heuristic. The price is linearity, which is a price economics already pays.

The deeper problem, which is also our opening. Every causal-emergence framework in the literature — effective information, dynamical independence, ΦID — assumes a fixed generative process. In our reflexive setting the macro description feeds back into the micro dynamics, so the transition kernel is itself a function of the coarse-graining. None of these theories handle that. Do not bury this. Stated honestly, it is a real contribution rather than a limitation, and it means we will be extending one of these frameworks rather than importing it. Extend Barnett & Seth's dynamical independence — its foundations are the cleanest and it is the only one that carries no inherited fight (see §19).

Implementation: the fragment store

class FragmentStore: """Central store for all world fragments. Versioned, queryable, composable.""" def __init__(self): self.fragments: Dict[str, WorldFragment] = {} self.transport_maps: Dict[Tuple[str,str], nn.Module] = {} self.history: List[Tuple[datetime, Dict]] = [] def compose(self, fid_a: str, fid_b: str) -> WorldFragment: wf_a, wf_b = self.fragments[fid_a], self.fragments[fid_b] if wf_a.fragment_type == wf_b.fragment_type: return self._same_type_compose(wf_a, wf_b) else: key = (wf_a.fragment_type, wf_b.fragment_type) rho = self.transport_maps[key] return self._cross_type_compose(wf_a, wf_b, rho) def snapshot(self) -> torch.Tensor: """Full world state as concatenation of all fragments (for loss computation).""" return torch.cat([wf.state for wf in self.fragments.values()])
Section 05

Belief Fields — How Beliefs Propagate

In standard agent models, each agent has an independent belief. In RCWM, beliefs form a field over the agent graph — they propagate, interfere, and create collective phenomena that no individual agent intends.

Belief Field Dynamics The belief field B(t) lives on a graph G = (V, E) where V = {CUi} and E = interaction edges. Each node's belief evolves as: bi(t+1) = (1-α) · U(bi(t), oi(t)) + α · Σj∈N(i) wij · bj(t) where: U(b, o) = Bayesian update of belief b given observation o α ∈ [0,1] = social influence weight (how much beliefs are contagious) wij = influence weight of agent j on agent i (normalized: Σj wij = 1) N(i) = neighbors of agent i in the interaction graph Narrative contagion occurs when α is high: beliefs synchronize regardless of private observations. This is how bubbles form. Divergence occurs when α is low: agents rely on private information, beliefs diversify. This is how price discovery works. The field has a coherence measure: χ(t) = 1 - H(B(t)) / Hmax where H is the entropy of the belief distribution across agents. χ → 1 means all agents believe the same thing (dangerous). χ → 0 means maximum belief diversity (healthy price discovery).
Critical insight: The belief coherence χ(t) is itself an input to the Reflexive Instability signal. When beliefs synchronize (χ rising) AND the reflexivity coefficient ε is high, you have the preconditions for a self-fulfilling crisis. This combination — high coherence + high reflexivity — is the mathematical signature of a bubble about to pop.
Section 06

Constraint Surfaces — The Possibility Landscape

Constraint surfaces define what economic transformations are possible and what are impossible. This is the constructor theory connection: instead of predicting what will happen, we classify what can happen.

Four constraint layers

1. Regulatory constraints Φreg

Capital adequacy: leverage(CUi) ≤ Lmax(typei) Position limits: |pos(CUi, assetk)| ≤ Pmax(k) Concentration: Σk ∈ sector |posk| / total_assets ≤ Cmax

2. Liquidity constraints Φliq

Market impact: slippage(order_size, depth) ≤ threshold Funding: available_funding(CUi) ≥ margin_requirement(action) Settlement: T+n settlement creates temporal constraints on re-use

3. Physical constraints Φphys

Time: actions take non-zero time to execute Capacity: production/processing has upper bounds Network: information propagates at finite speed through the system

4. Accounting identities Φacct

Balance sheet: assets(t) = liabilities(t) + equity(t) ∀ t, ∀ CU Flow conservation: Σi flowi→j = Σj flowj→i (for each asset) Stock-flow: stock(t+1) = stock(t) + Σ flows(t, t+1)

Constructibility Index — the first derived signal

Constructibility Index CI(t) = |{ a ∈ A(W(t)) : Φ(t)(a, W(t)) = feasible }| / |A(W(t))| In words: the fraction of all possible construction operators that are currently feasible under the constraint field. When CI(t) drops: - fewer transformations are possible - the economy is becoming "rigid" - path lock-in risk increases Estimate via Monte Carlo sampling: Sample N random construction operators uniformly from A(W(t)) Count how many pass the constraint field CI(t) ≈ count / N
Section 07

Construction Operators — Actions as World-Building

In RCWM, actions are not "buy" or "sell." They are construction operators — transformations that create, modify, or destroy world fragments.

Operator Taxonomy Create: Opcreate(params) → WFnew Example: IPO creates a new equity fragment Example: Central bank creates a new lending facility Transform: Optransform(WFexisting) → WFmodified Example: Large trade transforms liquidity fragment Example: Rate hike transforms policy fragment Compose: Opcompose(WFa, WFb) → WFab Example: CDO creation composes mortgage fragments Example: Merger composes corporate fragments Destroy: Opdestroy(WFexisting) → ∅ Example: Default destroys credit fragment Example: Delisting destroys equity fragment Each operator has: - preconditions: which fragments must exist - constraint check: must pass Φ(t) - success probability: κi(W(t)) - side effects: what other fragments are affected
For implementation in month 1: Start with Transform operators only. They are the most common (trades, policy changes) and the easiest to validate. Create/Compose/Destroy operators come in Phase 2.
Section 08

Reflexive Fixed Points — Where Systems Stabilize or Explode

A reflexive fixed point is a state where the belief-action-world cycle reaches equilibrium: agents' beliefs about the world are confirmed by the world their beliefs create.

Fixed Point Condition A reflexive fixed point exists at W* when: B* = U(B*, W*) // beliefs are consistent with the world they see A* = π(B*, S*) // actions follow from those beliefs W* = C(W*, A*, Φ) // the world produced by those actions IS the world believed This is a simultaneous fixed point across beliefs, actions, and world state. Stability analysis: Linearize around W*: δW(t+1) = J · δW(t) where J = ∂C/∂W · (I + ∂A/∂B · ∂B/∂W) = direct effect + reflexive amplification Eigenvalues of J determine stability: |λmax(J)| < 1 ⇒ stable fixed point (market equilibrium) |λmax(J)| = 1 ⇒ marginally stable (regime boundary) |λmax(J)| > 1 ⇒ unstable (crisis dynamics) Connection to the reflexivity coefficient: ε = spectral_radius(∂A/∂B · ∂B/∂W · ∂W/∂A) The condition ε · C < 1 from the compendium is equivalent to |λmax(J)| < 1
The fundamental limit of reflexive modeling: When ε · C ≥ 1, no model can reliably predict the system because the model's own predictions destabilize it. This is not a failure — it is a theorem. The Reflexive Instability signal reports exactly how close you are to this limit. When it approaches 1, the correct output is not a prediction but a warning.
Section 09

Prior Art — Reflexivity Already Has a Formal Home

Read this section before writing any paper. What we call "reflexivity" has been formalized since 2020 under the name performative prediction. It is an active ICML/NeurIPS-tier research area with theorems, convergence conditions, and impossibility results. If Paper 1 presents reflexive dynamics as novel without engaging this literature, a reviewer will reject it in the first round. We are not inventing this field — we are extending it into economics.

The lineage

Perdomo et al. (2020) introduced performative prediction: the setting where deploying a model changes the distribution the model is trying to predict. Hardt & Mendler-Dünner's 2025 survey in Statistical Science traces the idea back further, to Grunberg & Modigliani (1954) and Simon (1954), who proved via Brouwer's fixed-point theorem that a correct public forecast can exist even when the forecast influences the outcome.

That is the same fixed point we describe in §8. Our contribution is not the existence of the fixed point — it is the economic structure we put inside it: typed world fragments, constraint fields, and construction operators.

Our termEstablished termWhere it's formalized
Reflexive loopPerformative effectPerdomo et al. 2020
Reflexive fixed pointPerformative stabilityPerdomo et al. 2020; Hardt & Mendler-Dünner 2025
ε·C < 1 convergenceContraction under Lipschitz + strong convexityPerdomo et al. 2020 (repeated risk minimization)
Belief-driven world changeDecision-dependent distribution shiftStrategic classification literature
Endogenous vs. exogenous driftPartially performative predictionLee & Zrnic 2026
Model embedded in marketPerformative market makingKleitsikas, Leonardos & Ventre 2025

The hard bound we must confront

Performative Learning Theory (Rodemann, Fischer-Abaigar, Bailie & Muandet, ICML 2026) embeds performative prediction into statistical learning theory and proves generalization bounds under performative effects on the sample, on the population, and on both.

The Central Tension "The more a model affects data, the less it can learn from it." The proof intuition, in the authors' own framing: in the worst case, the population negates predictions, while the sample deceptively fulfills them. Formally, these are cast as risk functionals in Wasserstein space: self-negating predictions → min-max risk functional self-fulfilling predictions → min-min risk functional // Read that second line carefully. A model can look like it is // learning beautifully on its training sample precisely BECAUSE // it is causing the outcomes it predicts — while the broader // population moves the other way. Good in-sample fit is not // merely weak evidence here; under performativity it is an // actively misleading signal.
What this means for us concretely: our Reflexive Instability signal measures how performative the system is. This theorem says that as RI rises, our own model's capacity to learn from the data degrades. RI is therefore not only a product output — it is a confidence discount on everything else we produce. High RI should attenuate our own signal strength, not just warn the customer. Build that coupling in from the start.

What is genuinely unclaimed

The literature search found the formal machinery is mature on one side and the economics is mature on the other, with very little joining them:

  • Counterperformativity has no mathematics. MacKenzie & Bamford named it in 2018 — the case where deploying a model makes the world conform less to the model. Performative Market Making formalizes only the conformity-increasing direction. There is no formal condition for when deployment decreases conformity. This is a real open problem and it is squarely in our territory.
  • No benchmark scores a model on its own footprint. Every economic forecasting benchmark found is observational or synthetic-oracle. Boeken et al.'s performative divergence is the right quantity and nobody has instantiated it on economic data.
  • Reflexivity is still a prompt, not an architecture. The one 2026 paper joining reflexivity and frontier AI tests whether telling an LLM about Soros changes its behavior. No architecture, no invariance, no formal model.
Section 10

The Evaluation Problem — Why Standard Scoring Breaks

This section exists because of a 2025 result that invalidates the naive version of our validation plan. It does not block the 12-week backtests — but it does determine how we must evaluate once anything is deployed, and it needs to be designed in now rather than retrofitted.

Boeken, Zoeter & Mooij (2025) — arXiv:2510.21335 Setting: forecasts that influence the outcomes they predict. Problem 1 — well-posedness. If the forecast changes the target distribution, a "correct forecast" may not even be well-defined. Fix: condition forecasts on covariates that SEPARATE the forecast from the outcome. This renders the target distribution forecast-invariant and guarantees the forecasting problem is well-posed. Problem 2 — elicitation. This is the one that bites. Even once the problem is well-posed via separating covariates, classical proper scoring rules still fail to elicit correct forecasts. The authors prove a general impossibility result. // Brier score, log score, CRPS — all of them. Being "proper" // in the classical sense does not survive performativity. The two escape hatches: (i) Decision-theoretic settings: correct and incentive-compatible elicitation IS possible if forecasts are separating. (ii) Score against an unbiased estimate of the DIVERGENCE between the forecast and the induced distribution of the target. This yields correct forecasts. Applied to parameter estimation, this gives performatively stable estimation of performatively correct parameters — explicitly resolving the issues raised by Perdomo et al. (2020).

What this does and does not change for our 12 weeks

The backtests in weeks 7–11 are safe. During 2006–2026 our model was not deployed and had zero market impact, so the historical data is not performative with respect to us. Classical scoring is valid there. Do not let this section scare the team off the backtest plan — the backtest is exactly the right week-8 deliverable.
Everything after first deployment is affected. The moment a customer trades on our signals, our forecasts start influencing the outcomes we score ourselves against. From that point, in-sample accuracy is contaminated in the specific direction the ICML 2026 result identifies — the sample "deceptively fulfills" our predictions. We would look more accurate as we became more performative.

Three design requirements to build in now

  1. Identify separating covariates from day one. For each signal, we need variables that mediate the signal's causal effect on the outcome. For a signal delivered to N subscribers, subscriber count and AUM-weighted coverage are the natural candidates. Log them from the first customer — you cannot reconstruct this later.
  2. Implement divergence-based scoring alongside classical scoring. Track both. The gap between them is the performative divergence, and it is a direct empirical estimate of our own market footprint. Nobody has published this quantity on economic data.
  3. Version and freeze every deployed signal. Attributing a distribution change to our own deployment requires knowing exactly what was deployed, when, and to whom. Treat the deployment log as research data, not ops telemetry.
The opportunity hiding in this problem: requirement 2 is a paper. Instantiating performative divergence on real economic data — measuring how much a deployed forecast bends the thing it forecasts — has not been done. We would be the only group with the deployment log needed to do it. That is a genuine moat: it is not a dataset anyone can buy, and it accumulates the longer we operate.
Section 11

The Four Derived Signals — Complete Specification

These are the product. Each signal is computed from the RCWM internals and measures something no existing system can measure.

Signal 1: Constructibility Index (CI)

Question: How many transformations are feasible right now?

Computation: CI(t) = Ea~Uniform(A)[Φ(t)(a, W(t)) = feasible]

Range: [0, 1]. Estimated via 10,000 Monte Carlo samples per timestep.

Interpretation: CI = 0.8 means 80% of possible actions are feasible. CI = 0.2 means the system is highly constrained — most actions are blocked. CI dropping fast = economy becoming rigid.

Validate against: Financial Conditions Index (FCI), should lead it by 1–4 weeks.

Prior art on our flagship signal — engage it, do not walk into it. "What can this economy build next, given what it currently builds" is the core question of the economic complexity literature, and that literature is canon: Hidalgo, Klinger, Barabási & Hausmann, "The Product Space Conditions the Development of Nations," Science 317:482 (2007), ~2,169 citations; Hidalgo & Hausmann, "The building blocks of economic complexity," PNAS 106:10570 (2009), ~2,388 citations. The formal treatment of an expanding possibility space is Tria, Loreto, Servedio & Strogatz, "The dynamics of correlated novelties," Sci. Rep. 4:5890 (2014) — a Pólya-urn-with-triggering model of Kauffman's adjacent possible.

Any economist reviewing Paper 1 will know these on sight. Two required actions: (1) cite them explicitly and state precisely how the Constructibility Index differs — ours is a high-frequency financial feasibility measure computed from a constraint field, theirs is a low-frequency structural capability measure computed from trade data; (2) treat Economic Complexity Index as a baseline to beat in the week-8 validation, not merely as related work. If CI cannot outperform ECI on anything, that is a finding we need to know in week 8 rather than in review.

Signal 2: Reflexive Instability (RI)

Question: How sensitive is the system to belief changes?

Computation: RI(t) = ε(t) · χ(t) where ε = reflexivity coefficient, χ = belief coherence

Range: [0, ∞). Values above 0.7 are dangerous.

Interpretation: RI combines two things: how reflexive the system is (are beliefs causing reality?) and how synchronized beliefs are (is everyone believing the same thing?). Both high = self-fulfilling prophecy conditions.

Validate against: Should spike before major market dislocations. Backtest against 2008, 2020, 2023 SVB.

Signal 3: Composition Fragility (CF)

Question: Will combining subsystems break stability?

Computation: For all pairs (WFi, WFj), compute:

  CF(t) = maxi,j [ stability(WFi) + stability(WFj) - stability(WFi ⊗ WFj) ]

Range: [0, ∞). Positive values mean interaction creates instability that components lack individually.

Interpretation: CF > 0 means there exist sector combinations whose interaction is destabilizing even though each sector is independently stable. This is the mathematical definition of systemic risk.

Validate against: Cross-sector contagion episodes. Should flag before contagion becomes visible.

Signal 4: Path Lock-In Risk (PLR)

Question: Is the system entering an irreversible trajectory?

Computation: Run N forward simulations from current state with perturbed actions. Measure trajectory divergence:

  PLR(t) = 1 - (1/N) Σk overlap(trajectorybaseline, trajectoryk)

Range: [0, 1]. PLR = 0 means all perturbations converge back. PLR = 1 means every perturbation leads to a different future.

Interpretation: High PLR means the system is at a bifurcation — small differences in actions now lead to radically different outcomes. This is the non-ergodicity signal.

Validate against: Should be high before major regime transitions, low during stable periods.

Section 12

State Estimation (Layer 1) — The VAE Architecture

Layer 1 decomposes raw economic data into world fragments. The architecture is a structured Variational Autoencoder with fragment-specific decoders.

Fragment VAE Architecture Encoder: x(t) → {μj(t), σj(t)}j=1..K Input x(t) ∈ ℝD: concatenation of all raw data at time t Output: K sets of (mean, variance) — one per fragment type The encoder is NOT a single bottleneck. It has K parallel heads, one per fragment type, each producing a fragment-specific latent. zj(t) ~ N(μj(t), diag(σj(t)²)) for j = 1..K Decoder: {zj(t)}j=1..K → x̂(t) Each fragment is decoded through its own decoder head, then combined to reconstruct the input: x̂(t) = Σj gj(zj(t)) Loss — REVISED, see §21 before implementing: L = Lrecon + β · LKL + δ · Ltemporal + α · Lsparsity Lrecon = ||x(t) - x̂(t)||² LKL = Σj KL(q(zj|x) || p(zj|z(t-1))) // NOTE: conditional prior, not N(0,I) Ltemporal = ||zj(t+1) - fj(z(t))||² Lsparsity = ||supp(Jdecoder)||0 + ||Gz||0 // THIS is what buys identifiability // The total-correlation term from the earlier draft has been REMOVED. // TC penalties are provably insufficient for identifiability (Locatello // et al. 2019), and actively counterproductive when the true factors are // correlated — which macro factors always are. See §21.

Adding path signatures for non-Markovian dynamics

Financial data is non-Markovian — volatility has Hurst parameter H ≈ 0.1, meaning the current state depends on the entire history, not just the last observation. Path signatures capture this.

Path Signature Integration Instead of feeding raw x(t) to the encoder, we feed: x̃(t) = [x(t), Sig≤N(x[t-L:t])] where Sig≤N is the truncated path signature of depth N over a lookback window L. The signature S(path) = (1, S1, S2, ..., SN) where: Ski1...ik = ∫ ... ∫ dxi1 ... dxik t1<..<tk Properties that matter: - Complete: captures ALL information about the path (up to tree-like equivalence) - Reparametrization-invariant: same signature regardless of sampling frequency - Graded: depth N controls resolution Practical choices: N = 3 (the field's most common default; sweep 2 and 4) Windows: HIERARCHICAL DYADIC, not sliding (see §14) Library: pysiglib or iisignature-from-git — NOT signatory
Section 13

Ergodic Objectives — Corrected

Correction to an earlier draft of this briefing. A previous version told you to implement E[log(loss)] as a one-line change on day 1. That was wrong, and it is wrong in a way that would have quietly damaged the models. The section below replaces it. The underlying idea — that ensemble averages are the wrong objective for compounding processes — is sound and important. The prescription was not.

The problem, which is real

Why Ensemble Averages Mislead Standard ML minimizes the ensemble average: E[L] = (1/N) Σn Ln — the average across infinitely many parallel trajectories. But wealth compounds multiplicatively: W(T) = W(0) · Πt (1 + rt) The canonical example: 50% chance of +60%, 50% chance of −40% E[return] = +10% → looks great After 2 rounds: 25%: 1.6 × 1.6 = 2.56 50%: 1.6 × 0.6 = 0.96 ← the typical path LOSES money 25%: 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36 The median outcome loses money despite positive expected return. The ensemble average is dominated by rare extreme paths that almost surely do not happen to you.

Why "just take the log of the loss" is the wrong fix

Three Separate Errors 1. The sign is backwards. log is concave and increasing. Applying it to a LOSS (where large = bad) makes large losses contribute sub-linearly — so E[log L] is MORE tolerant of catastrophic losses than plain E[L], not less. The entire point of the ergodicity correction is to punish ruin. Applied to a loss, log does the opposite. // log is the right transform for WEALTH (high = good), where // concavity punishes low outcomes. A loss is not wealth. The // orientation of the quantity is what makes the transform work, // and flipping it inverts the intent. 2. Wrong object. The ergodicity correction applies to a quantity that COMPOUNDS MULTIPLICATIVELY across time — portfolio value, capital, output. A training loss does not compound across gradient steps the way capital compounds across bets. 3. log is a special case, not the general answer. The general object is an ergodicity transformation h, chosen so that h's increments have equal ensemble and time averages. Then: h = log ⇔ multiplicative / GBM dynamics h = identity ⇔ additive dynamics h = something else otherwise Peters & Adamou prove the transformation IS the utility function under the time interpretation. So "just use log" silently assumes log utility, i.e. assumes GBM wealth. That is circular unless the dynamics justify it.

What to actually do

The Defensible Version For compounding state variables (portfolio value, capital, market share, output) — optimize the time-average growth rate: maximize E[ Δ log x ] where x is the compounding quantity When the dynamics are unknown — learn the transformation rather than assuming it. Baumann et al. (TMLR 2025) estimate h as a variance-stabilizing transform: 1. Regress log( (R(tk+1) − R(tk))² ) on R(tk), fit with LOESS → gives an estimate of the variance function v 2. Set h(x) = ∫0x 1/√v(u) du 3. Optimize increments of h(R) log falls out analytically for the multiplicative coin-toss game — as a SPECIAL CASE, not as the general prescription. For ordinary prediction losses — leave them alone. Use standard MSE / NLL. If you want tail sensitivity in a forecast loss, that is a separate and well-understood design choice (quantile loss, CVaR, focal-style reweighting) and it should be argued on its own terms, not smuggled in under the ergodicity banner.
Scope limits worth knowing before you build on it: Baumann et al. carries no formal convergence guarantees for the learning algorithm — it is a well-motivated empirical method with a clean theoretical story, not a theorem. It also requires episodic data (full trajectories before updating). And a 2026 follow-up (Verbruggen, Vanhoyweghen & Ginis, arXiv:2601.08726) criticizes this whole line for relying on ex-ante knowledge of the underlying dynamic, proposing instead to feed temporal information directly to the function approximator. Read both before committing the architecture.

Citation hygiene on this topic

The mathematics here is uncontroversial and predates the "ergodicity economics" branding by decades — Kelly (1956), Breiman (1961), Thorp, Merton. What is contested is the claim that economics has been making an error, and there is a live dispute on the record in Nature Physics (Doctor, Wakker & Wang 2020, with a reply from Peters).

Practical guidance: cite Kelly/Breiman for the growth-optimality mathematics, Peters & Adamou for the formal transformation-equals-utility correspondence, and lead with Baumann et al. (TMLR 2025) for the learned-transformation method — it is peer-reviewed, ships code, and has Peters as a co-author, so it cannot be dismissed as someone misreading the literature. Do not adopt the movement's rhetoric about economics being fundamentally wrong; one of our referees may well be a disputant.

The composition worth claiming. The ergodicity thread and the performativity thread (§9) are formally independent — Peters says nothing about performativity, and Perdomo says nothing about ergodicity. They compose cleanly: performativity determines which distribution you face; ergodicity determines which functional of that distribution you should optimize. Neither implies the other, and as far as the literature search found, that composition is unclaimed. It is a more defensible framing than implying either literature already contains the other.
Section 14

Path Signatures — Complete Technical Reference

Path signatures are to sequences what Fourier transforms are to periodic functions — a complete, canonical representation. They are central to L1 because financial data is inherently path-dependent.

Mathematical Definition Given a path X: [0,T] → ℝd, its signature is the infinite sequence: Sig(X) = (1, Sig1(X), Sig2(X), ...) ∈ T((ℝd)) where T((ℝd)) is the tensor algebra, and: Sigk(X)i1,...,ik = ∫0<t1<...<tk<T dXi1(t1) ⊗ ... ⊗ dXik(tk) Depth 1 (d terms): Sig1i = ∫0T dXi = Xi(T) - Xi(0) // Just the total displacement. Not very informative. Depth 2 (d² terms): Sig2ij = ∫∫s<t dXi(s) dXj(t) // Captures "i moved, then j moved" — the ordering of changes. // The antisymmetric part Sig2ij - Sig2ji = signed area = "lead-lag" Depth 3 (d³ terms): // Captures third-order path effects — how the lead-lag itself changes. // Sufficient for most financial applications. Log-signature (compressed): log-Sig(X) = log(Sig(X)) in the tensor algebra Dimension: much smaller than Sig. For d=5, depth 3: Sig has 1+5+25+125 = 156 terms log-Sig has 5+10+20 = 35 terms // 4.5x compression

Library choice — verified August 2026

Do not use signatory. It is the library most tutorials still reference, but its last release (1.2.7) supports only Python 3.7–3.9 and PyTorch 1.8.0–1.11.0. It will not install against the PyTorch 2.x stack in §16. Verified on the project page, August 2026.

Use pysiglib (Shmelev & Salvi, arXiv:2509.10613) instead. Python 3.9+, NumPy/PyTorch/JAX backends, CUDA kernels, autograd on both PyTorch and JAX, and — critically for us — signature streams with constant-time interval queries.

# pip install "pysiglib[cuda]" import torch from pysiglib.torch_api import log_sig def compute_signature_features(data: torch.Tensor, degree: int = 3) -> torch.Tensor: """ data: (batch, path_length, channels) — computation runs on the device the input already lives on, so keep it on GPU. Returns log-signature features for each batch element. """ # Time-augment the path: makes the signature sensitive to # parametrization speed, which matters for financial paths # (the same price move over 1 day vs 20 days is not the same event). b, t, _ = data.shape time = torch.linspace(0, 1, t, device=data.device) time = time.view(1, t, 1).expand(b, -1, 1) augmented = torch.cat([time, data], dim=-1) return log_sig(augmented, degree=degree) # (batch, logsig_channels)

The rolling-window optimization — do not skip this

The naive way to build a 20-year backtest is to recompute a 60-day log-signature at every one of ~5,000 trading days. That is O(T · L) work and it will dominate your week-8 to week-11 compute budget.

pysiglib exposes LogSigWindowStream, which maintains a sliding window incrementally using Chen's identity — signatures concatenate, so you can append the new day and drop the old one rather than recomputing the whole window. This turns the rolling computation into O(T).

from pysiglib import LogSigWindowStream # Rolling 60-day log-signature across the full history — O(T), not O(T*L) stream = LogSigWindowStream(dim=n_channels + 1, degree=3, window=60) features = [] for day in augmented_path: # iterate once over history stream.update(day) if stream.ready: features.append(stream.value())

Why log-signatures, not raw signatures: Log-signatures are the independent coordinates of the signature — they strip the redundancy that the tensor-algebra structure forces into the full signature. For d=5 at depth 3 this is 156 terms → 35 terms, a 4.5× compression with no information loss. Always use log-signatures as model inputs — in a latent-variable model the compactness is not optional. This is exactly what the closest prior-art market simulator (Buehler et al., see below) does.

Practitioner defaults — from the definitive 9,984-configuration ablation

Morrill, Fermanian, Kidger & Lyons (arXiv:2006.00873) swept depth, augmentation, window, and rescaling across 26 datasets and four model classes. The findings are specific and some are counterintuitive:

  • Depth 2–4, default 3. Average rank improves through depth 4–5 then degrades at 6 — a real bias-variance ceiling, more information but worse generalization. The tuned pipeline picks depth 1–3 for 24 of 30 datasets. Sweep 2 and 4; start at 3.
  • Augmentation matters more than depth. Time + basepoint is near-mandatory and significantly beats none. For financial data, the finance-standard stack is lead-lag → append time → I-visibility → signature. Lead-lag makes the signature capture quadratic variation — but note it doubles the channel count before exponentiation, so include a no-lead-lag ablation.
  • Hierarchical dyadic windows beat sliding and global windows, significantly. This is one of the most actionable findings, because sliding/global is what most people reach for by default.
  • Do not pre-scale the path. The obvious fix for the 1/k! factorial decay — multiplying the input path by α=(N!)1/N — is significantly worse than doing nothing (it blows up the mid-levels as O(2N/2)). Post-signature k! scaling is statistically indistinguishable from no scaling. Just normalize input channels to zero-mean/unit-variance and leave the signature alone.
The dimension trap — the real binding constraint. Signature dimension is Σk=1..N dk, and augmentations multiply d before you exponentiate it. Five assets + time + Hoff lead-lag gives d=12, so a depth-3 signature is 1,884 features and depth-4 is 22,620. Published work excludes configs producing >105 features and drops datasets with d>60. Take signatures of factors, not raw series — the GDP-nowcasting result that beat the NY Fed did depth-3 signatures on PCA/DFM factors of 33 variables, sidestepping the blow-up entirely. For us: signatures of the fragment latents, never the raw data panel.
Correction to my earlier claim, and a benchmark to run in week 2. I called signature-MMD a cheap free win. It is not free. A June 2026 paper from Cass's own rough-path group — Generating Financial Time Series by Matching Random Convolutional Features (SOCK, arXiv:2606.05138) — found random convolutional features beat properly-tuned signature features on financial generation, and that signatures are "very sensitive to hyperparameters" where random features are robust. Separately, an untruncated signature-kernel MMD has a documented failure to converge on this exact task.

Action: benchmark the signature approach against a MultiROCKET / random-convolutional-feature baseline from week 2. If a signature VAE cannot beat random features on our data, that is a fact we want in week 2, not month 6. And if we use a signature kernel loss, use the truncated DP kernel at level 5, not the untruncated PDE kernel.

Closest prior art — study it before designing the encoder. Buehler, Horvath, Lyons, Perez Arribas & Wood, A Data-driven Market Simulator for Small Data Environments (arXiv:2006.14498), is a VAE on log-signatures of lead-lag-transformed paths — structurally almost exactly what we are building. Their architecture is deliberately tiny (one 50-unit hidden layer each side); the signature does the representational work. The most transferable idea: condition the VAE on the log-signature of the previous path segment — a path-aware conditioning variable that maps directly onto our reflexive setup. Note their honest caveat that inverting a signature back to a path is "a highly non-trivial task"; if our decoder emits signatures, use the Insertion Method (Fermanian et al. 2024), or avoid inversion by scoring directly in signature space.
Library note — an unresolved discrepancy, flagged not hidden. §12 recommends pysiglib, which I verified directly (v3.1.0, June 2026, PyTorch 2.x, CUDA, autograd). This research sweep independently converged on a different live stack — iisignature installed from git (CPU, actively developed, the only mature Lyndon-basis log-signature implementation) and signax from git (JAX/GPU) — and did not surface pysiglib at all, plausibly because pysiglib is newer than most of the corpus. Both stacks are current as of the checks; the PyPI releases of iisignature and signax are years stale, so those must be installed from git, not pip. Do a one-day bake-off in week 3 — pysiglib vs iisignature/signax on our actual paths — and let correctness and speed on our data decide. What is not in dispute: signatory is dead (no PyTorch 2.x) and torchcde's log-ODE path is broken because it depends on it.
Section 15

Convergence Theory — When Does RCWM Work?

The reflexive fixed point equation has convergence conditions that must be proved. This is both a mathematical requirement and a practical safeguard.

Convergence Theorem (to prove) Theorem (Reflexive Convergence): The RCWM evolution equation W(t+1) = C(W(t), A(B(t)), Φ(t)) converges to a fixed point W* provided: (i) ε(t) · Cmodel < 1 // reflexivity × model complexity < 1 (ii) C is Lipschitz continuous in W with constant LC < 1/ε (iii) Φ(t) is measurable and bounded (iv) Belief updates U(b, o) are contractive: d(U(b,o), U(b',o)) ≤ λ · d(b,b') with λ < 1 Proof sketch (Banach fixed-point theorem application): Define F(W) = C(W, A(B(W)), Φ) Show F is a contraction mapping on the metric space (W, d): d(F(W1), F(W2)) ≤ LC · (1 + ε) · d(W1, W2) Contraction requires: LC · (1 + ε) < 1 Which simplifies to: ε < 1/LC - 1 Interpretation: - More reflexive systems (ε higher) require simpler models (LC lower) - There is a FUNDAMENTAL tradeoff: model expressiveness vs. reflexive stability - This is NOT a limitation of our approach — it is a property of the system being modeled
Positioning correction — read with §9. This theorem is not new. Perdomo et al. (2020) proved essentially this result for performative prediction: repeated risk minimization converges to a performatively stable point under Lipschitz continuity of the distribution map plus strong convexity of the loss. Our ε·C < 1 is a restatement of their contraction condition in our notation.

Do not claim it as a contribution. Claim the specialization: what the Lipschitz constant of the distribution map is when the map is generated by constraint-filtered construction operators over typed world fragments. That is a genuinely new object, and bounding it is real work.

Research task for weeks 3–4 (revised): Do not re-derive Banach. Instead: (1) state our evolution equation in the standard performative-prediction formalism so the mapping is explicit and checkable; (2) derive the Lipschitz constant LC of our constructive operator in terms of constraint-field tightness — the conjecture worth testing is that a tighter constraint field reduces LC, because fewer feasible actions means less distributional movement per step; (3) if that holds, we get a genuinely novel result: constraints buy stability, and the Constructibility Index becomes a direct read on how far the system is from the convergence boundary. That is a Paper 3 contribution rather than a rediscovery.

Practical convergence monitoring

def check_convergence(W_history: List[torch.Tensor], window: int = 10) -> dict: """Monitor convergence of the RCWM evolution at runtime.""" if len(W_history) < window: return {"status": "warming_up"} recent = W_history[-window:] deltas = [torch.norm(recent[i+1] - recent[i]) for i in range(len(recent)-1)] # Check if deltas are decreasing (contraction) contracting = all(deltas[i+1] < deltas[i] for i in range(len(deltas)-1)) # Estimate contraction rate rates = [deltas[i+1] / (deltas[i] + 1e-8) for i in range(len(deltas)-1)] avg_rate = sum(rates) / len(rates) return { "status": "converging" if contracting else "diverging", "contraction_rate": avg_rate.item(), "epsilon_C": avg_rate.item(), # empirical estimate of ε·C "safe": avg_rate.item() < 0.95, }

Section 17

Paper 1 Strategy — A Decision to Make in Week 2

The literature review changed this section. The original plan was a Fragment VAE paper. That is still viable, but the research surfaced a second option with a materially better risk-adjusted return, and the choice affects what weeks 5–12 optimize for. Decide by end of week 2 — after that, the two paths diverge in what data and code you build.

Context: the field was formally named four days before this briefing

Han et al., "From Economic Agents to Agentic Economies: A Systems Blueprint for Economic World Models" (arXiv:2608.06020, 6 August 2026) is the field-defining paper. It establishes a capability ladder — L1 fixed-rule agents through L6 sim-to-real economic twins with online correction — and states that L5–L6 remain "nearly absent."

Two consequences. First, cite this in our first paragraph and position RCE explicitly at L6; the taxonomy is going to become standard and we want to be placed on it by our own hand rather than someone else's. Second, the timing is unusually good: a field that just got its vocabulary has no established benchmark, and benchmarks published into that window become the measuring stick.

Option A — Fragment VAE (the original plan)

Risk: this competes in a crowded space. PRISM-VQ, FactorVQVAE, FactorQVAE, and the broader disentangled-representation literature are all adjacent, several with released code and reported numbers. Our differentiator is the typed-fragment ontology, which is a framing contribution — reviewers discount those unless the empirical work is decisive.

There is also an identifiability exposure. The paper claims fragments are "interpretable." Unconstrained disentanglement is provably non-identifiable without auxiliary structure. We would need to ground the claim in the iVAE/nonlinear-ICA line and show our conditions are met, or soften the claim to "empirically interpretable." A reviewer who knows this literature will go straight at it.

Option B — The interventional benchmark RECOMMENDED

The literature search found a specific, confirmed hole: there is no vintage-consistent, real-data interventional benchmark for economic models scored on causal response accuracy to historical policy shocks.

What exists instead, and why none of it closes the gap:

  • DSGE-Gym — the closest artifact, but entirely synthetic. Ground truth is a DSGE solution, not the world.
  • ForecastBench-Sim — genuinely interventional with paired rollouts, but the world is Freeciv. The authors themselves flag whether game-world patterns generalize to real policy domains.
  • A calibrated-ABM counterfactual benchmark with real demographic and mobility data, time-varying interventions, 150+ counties — exactly the right design, built for epidemiology. It is a template to port, not a competitor.
  • EconCausal, InterveneBench — test whether LLMs can reason about published causal findings in text. Not whether a dynamical model gets the impulse response right.
  • Prophet Arena, ForecastBench, QuantBench — all observational.

Meanwhile every component needed to build the real thing is public and mature: Philadelphia Fed real-time data vintages, Greenbook vintages, the monetary-shock identification literature (Romer–Romer, high-frequency identification, Miranda-Agrippino/Ramey), and McKay & Wolf (Econometrica 2023), whose result that estimable causal effects of policy shocks are sufficient statistics for counterfactual analysis is precisely the theoretical license to score models this way.

Why this is the better Paper 1. Data cost is zero and the sources are public and citable. It has no direct competitor, where Option A has several. It is the kind of artifact the whole field cites regardless of whether they like our model — benchmarks accrue citations from people who disagree with you. It establishes us as the group that defines how economic world models are measured, which is a stronger position than having one more architecture. And it directly de-risks everything downstream: we need this evaluation harness internally anyway to know whether RCWM works, so we build it either way. Option B publishes the thing we were going to build regardless.

Working title: Can Economic World Models Answer "What If?" A Vintage-Consistent Interventional Benchmark on Historical Policy Shocks

Sequencing if we take Option B: the Fragment VAE does not disappear — it becomes one of the entrants we evaluate, and Paper 2 rather than Paper 1. That ordering is strictly better: the VAE paper then arrives with an established benchmark to report numbers on, which is a much stronger empirical position than inventing your own evaluation alongside your own method.

The honest counterargument, so the decision is made with eyes open. Benchmarks are more work than they look — the vintage alignment and shock identification are genuinely fiddly, and a benchmark nobody adopts is worth little. Option B also delays our first architectural claim by roughly a quarter, which matters if fundraising needs a model result rather than an evaluation result. If the near-term priority is demonstrating that our architecture works, take Option A and keep the benchmark as Paper 2. This is a real trade, not a formality.

Option A outline, retained

World Fragment Decomposition: Learning Composable Economic States via Structured Variational Inference

Abstract structure (150 words)

  1. Problem: Economic states are monolithically represented, losing compositional structure
  2. Method: Structured VAE that decomposes state into typed, multi-scale, composable fragments with path signature inputs
  3. Results: Fragments outperform HMM/threshold baselines on regime detection; Constructibility Index leads FCI by 2–3 weeks; fragments are interpretable and correspond to economic intuition
  4. Contribution: New ontology (world fragments), new signal (Constructibility Index), connection to constructor theory

Section outline

SectionPagesContent
1. Introduction1.5Monolithic state representations miss compositional structure of economies. Preview fragments, CI, results.
2. Related Work1Regime-switching models, disentangled VAEs, economic state spaces, constructor theory (briefly)
3. World Fragment Ontology1.5Formal definitions: WF, composition, constraints. This section defines the field's vocabulary.
4. Fragment VAE Architecture2K-head encoder/decoder, path sig inputs, ergodic loss, transport maps, disentanglement

Writing strategy: The paper's job is to make "world fragment" a standard term. Every subsequent paper you write will cite this one. Optimize for clarity and citeability over impressiveness. The math should be accessible to an ML audience that doesn't know economics.

Section 19

Citation Strategy — What to Build On, What to Avoid

The research compendium that seeded this project draws on several exotic theoretical frameworks. Some are load-bearing and safe. Others carry active pseudoscience accusations that would follow our papers into review. This section is the filter. It exists so nobody spends a month building on a foundation that a referee can dismiss in one sentence.

Tier 1 — Build on these

FrameworkAnchor citationWhy it's safe
Performative predictionPerdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner & Hardt, ICML 2020Top-tier, uncontested, and it is our formal core. Lead with it.
Dynamical independenceBarnett & Seth, Phys. Rev. E 108:014304 (2023)Built on Granger causality / transfer entropy. No arbitrary intervention distribution. Transformation-invariant. MATLAB code ships. The cleanest thing in the emergence field.
Exact CE, linear systemsLiu, Yuan & Zhang, Entropy 26(8):618 (2024)Closed form on exactly the model class economics uses. Our computational workhorse.
ΦID emergence criteriaRosas et al., PLOS Comp Biol 16:e1008289 (2020); Mediano et al., PNAS 122 (2025)Tests a macro variable you nominate rather than searching for one — sidesteps the combinatorics. PNAS gives citation armor.
Growth optimalityKelly (1956), Breiman (1961)The actual mathematics behind ergodicity economics, 70 years old and uncontroversial.
Path signaturesStandard rough-path literature; pysiglib for implementationMature, mathematically settled.

Tier 2 — Cite carefully, position deliberately

Ergodicity economics

Cite the mathematics and Peters & Adamou's transformation-equals-utility correspondence. Lead with Baumann et al. (TMLR 2025) — peer-reviewed, ships code, Peters is a co-author. Do not adopt the movement's rhetoric about economics being fundamentally in error. There is a live dispute on the record in Nature Physics (Doctor, Wakker & Wang 2020, with a reply from Peters), and one of our referees may be a disputant. Also note Peters' 2019 Nature Physics piece is a Perspective, not a research article — do not cite it as if it proves something.

Hoel's causal emergence

Cite the 2013 PNAS paper as the origin of the question — reviewers will expect it — but cite the critiques in the same sentence. Two peer-reviewed objections stand largely unanswered: Dewhurst (Thought, 2021) argues it supports only epistemic emergence, and Eberhardt & Lee (Philosophies, 2022) show the uniform intervention distribution is extraneous and that marginalization and abstraction do not commute. Pre-empting this signals sophistication instead of naivety.

Tier 3 — Do not build on, do not cite prominently

Assembly theory — avoid. The compendium proposed a "Copresheaf Assembly Constructor" architecture built on it. Do not pursue that. Zenil et al. argue the assembly index is reproducible by LZ-family compression, making it equivalent to a Shannon-entropy statistical measure rather than a new theory of selection; there is a critical review in BioSystems (2024); and the dispute is unsettled as of 2026 with named critics including Tour, Benner, Hazen and Jaeger. There is no quality economics application. It imports a live pseudoscience accusation in exchange for nothing formal.

Use instead, for "how much construction history is in this object": Bennett's logical depth, or Crutchfield & Young statistical complexity / ε-machines. The latter has real algorithms (CSSR), was designed for time series, and carries 40 years of standing with zero controversy. It does the same conceptual work.

IIT and Φ — do not cite. 124 signatories called it pseudoscience in 2023; that document became a Nature Neuroscience paper in April 2025 with 132+ named authors including Yoshua Bengio. Bengio's signature is precisely what makes this a problem in an ML venue — reviewers there treat him as an authority and will not adjudicate the consciousness debate. Φ is also computationally hopeless: O(n5·3n), practical limit around 10–12 nodes. We gain nothing and pay a real cost.

Note the entanglement: Hoel is a co-author on the IIT defense paper, and effective information is lifted from IIT machinery. That is a reason to prefer Barnett & Seth as our emergence anchor — same job, no inherited fight. ΦID is fine despite the name: it is a PNAS-published general information-theoretic decomposition, and the Φ is inheritance, not endorsement.

Constructor theory — low risk, near-zero payoff. Real venues (Deutsch, Synthese 2013; Deutsch & Marletto, Proc. R. Soc. A 2015), not fringe. But ~13 years in, uptake outside the originating circle is minimal and there is no economics application at all. A reviewer will ask what it buys us formally, and the honest answer today is "framing." It costs a paragraph and earns nothing. The possible/impossible transformation framing is genuinely useful to us as internal vocabulary for the constraint field — just don't hang the paper on it.

Direct substitutions — same idea, canonical instead of contested

Every exotic framework in the compendium has a mainstream equivalent that does the same conceptual work with an order of magnitude more citations and no baggage. Use the right column.

Instead of…Use…Citations
Assembly theory — "possibility space of what can be built next"Tria, Loreto, Servedio & Strogatz, Sci. Rep. 4:5890 (2014), "The dynamics of correlated novelties" — the formal Pólya-urn treatment of the adjacent possible~152
Assembly theory — economic version of the sameHidalgo & Hausmann, PNAS 106:10570 (2009); Hidalgo et al., Science 317:482 (2007)~2,388 / ~2,169
Assembly index — "construction history embodied in an object"Bennett, "Logical Depth and Physical Complexity" (1988) — the actual intellectual ancestor, 37 years unchallengedundercounted
Assembly index as a computable measureCrutchfield & Young, PRL 63:105 (1989); Shalizi & Crutchfield, J. Stat. Phys. 104:817 (2001) — statistical complexity / ε-machines, with real algorithms, built for time series~741 / ~328
Constructor theory — "a model that takes interventions"Barnett & Crutchfield, J. Stat. Phys. 161:404 (2015) — ε-transducers, the closest well-founded formal object to an intervention-capable world model~54
IIT / ΦTransfer entropy — Marschinski & Kantz, Eur. Phys. J. B 30:275 (2002). Already mainstream econophysics; nobody will blink.~395
The trade in one line: this substitution loses nothing conceptual and swaps ~150-citation contested work for 700–2,400-citation canon. The ε-transducer row is the one to look at hardest — it is a better formal fit for what we are actually building than constructor theory ever was.
Two things not to do, learned the expensive way. First: the constructor-theory thermodynamics paper (arXiv:1608.02625) has sat on arXiv for ten years across five versions with no journal reference — it is the paper you would want to lean on for entropy/irreversibility, and it has never passed peer review. Second: there is one preprint connecting both constructor theory and assembly theory to macroeconomic forecasting (arXiv:2603.24559, marked "draft"). It is not a citable precedent. If our paper becomes the second item in that reference class, that is the company we keep.

One attribution error to fix everywhere

Our internal notes record the convergence condition ε < γ/β as due to Hardt & Mendler-Dünner (2025). That is wrong. It is Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner & Hardt, ICML 2020, Theorem 3.5. Hardt & Mendler-Dünner (Statistical Science, 2025) is the survey. A referee in this area will catch the misattribution immediately, and it would cost us credibility across the whole related-work section. Fix it in every document before anything ships.

The three thresholds — keep them straight

ConditionWhat it guaranteesSource
ε < γ/βRepeated risk minimization contracts; a unique performatively stable point exists and is reachablePerdomo Thm 3.5
ε < γ/[(β+γ)(1+1.5ηβ)]Repeated gradient descent converges — strictly tighterPerdomo Thm 3.8
ε ≤ γ/(2β)Performative risk is convex, so the optimum is findableMiller, Perdomo & Zrnic, ICML 2021, Thm 3.1
The gap worth naming. Between γ/(2β) and γ/β there is a regime where you can find the reflexive fixed point but the performative risk is non-convex — stable but not optimizable. That regime is unnamed in the literature, and it is plausibly where any interesting economy actually lives. Characterizing it is cheap, honest novelty and it is sitting there unclaimed.

Where genuine extension is available, ranked by defensibility

  1. Endogenous ε — the strongest slot. In Perdomo, ε is a fixed environmental constant. In a real economy sensitivity is state- and regime-dependent. A model where εt is learned and endogenous, so the system crosses γ/β dynamically, converts a static condition into a crisis mechanism. Nobody has done this, and it is exactly what our Reflexive Instability signal measures.
  2. The differentiable equilibrium layer, made rigorous. Implicit-function-theorem differentiation through a fixed point requires (I − ∂G/∂θ) invertible — which is the contraction condition. So ε < γ/β becomes the well-posedness criterion for a differentiable performative-equilibrium layer. That reframes a borrowed condition as load-bearing in a new construction: legitimate, clean, and publishable. The DEQ machinery is mature and the performative-equilibrium definition is settled; searching the intersection returns the two literatures separately, with no paper joining them.
  3. Reflexive causal emergence. Per §4 — every emergence framework assumes a fixed generative process. Ours does not. Extending Barnett & Seth to a setting where the coarse-graining feeds back into the dynamics is a real open problem.
  4. Formal counterperformativity. Named by MacKenzie & Bamford in 2018, still qualitative in the 2025 meta-review, and the performative-prediction survey explicitly lists MacKenzie-style performativity as out of scope. Confirmed vacant by the field's own survey.
Section 20

Evaluation Protocol & Baselines — The Week-7 Bar

Our Fragment VAE is a structured latent-variable model with typed sub-states. That places it in a specific, well-benchmarked literature with published numbers. This section is the bar. Everything here is a real reported score from a real paper — these are not targets we invented.

The single most important fact in this literature. On the Turing Change Point Dataset — 37 real series, each annotated by 5 humans — a baseline called zero, which predicts no change points at all, outperforms 9 of the 13 published algorithms in the default-hyperparameter setting (covering 0.583, F1 0.669). The authors' reading: most methods return a flood of false positives.

Include a do-nothing baseline in week 7. If we don't, a reviewer will, and it will be in the rebuttal rather than the paper.

Direct competitors — structured switching models

RED-SDS and SNLDS are the closest published architectures to what we are building, and they are the only literature that evaluates regime decomposition against known ground truth with ARI/NMI. Frame-wise accuracy after Hungarian label matching:

MetricModelBouncing ball3-mode systemDancing bees (K=3)
AccuracySNLDS0.970.820.44
RED-SDS0.970.980.73
NMISNLDS0.830.630.10
RED-SDS0.810.910.48
ARISNLDS0.900.670.10
RED-SDS0.880.950.53

Two things to take from this literature. First, ARI / NMI / Hungarian-matched accuracy is the honest metric set for an unsupervised state decomposition — adopt it. Second, RED-SDS's entire advantage over SNLDS is explicit duration modelling (0.73 vs 0.44 on dancing bees). Our fragments have characteristic timescales τj by construction, which is the same idea. That is an argument we can make and test.

A warning from the same literature: in the SNLDS paper, a naive Gumbel-Softmax relaxation of the discrete variable collapses to F1 5.0 where proper forward-backward marginalization reaches 78.1. If any part of our architecture discretizes, marginalize it properly — do not reach for a straight-through relaxation.

Signature-MMD — a strong published competitor, not a freebie

§14 flagged signature kernels as a cheap extra baseline. The literature is more demanding than that. Issa & Horvath's non-parametric online detector reports, over 100 runs on regime-switching paths:

DetectorTotal accuracyROC AUCRuntime
Truncated signature (N=5)72.7%0.8755.1s
SIG-CON (Cochrane et al.)82.2%0.83545.0s
Untruncated sig-MMD93.6%0.9923.9s

Note that the untruncated signature kernel beats the truncated one decisively (93.6% vs 72.7%) and runs faster. If we use signature MMD, use the kernel — not truncated signature features fed to a distance.

Where to pick the fight

This is the most strategically useful finding in the whole literature review. Classical methods dominate mean-shift detection — BinSeg (1974) wins the TCPD default benchmark outright, and a 1970s generalized likelihood ratio test beats the celebrated deep KL-CPD method, whose average AUC of 0.48 is below chance. Learned methods only earn their keep on two things: covariance-structure change (neural 0.90–0.93 F1 vs classical 0.62–0.85) and long-range duration structure (RED-SDS 0.73 vs SNLDS 0.44).

Economic regimes are exactly covariance-structure and duration phenomena. Frame the contribution there and we are arguing on favourable ground. Frame it as general-purpose change detection and we lose to an algorithm from 1974.

Macro baselines — the numbers to beat

Real-time turning-point detection delay (months; negative = anticipates the NBER call). Barigozzi & Massacci's Markov-switching factor model on FRED-MD is best-in-class:

Turning pointChauvet & Piger (2008)Barigozzi–Massacci (2024)
Recession Feb-8061
Expansion Nov-826−7
Recession Jan-08139
Expansion Jul-097−4
Recession Mar-2001

Concordance with NBER: DoC 0.7718 on FRED-MD macro series, 0.8048 on stock returns. Chauvet–Piger's smoothed recession probabilities are live on FRED as RECPROUSM156N — a free, continuously updated real-time baseline with no excuse for omitting it.

Use PR AUC, not ROC AUC. The US recession base rate is ~0.086, so that is the random-guess floor for PR AUC. In the best current recession-prediction paper, ROC AUC compresses every model into 0.75–0.95 and hides real differences, while PR AUC spreads the same models across 0.17–0.72. A ROC AUC of 0.9 here is unremarkable; a PR AUC of 0.5 is genuinely strong. Reporting ROC AUC on a 9%-base-rate problem reads as either naive or evasive.

The corner-solution trap

A 2024 deep regime-detection paper on SPD manifolds reports 98.90% out-of-sample accuracy. It is a corner solution — the model classifies almost everything as "normal" — and a plain mean-variance benchmark still beat all their models on cumulative return. Their own conclusion: "using a singular performance metric is misleading."

Elsewhere in the same literature, a model posts accuracy 0.876 with F1 exactly 0.000 — it never predicts a recession at all. Report confusion matrices, always. And report downstream task performance separately, without claiming it validates the segmentation: the one paper that measured both found them decoupled.

The week-7 checklist

  1. Synthetic regime-switching data with known labels → ARI + NMI + Hungarian-matched accuracy, against: Gaussian HMM, HSMM, SNLDS, RED-SDS, Wasserstein k-means, BinSeg, PELT, BOCPD, sig-MMD, and zero.
  2. Confusion matrices for everything, to prove we have not found a corner solution.
  3. FRED-MD → NBER concordance + false-positive/false-negative rates + per-turning-point signed detection delay.
  4. PR AUC and F2 (a missed regime shift costs more than a false alarm), not accuracy and not ROC AUC alone.
  5. Default and tuned hyperparameters for every baseline. One kernel method on TCPD swings from 0.062 to 0.626 on tuning alone — reporting only one setting is not a result.
  6. Sensitivity to K (number of fragments) and to random seed. HMM initialization sensitivity is real and papers disclose it.
The opening this creates. The field's most-cited unsupervised regime-clustering paper reports no comparative accuracy table at all — its "vastly outperforms all competitors" claim is backed by two figures and a qualitative reading of three crises. Meanwhile the ML segmentation community has clean ARI/NMI protocols that nobody in finance has imported. Bringing RED-SDS-grade evaluation rigor to FRED-MD would be a contribution on evaluation methodology alone, independent of whether our architecture wins. That is a second, cheaper claim to novelty sitting inside work we are already committed to doing.
