1. Extended Kalman Filter for Nonlinear State Estimation

The Kalman filter (KF) is the minimum-variance linear estimator for linear-Gaussian state-space models. For nonlinear dynamics, the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) linearizes around the current estimate. Consider the state-space model:

State-Space Model xt = f(xt-1) + wt,   wt ~ N(0, Q)
yt = h(xt) + vt,   vt ~ N(0, R)

where f is the state transition function, h is the observation function, and Q, R are the process and measurement noise covariances respectively.

EKF Prediction Step x̂t|t-1 = f(x̂t-1|t-1)
Pt|t-1 = Ft Pt-1|t-1 FtT + Q

where Ft = ∂f/∂x |x̂t-1|t-1   (Jacobian of f evaluated at current estimate)
EKF Update Step et = yt - h(x̂t|t-1)   (innovation)
St = Ht Pt|t-1 HtT + R   (innovation covariance)
Kt = Pt|t-1 HtT St-1   (Kalman gain)
x̂t|t = x̂t|t-1 + Kt et
Pt|t = (I - Kt Ht) Pt|t-1

where Ht = ∂h/∂x |x̂t|t-1   (Jacobian of h)

Limitations of the EKF

  • Linearization error: The first-order Taylor expansion of f and h introduces bias. When the nonlinearity is strong or the covariance P is large (so the "operating region" is wide), the linearized approximation can be poor.
  • Divergence: Accumulated linearization errors cause the filter's covariance P to become inconsistent with the true estimation error, leading to overconfidence and eventual divergence.
  • Jacobian computation: Requires analytical or numerical derivatives of f and h, which may be expensive or unavailable.
  • Non-Gaussian distributions: The EKF maintains a Gaussian approximation; heavy tails or multimodality are lost.

The Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF)

Julier and Uhlmann (1997) introduced the UKF to avoid Jacobian computation and reduce linearization error. The key insight: it is easier to approximate a probability distribution than to approximate an arbitrary nonlinear function.

UKF core idea: Choose a set of sigma points {Xi} deterministically to capture the mean and covariance of the state distribution. Propagate these through the true nonlinear function f (or h), then recover the transformed mean and covariance from the propagated points. This captures second-order effects of the nonlinearity without requiring Jacobians.

For an n-dimensional state, the UKF uses 2n+1 sigma points. The predicted mean and covariance are weighted sums over the propagated sigma points. The UKF achieves third-order accuracy for Gaussian inputs (vs. first-order for EKF) and has similar computational cost to the EKF for moderate state dimensions.

Julier, S.J. & Uhlmann, J.K.
New Extension of the Kalman Filter to Nonlinear Systems.
Proc. SPIE 3068, Signal Processing, Sensor Fusion, and Target Recognition VI, 1997.
DOI: 10.1117/12.280797
Introduced sigma-point sampling as an alternative to Jacobian-based linearization; demonstrated superior performance on strongly nonlinear problems.
Wan, E.A. & van der Merwe, R.
The Unscented Kalman Filter for Nonlinear Estimation.
Proc. IEEE Adaptive Systems for Signal Processing, Communications, and Control Symposium (AS-SPCC), 2000.
DOI: 10.1109/ASSPCC.2000.882463
Formalized the UKF algorithm and demonstrated its application to state and parameter estimation; showed consistent improvement over EKF on benchmark problems.

Other alternatives include the Cubature Kalman Filter (CKF) of Arasaratnam & Haykin (2009), which uses cubature rules for integration, and particle filters (sequential Monte Carlo), which handle arbitrary distributions but scale poorly with state dimension.

Arasaratnam, I. & Haykin, S.
Cubature Kalman Filters.
IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 54(6):1254-1269, 2009.
DOI: 10.1109/TAC.2009.2019800
Derived spherical-radial cubature rules for Gaussian-weighted integrals; CKF avoids the tuning parameters of UKF (alpha, beta, kappa) and is numerically more stable in high dimensions.

2. Adaptive Kalman Filtering: Online Q and R Estimation

The standard KF/EKF assumes Q and R are known. In practice they are rarely known precisely, and misspecification has severe consequences:

  • Q too small: The filter trusts the model too much, responds too slowly to real state changes, and P collapses (overconfidence).
  • Q too large: The filter overreacts to noise, producing noisy estimates.
  • R too small: The filter trusts observations too much, chasing measurement noise.
  • R too large: The filter ignores informative observations.
The adaptive KF problem: Estimate Q and/or R online, concurrently with the state x, using only the observable innovation sequence et = yt - Ht x̂t|t-1.

2a. The Sage-Husa Adaptive Filter

The foundational work on online adaptive noise estimation within the Kalman filter framework.

Sage, A.P. & Husa, G.W.
Adaptive Filtering with Unknown Prior Statistics.
Proc. Joint Automatic Control Conference (JACC), pp. 760-769, 1969.
No DOI available (conference proceedings, pre-digital era)
First systematic algorithm for online maximum-likelihood estimation of Q and R within the Kalman filter recursion. Proposed using innovation and residual sequences to adaptively update noise covariance matrices.

The Sage-Husa algorithm augments the standard KF with recursive estimators for the noise statistics. The core idea: under correct filter tuning, the innovation sequence et should be a zero-mean white noise with covariance St = Ht Pt|t-1 HtT + R. Deviations from this indicate misspecified Q or R.

Sage-Husa R Update R̂t = (1 - dt) R̂t-1 + dt (et etT - Ht Pt|t-1 HtT)

where dt = (1 - b) / (1 - bt)   for a forgetting factor b ∈ (0,1)
Sage-Husa Q Update Q̂t = (1 - dt) Q̂t-1 + dt (Kt et etT KtT + Pt|t - Ft Pt-1|t-1 FtT)

In the simplest form (without forgetting), dt = 1/t, which gives a running average. The forgetting factor b (typically 0.95-0.99) allows tracking of slowly time-varying noise statistics.

Known stability issues: The Sage-Husa filter can produce negative-definite estimates of Q or R because the update equations do not enforce positive semi-definiteness. This causes filter divergence. The problem is particularly acute when: (a) the state dimension is high relative to observation dimension, (b) the initial noise estimates are far from the true values, or (c) the system is strongly nonlinear.

2b. Innovation-Based and Residual-Based Methods

Mehra's Classification (1970-1972)

Mehra, R.K.
On the Identification of Variances and Adaptive Kalman Filtering.
IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 15(2):175-184, 1970.
DOI: 10.1109/TAC.1970.1099422
Classified adaptive KF methods into four categories: (1) Bayesian, (2) maximum likelihood, (3) correlation (innovation-based), and (4) covariance matching. Showed that the innovation sequence contains all information needed for noise identification in LTI systems.
Mehra, R.K.
Approaches to Adaptive Filtering.
IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 17(5):693-698, 1972.
DOI: 10.1109/TAC.1972.1100100
Extended the classification and compared methods; showed innovation-based methods are most practical for real-time applications.

Innovation-based (covariance matching) method for R: The theoretical innovation covariance is St = H Pt|t-1 HT + R. Over a window of N innovations:

Windowed R Estimation Ĉe = (1/N) Σi=t-N+1t ei eiT
R̂t = Ĉe - H Pt|t-1 HT

Residual-based method for Q: The smoothed residual rt = x̂t|t - x̂t|t-1 = Kt et carries information about the process noise. The autocovariance of the innovation sequence at lag j, denoted Ce(j), is theoretically zero for j ≥ 1 when Q is correct. Non-zero lag-1 autocovariance indicates Q misspecification:

Q Estimation via Innovation Autocovariance Ce(1) = H F (Pt|t - Pt|t-1 + Q) HT
When Ĉe(1) ≠ 0, one can solve for Q (assuming observability conditions hold).

2c. Stability Fixes and Fading Memory

Fading Memory / Exponential Forgetting

The most widely used fix for adaptive KF instability is the fading memory approach, which inflates P to prevent overconfidence:

Fading Memory Prediction Pt|t-1 = α2 Ft Pt-1|t-1 FtT + Q

where α ≥ 1 is the fading factor (typically 1.001 to 1.05)

This prevents the filter from becoming overconfident when Q is underestimated, at the cost of slightly noisier estimates.

Jazwinski, A.H.
Stochastic Processes and Filtering Theory.
Academic Press, New York, 1970.
ISBN: 978-0-12-381550-7
Comprehensive treatment of stochastic filtering including limited-memory and fading-memory filters; remains the standard reference for the theoretical foundations of adaptive filtering.

Positive Definiteness Enforcement

To fix the Sage-Husa negative-definiteness problem, common approaches include:

  • Projection: After each update, project Q̂ and R̂ onto the positive semi-definite cone (eigenvalue clipping).
  • Diagonal constraint: Estimate only the diagonal elements of Q and R, enforcing positivity element-wise.
  • Square-root formulations: Parameterize Q = LQ LQT and estimate LQ instead.
Mohamed, A.H. & Schwarz, K.P.
Adaptive Kalman Filtering for INS/GPS.
Journal of Geodesy, 73(4):193-203, 1999.
DOI: 10.1007/s001900050236
Proposed practical modifications to the Sage-Husa filter for INS/GPS integration, including positive-definiteness enforcement and windowed estimation; widely cited in navigation applications.

2d. Variational and EM-Based Approaches

More principled approaches treat the noise covariances as latent variables and use Bayesian or EM methods:

Shumway, R.H. & Stoffer, D.S.
An Approach to Time Series Smoothing and Forecasting Using the EM Algorithm.
Journal of Time Series Analysis, 3(4):253-264, 1982.
DOI: 10.1111/j.1467-9892.1982.tb00349.x
Applied EM to estimate state-space model parameters including Q and R by iterating between Kalman smoothing (E-step) and parameter MLE (M-step). Foundational for offline parameter estimation in state-space models.
Ghahramani, Z. & Hinton, G.E.
Parameter Estimation for Linear Dynamical Systems.
Technical Report CRG-TR-96-2, University of Toronto, 1996.
Available at: https://mlg.eng.cam.ac.uk/zoubin/papers/tr-96-2.pdf
Detailed EM algorithm for learning all parameters of a linear dynamical system (A, B, C, Q, R, initial conditions); clean derivation widely used as a reference.
Sarkka, S. & Nummenmaa, A.
Recursive Noise Adaptive Kalman Filtering by Variational Bayesian Approximations.
IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 54(3):596-600, 2009.
DOI: 10.1109/TAC.2008.2008348
Used variational Bayes with inverse-Wishart priors on R to derive an online adaptive KF that is more stable than Sage-Husa; the posterior over R is updated jointly with the state at each time step.
Huang, Y., Zhang, Y., Wu, Z., Li, N. & Chambers, J.
A Novel Adaptive Kalman Filter with Inaccurate Process and Measurement Noise Covariance Matrices.
IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 63(2):594-601, 2018.
DOI: 10.1109/TAC.2017.2730480
Extended the variational Bayesian approach to jointly estimate both Q and R online using inverse-Wishart priors on both; showed improved robustness over single-covariance adaptive methods.

3. Kalman Filtering and Online Learning

3a. KF as Bayesian Online Learning

The Kalman filter is exact Bayesian online learning for linear-Gaussian models. The posterior at time t is:

Bayesian Interpretation p(xt | y1:t) = N(x̂t|t, Pt|t)

The prediction step computes the prior via Chapman-Kolmogorov:
p(xt | y1:t-1) = ∫ p(xt | xt-1) p(xt-1 | y1:t-1) dxt-1

The update step applies Bayes' rule:
p(xt | y1:t) ∝ p(yt | xt) p(xt | y1:t-1)

For linear-Gaussian models, both operations preserve Gaussianity exactly.

This interpretation immediately connects to online Bayesian regression: if the state xt represents regression coefficients that evolve as a random walk, the Kalman filter performs exact Bayesian online linear regression with time-varying parameters.

3b. KF and Online Linear Regression

Consider the special case where xt = xt-1 + wt (random walk state) and yt = htT xt + vt (linear observation). This is equivalent to online linear regression where the true coefficients drift. The connection to recursive least squares (RLS) is exact:

RLS as KF Special Case When Q = 0 (static parameters), the Kalman filter reduces to RLS:
Pt-1 = Pt-1-1 + ht htT / σ2
x̂t = x̂t-1 + Pt ht (yt - htT x̂t-1) / σ2

This is the standard RLS update with Pt playing the role of the inverse Hessian.

With Q ≠ 0, the KF effectively "forgets" old data at a rate governed by Q, enabling tracking of non-stationary parameters. This is the adaptive online learning interpretation: Q controls the effective memory length of the estimator.

3c. Regret Bounds and the OCO Connection

Abbasi-Yadkori, Y. & Szepesvari, Cs.
Regret Bounds for the Adaptive Control of Linear Quadratic Systems.
Proc. 24th Annual Conference on Learning Theory (COLT), pp. 1-26, 2011.
Available in JMLR Proceedings, Vol. 19
Proved O(sqrt(T)) regret bounds for adaptive LQR using online least squares (which is the KF with Q=0). The confidence sets for the unknown system matrices are constructed using the KF's covariance matrix P, establishing a direct link between KF estimation quality and control regret.
Hazan, E. & Singh, K.
Introduction to Online Convex Optimization.
Foundations and Trends in Optimization, 2(3-4):157-325, 2016. (2nd ed. as monograph, MIT Press, 2022.)
arXiv: 1909.05207 (survey version)
Comprehensive framework for OCO; discusses online Newton step (ONS) which uses a matrix that evolves identically to the KF precision matrix P^{-1} for squared loss.
Hazan, E., Singh, K. & Zhang, C.
Learning Linear Dynamical Systems via Spectral Filtering.
Proc. NeurIPS, 2017.
arXiv: 1711.00946
Proposed an online learning approach to linear dynamical system prediction that achieves sublinear regret without system identification; provides an alternative to the Kalman filter approach that works under adversarial noise.
Hazan, E., Lee, H., Singh, K., Zhang, C. & Zhang, Y.
Spectral Filtering for General Linear Dynamical Systems.
Proc. NeurIPS, 2018.
arXiv: 1802.03981
Extended spectral filtering to general (non-symmetric) LDS with polynomial regret bounds; provided online learning guarantees competitive with the optimal KF in hindsight.
Kozat, S.S. & Singer, A.C.
Universal Switching Linear Least Squares Prediction.
IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing, 56(1):189-204, 2008.
DOI: 10.1109/TSP.2007.906iembre
Connected the Kalman filter to universal prediction and minimax regret in the context of switching linear models.
The OCO-KF correspondence: For the squared loss ℓt(θ) = (yt - htTθ)2, the Online Newton Step (ONS) algorithm of Hazan et al. (2007) maintains a precision matrix At = λI + Σi=1t hihiT that is identical to the KF precision matrix Pt-1 (with Q=0 and R=I, λ = P0-1). The ONS achieves O(d log T) regret for exp-concave losses, which is the best possible for online linear regression. The Kalman filter thus achieves optimal regret in the static-parameter case.

3d. Kalman Gain as Adaptive Learning Rate

The Kalman gain Kt can be interpreted as an adaptive, matrix-valued learning rate in online gradient descent. Compare:

Online GD Kalman Filter
θt = θt-1 - ηt ∇ℓt(θt-1) x̂t|t = x̂t|t-1 + Kt et
Scalar step size ηt Matrix gain Kt = Pt|t-1 HtT St-1
Decays as O(1/t) or O(1/√t) Kt converges to steady-state gain (for stable systems)
Isotropic: same rate for all dimensions Anisotropic: adapts per-dimension based on uncertainty

Key properties of the Kalman gain as a learning rate:

  • Second-order: Kt effectively preconditions by the inverse Hessian (via Pt), analogous to natural gradient or Newton's method.
  • Uncertainty-aware: The gain is large in uncertain dimensions and small in well-estimated ones.
  • Observation-adaptive: The gain adapts to the current observation matrix Ht, automatically handling missing data or varying observation quality.
  • With Q ≠ 0: The gain never decays to zero -- P is bounded below by Q, maintaining a minimum learning rate. This is the KF's built-in mechanism for continual learning / non-stationarity tracking.
Ollivier, Y.
Online Natural Gradient as a Kalman Filter.
Electronic Journal of Statistics, 12(2):2930-2961, 2018.
arXiv: 1703.00209 · DOI: 10.1214/18-EJS1468
Proved that online natural gradient descent on a probabilistic model is equivalent to a Kalman filter on the model parameters, with the Fisher information matrix playing the role of H^T R^{-1} H. This formalizes the "KF gain = adaptive preconditioned learning rate" intuition.
Haykin, S.
Kalman Filtering and Neural Networks.
Wiley, 2001.
ISBN: 978-0-471-36998-1
Collected chapters on using the (extended) Kalman filter for neural network training, where the KF is applied to the parameter space of the network; demonstrated superior convergence to backpropagation in small networks.

4. Continual State Estimation in Economic Models

4a. Multi-Rate and Mixed-Frequency Kalman Filtering

Economic state variables evolve at different timescales: daily asset prices, monthly employment, quarterly GDP. The state-space formulation handles this naturally by treating slow variables as having missing observations at high-frequency time steps.

Mariano, R.S. & Murasawa, Y.
A New Coincident Index of Business Cycles Based on Monthly and Quarterly Series.
Journal of Applied Econometrics, 18(4):427-443, 2003.
DOI: 10.1002/jae.695
Constructed a coincident economic index using a state-space model with mixed-frequency data (monthly and quarterly); the Kalman filter handles missing quarterly observations naturally by skipping the update step.
Banbura, M., Giannone, D. & Reichlin, L.
Nowcasting.
In: M.P. Clements & D.F. Hendry (Eds.), Oxford Handbook of Economic Forecasting, Oxford University Press, 2011.
ECB Working Paper No. 1275
Survey of nowcasting methods based on large-dimensional factor models estimated via the Kalman filter with mixed-frequency data; established the state-space/KF approach as the standard for real-time macroeconomic monitoring.
Banbura, M. & Modugno, M.
Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Factor Models on Datasets with Arbitrary Pattern of Missing Data.
Journal of Applied Econometrics, 29(1):133-160, 2014.
DOI: 10.1002/jae.2306
Extended the EM algorithm for factor model estimation with the Kalman smoother to handle arbitrary missing-data patterns, as arise naturally in mixed-frequency economic datasets.
Multi-rate KF for RCWM: In a typed-step-size S5 model, each state dimension has an associated timescale (step size). This is structurally analogous to multi-rate KF: fast state components (e.g., market microstructure) are updated at every tick, while slow components (e.g., structural economic parameters) have their observation matrices effectively zeroed out between quarterly releases. The S5 discretization with different step sizes per dimension naturally implements this multi-rate structure.

4b. DSGE Estimation via the Kalman Filter

The Kalman filter is the workhorse of Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) model estimation. The log-linearized DSGE model produces a linear state-space form, and the Kalman filter computes the likelihood p(y1:T | θ) via the prediction error decomposition:

Prediction Error Decomposition log p(y1:T | θ) = -½ Σt=1T [m log(2π) + log|St| + etT St-1 et]

This decomposes the likelihood into contributions from each time step's innovation et and its predicted covariance St.
Smets, F. & Wouters, R.
An Estimated Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium Model of the Euro Area.
Journal of the European Economic Association, 1(5):1123-1175, 2003.
DOI: 10.1162/154247603770383415
Landmark medium-scale DSGE model estimated via Bayesian methods using the Kalman filter for likelihood evaluation; demonstrated that DSGE models with enough frictions can match VAR forecasting performance.
Smets, F. & Wouters, R.
Shocks and Frictions in US Business Cycles: A Bayesian DSGE Approach.
American Economic Review, 97(3):586-606, 2007.
DOI: 10.1257/aer.97.3.586
US version of their Euro Area model; became the benchmark medium-scale DSGE model. The KF-based likelihood evaluation combined with MCMC (Random Walk Metropolis-Hastings) remains the standard estimation approach.
Herbst, E.P. & Schorfheide, F.
Bayesian Estimation of DSGE Models.
Princeton University Press, 2015.
ISBN: 978-0-691-16108-2
Comprehensive textbook on Bayesian DSGE estimation; covers KF likelihood evaluation, sequential Monte Carlo (particle filter) for nonlinear DSGE, and practical implementation details including handling of stochastic singularity.

Stochastic singularity: A common issue in DSGE estimation: if the model has fewer shocks than observables, R is singular, and the KF likelihood is undefined for some data realizations. The fix is either to add measurement errors (non-zero R) or to reduce the number of observables. This is directly relevant to RCWM: the noise covariance structure must be carefully designed to avoid singularity while maintaining economic interpretability.

4c. Harvey's Structural Time Series

Harvey, A.C.
Forecasting, Structural Time Series Models and the Kalman Filter.
Cambridge University Press, 1989.
ISBN: 978-0-521-40573-7
The standard reference for structural time series models (unobserved components models) estimated via the Kalman filter. Decomposes time series into trend, seasonal, cyclical, and irregular components, each modeled as a separate state-space block.

Harvey's framework decomposes an economic time series as:

Structural Decomposition yt = μt + γt + ψt + εt

μt = trend (local level or local linear trend)
γt = seasonal component
ψt = cyclical component
εt = irregular (measurement noise)

Each component has its own state-space dynamics and process noise variance. The combined model is a block-diagonal state-space model estimated by the Kalman filter. The relative magnitudes of the process noise variances Qμ, Qγ, Qψ determine the smoothness of each component -- directly analogous to typed step sizes in S5.

Durbin, J. & Koopman, S.J.
Time Series Analysis by State Space Methods.
Oxford University Press, 2nd edition, 2012.
ISBN: 978-0-19-964117-8
Modern comprehensive treatment of state-space time series analysis; covers the Kalman filter, smoothing, missing data, non-Gaussian extensions, and computational methods. Includes treatment of multivariate models with common trends/cycles.
Commandeur, J.J.F. & Koopman, S.J.
An Introduction to State Space Time Series Analysis.
Oxford University Press, 2007.
ISBN: 978-0-19-922887-4
Accessible introduction to Harvey-style structural time series with worked examples; useful for implementation reference.

5. Modern Neural Extensions

5a. KalmanNet

Revach, G., Shlezinger, N., Ni, X., Escoriza, A.L., van Sloun, R.J.G. & Eldar, Y.C.
KalmanNet: Neural Network Aided Kalman Filtering for Partially Known Dynamics.
IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing, 70:1532-1547, 2022.
arXiv: 2107.10043 · DOI: 10.1109/TSP.2022.3158588 Code github.com/KalmanNet/KalmanNet_TSP
Replaced the Kalman gain computation K_t with a recurrent neural network (GRU-based) that learns the gain directly from data. The network takes as input the innovation e_t and the difference between consecutive innovations, and outputs the Kalman gain matrix. Achieves near-optimal KF performance when the model is known, and significantly outperforms model-based KF when Q and R are misspecified. Key insight: the network learns to implicitly adapt Q and R without explicitly estimating them.
Revach, G., Shlezinger, N., van Sloun, R.J.G. & Eldar, Y.C.
Unsupervised Learned Kalman Filtering.
Proc. International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2023.
arXiv: 2110.09005 Code github.com/KalmanNet/Unsupervised_ICLR_2023
Extended KalmanNet to the unsupervised setting where ground-truth states are unavailable during training. Trained using the innovation-based loss (the innovation should be white with known covariance under correct filtering). This directly connects to the adaptive KF literature: the innovation whiteness criterion is the same principle underlying Mehra's methods and the Sage-Husa filter.
KalmanNet architecture: The GRU network receives features derived from et (innovation), et - et-1 (innovation difference, carrying second-order information about the gain's evolution), and Σt (forward evolution of state covariance). It outputs Kt ∈ Rn×m. The rest of the KF equations (prediction, state update) use the model-based f and h. This preserves the KF's interpretable structure while making the gain computation data-driven.

5b. Differentiable Kalman Filters

Kloss, A., Schaal, S. & Bohg, J.
How to Train Your Differentiable Filter.
Autonomous Robots, 45:561-578, 2021.
arXiv: 2012.14313 · DOI: 10.1007/s10514-021-09990-9
Compared differentiable EKF, UKF, and particle filters for end-to-end learning of state estimation from raw observations; found that backpropagation through the KF equations enables learning observation models and noise parameters jointly.
Haarnoja, T., Ajay, A., Levine, S. & Abbeel, P.
Backprop KF: Learning Discriminative Deterministic State Estimators.
Proc. NeurIPS, 2016.
arXiv: 1605.07148
Backpropagated through the KF update equations to learn observation and transition models end-to-end; demonstrated on visual tracking tasks. Showed that the structured KF inductive bias improves data efficiency compared to generic RNNs.
Becker, P., Pandya, H., Gebhardt, G., Zhao, C., Taylor, C.J. & Neumann, G.
Recurrent Kalman Networks: Factored Inference in High-Dimensional Deep Feature Spaces.
Proc. ICML, 2019.
arXiv: 1905.07357
Factored the state space into independent subspaces to make KF tractable in high dimensions; used a neural encoder for observations and learned transition/observation models. The factored structure is analogous to block-diagonal Q in Harvey's structural models.

The differentiable KF approach is directly relevant to RCWM: by making the entire Kalman filter differentiable, one can learn Q, R, and the state-space model parameters end-to-end from data, using gradient descent. This subsumes adaptive KF: rather than using moment-matching heuristics (Sage-Husa) or EM, the noise covariances are learned by backpropagation through the filter.

5c. Connections to S4/S5 State-Space Models

The structured state-space sequence models (S4, S5) used in deep learning share the mathematical form of classical state-space models but differ in purpose: they are trained as sequence-to-sequence maps rather than as probabilistic state estimators. However, key connections exist:

Gu, A., Goel, K. & Re, C.
Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces.
Proc. ICLR, 2022.
arXiv: 2111.00396 Code github.com/state-spaces/s4
Introduced S4: a deep state-space model using the HiPPO initialization for the state matrix A, diagonal-plus-low-rank structure, and parallel scan for efficient training. The discretization uses a zero-order hold (ZOH) with step size Delta that controls the timescale of each state dimension.
Smith, J.T.H., Warrington, A. & Linderman, S.W.
Simplified State Space Layers for Sequence Modeling.
Proc. ICLR, 2023.
arXiv: 2208.04933 Code github.com/lindermanlab/S5
Introduced S5: simplified S4 with a single MIMO state-space model (vs. S4's stacked SISO), diagonal state matrix, and efficient parallel scan. The step size Delta_i per state dimension controls the timescale -- directly analogous to per-component process noise variance Q_ii in the Kalman filter.
S5 step sizes and Kalman filter Q: In S5, the discretized state transition is Āi = exp(Δi Ai). A large Δi means dimension i integrates over longer timescales (is "slower"). In the Kalman filter, the effective process noise for dimension i is Qii, and a larger Qii means the filter expects more state change per step -- making that dimension "faster" (more responsive). The correspondence: S5's Δi controls the discretization timescale, while KF's Qii controls the forgetting/adaptation rate. For RCWM, typed step sizes that differ by state type (fast for market variables, slow for structural parameters) implement a multi-timescale state estimation architecture where Δi and Qii are jointly determined by the economic type of state i.
Gu, A. & Dao, T.
Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces.
Proc. ICLR (notable-top-5%), 2024.
arXiv: 2312.00752 Code github.com/state-spaces/mamba
Made the step size Delta and the B, C matrices input-dependent (selective), enabling the model to adaptively filter information based on the current input. This is directly analogous to the EKF where the Kalman gain K_t adapts at each time step based on the current observation. Mamba's selectivity mechanism is, at its core, an adaptive gain.
Linderman, S.W.
Bayesian Learning and Inference in Recurrent Switching Linear Dynamical Systems.
PhD Thesis, Harvard University, 2016.
Available via Harvard DASH
Developed switching linear dynamical systems (rSLDS) with Bayesian inference via message passing (Kalman filtering within each regime). Relevant to RCWM as a principled way to handle regime changes in economic state estimation within the state-space framework.
Rangapuram, S.S., Seeger, M.W., Gasthaus, J., Stella, L., Wang, Y. & Januschowski, T.
Deep State Space Models for Time Series Forecasting.
Proc. NeurIPS, 2018.
arXiv: 1803.01271
Combined deep learning (for learning state-space model parameters from covariates) with classical Kalman filtering (for inference). The neural network outputs the parameters of a linear state-space model, and the Kalman filter provides exact posterior inference. Directly relevant to RCWM: neural networks can parameterize the state-space model, while the KF provides principled uncertainty quantification.

6. Synthesis: Implications for RCWM with S5 and Typed Step Sizes

The following table maps the classical KF/adaptive KF concepts to their RCWM counterparts:

Classical KF Concept RCWM / S5 Counterpart Design Implication
Process noise Qii S5 step size Δi per state type Typed step sizes implement multi-timescale Q; fast economic variables (prices) get large Δ / large Q, slow variables (institutions) get small values
Measurement noise R Observation uncertainty per data source Different economic data sources (BLS surveys vs. transaction data vs. sentiment) have different R; adaptive R estimation handles time-varying data quality
Kalman gain Kt Adaptive learning rate / selectivity The Mamba-style input-dependent Δ is an adaptive gain; for RCWM, the gain should be type-aware (different adaptation logic for different state types)
Innovation sequence et Prediction error signal for adaptation The innovation drives both state updates and adaptive noise estimation; its whiteness is the diagnostic for correct model specification (Mehra's insight)
Sage-Husa adaptive Q/R Online noise adaptation in S5 Can be implemented as a differentiable layer (a la KalmanNet) that adjusts Δi and R based on innovation statistics, avoiding the positive-definiteness issues of classical Sage-Husa
Multi-rate KF Mixed-frequency economic data fusion S5's parallel scan naturally handles irregular/missing observations; the state evolves continuously, observations arrive at mixed frequencies
Harvey's structural decomposition Typed state blocks (trend, cycle, seasonal per sector) Block-diagonal structure in S5 state matrix, with each block having its own type-appropriate Δ and dynamics
Prediction error decomposition (likelihood) Training objective for S5 The KF likelihood provides a principled training signal that accounts for observation uncertainty; can be combined with the S5 sequence loss

Concrete Design Recommendations

  1. Typed step sizes as typed Q: Initialize S5 step sizes Δi by economic state type. Use the Harvey-style decomposition as a structural prior: trend components get small Δ (slow evolution), cyclical components get medium Δ, and irregular/market components get large Δ.
  2. KalmanNet-style adaptive gain: Rather than classical Sage-Husa (fragile), use a small neural network (GRU or MLP) to output per-type gain adjustments conditioned on the innovation. This makes the adaptation differentiable and avoids positive-definiteness issues. Train end-to-end.
  3. Innovation whiteness as a regularizer: Add a loss term penalizing autocorrelation in the innovation sequence (Mehra's criterion). This acts as a self-consistency check: if the model's Q and R are correct, innovations should be white. The unsupervised KalmanNet paper (Revach et al. 2023) demonstrates this works in practice.
  4. Online learning regret perspective: The OCO connection (Section 3c) provides regret guarantees for the static-parameter case. For the time-varying case relevant to RCWM, the appropriate benchmark is the comparator class of piecewise-constant or slowly-varying parameter sequences. The dynamic regret literature (Zinkevich 2003, Jadbabaie et al. 2015) provides the relevant bounds, with the path length of the comparator playing the role of Q.
  5. Multi-rate fusion: Implement the mixed-frequency approach of Banbura & Modugno (2014) within the S5 framework: the observation mask Mt at each time step indicates which variables are observed, and the update step is applied only to observed dimensions. This is trivially compatible with the parallel scan.

Experience Replay Methods for Continual Learning

Research survey for the RCWM program — August 2026

Contents

  1. Reservoir Sampling — Vitter 1985
  2. Prioritized Experience Replay — Schaul et al. 2016
  3. Deep Generative Replay — Shin et al. 2017

1. Reservoir Sampling

Citation

Primary Reference
Jeffrey S. Vitter. "Random Sampling with a Reservoir." ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software, 11(1):37–57, March 1985. DOI: 10.1145/3147.3165
Optimized Variant
Kim-Hung Li. "Reservoir-Sampling Algorithms of Time Complexity O(n(1 + log(N/n)))." ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software, 21(4):478–493, December 1995. DOI: 10.1145/198429.198435

Algorithm R — Step by Step

-- Reservoir Sampling, Algorithm R (Vitter 1985) -- Input : stream S of unknown length, reservoir size k -- Output: array R[1..k] containing a uniform random sample procedure ALGORITHM_R(S, k): -- Phase 1: fill the reservoir with the first k items for i = 1 to k: R[i] ← S[i] -- Phase 2: for each subsequent item, include with decreasing probability for i = k+1 to n: j ← RANDOM(1, i) -- uniform integer in {1, 2, ..., i} if j ≤ k: R[j] ← S[i] -- replace the j-th reservoir element -- else: discard S[i], reservoir unchanged return R

Complexity: O(n) time, O(k) space. Each stream element is examined exactly once. Vitter also introduced Algorithm X, Y, and Z in the same paper, with Algorithm Z achieving optimal O(k(1 + log(n/k))) time by computing random skip distances instead of generating a random number per element.

Unbiasedness Guarantee

Theorem. After processing all n items, each item has exactly probability k/n of being in the reservoir.

Proof by induction on stream position i

Base case (i = k): The reservoir contains all k items. Each has probability k/k = 1 of inclusion. ✓ Inductive hypothesis: After processing item i, every item seen so far has probability k/i of being in the reservoir. Inductive step (i → i+1): Item i+1 enters the reservoir with probability k/(i+1). ✓ For any prior item already in the reservoir, the probability it survives step i+1: P(survives) = P(item i+1 does not replace it) = 1 − P(item i+1 enters) × P(this slot chosen | entry) = 1 − (k/(i+1)) × (1/k) = 1 − 1/(i+1) = i/(i+1) By the inductive hypothesis, the item was in the reservoir with probability k/i. So after step i+1: P(in reservoir) = (k/i) × (i/(i+1)) = k/(i+1) ✓ □

Modern Extensions

  • Algorithm L (Kim-Hung Li, 1995): Computes random skip distances using geometric sampling, achieving O(k(1 + log(n/k))) time — sublinear in n.
  • Weighted reservoir sampling (Efraimidis & Spirakis, 2006): Each item i gets key ri1/wi where ri ~ Uniform(0,1) and wi is its weight. The top-k keys form the sample.
  • Partitioning Reservoir Sampling (PRS) (Kim et al., ECCV 2020): Partitions the buffer by class to handle class-imbalanced continual learning streams.
  • Time-Decayed Reservoir Sampling: Prioritizes recent items for evolving distributions — relevant for non-stationary economic regimes.

Implementations in CL Frameworks

aimagelab/mammoth ContinualAI/avalanche cdjkim/PRS

Both Mammoth and Avalanche implement reservoir sampling as their default buffer management strategy for experience replay baselines (ER, DER, DER++, A-GEM).

Application to RCWM

Reservoir sampling provides the buffer management substrate for all replay-based approaches in RCWM. For multi-timescale economic data, stratified reservoir sampling is essential: maintain separate reservoirs per temporal granularity (tick, daily, monthly, macro-cycle) so that rare slow-timescale regime transitions are not washed out by high-frequency observations. The class-balanced PRS variant maps directly to regime-balanced buffers. Time-decayed weighting addresses non-stationarity inherent in economic series.

2. Prioritized Experience Replay

Citation

Primary Reference
Tom Schaul, John Quan, Ioannis Antonoglou, David Silver. "Prioritized Experience Replay." Proceedings of the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2016. arXiv: 1511.05952

Core Idea

Not all transitions are equally useful for learning. PER replays transitions in proportion to their "surprise" — measured by the magnitude of the temporal-difference (TD) error — so the agent learns more from unexpected outcomes.

Priority Definitions

Variant 1: Proportional Prioritization

pi = |δi| + ε where δi is the TD-error for transition i, and ε > 0 is a small constant preventing zero-priority transitions.

Variant 2: Rank-Based Prioritization

pi = 1 / rank(i) where rank(i) is the position of transition i when sorted by |δi| descending.

Sampling Probability

P(i) = piα ⁄ Σk pkα where α ∈ [0, 1] controls prioritization intensity: α = 0 → uniform sampling (standard replay) α = 1 → full prioritization

Importance Sampling Correction

Prioritized sampling introduces bias (the expected update no longer equals the uniform-sampling expected update). This is corrected with importance-sampling weights:

wi = ( (1/N) · (1/P(i)) )β Normalized weights: ŵi = wi / maxj wj where N = replay buffer size, and β is annealed linearly from β0 to 1 over the course of training. At β = 1, importance sampling fully compensates for the non-uniform distribution. The gradient update is then scaled: Δθ = ŵi · δi · ∇θ Q(si, ai)

Sum Tree Data Structure

Efficient proportional sampling uses a sum tree (binary segment tree):

  • Leaf nodes store transition priorities piα
  • Internal nodes store the sum of their children
  • Root stores the total priority: ptotal = Σi piα
  • To sample a minibatch of size k: divide [0, ptotal] into k equal segments, uniformly sample one value from each segment, traverse the tree to find the corresponding leaf
  • Update and sampling are both O(log N)

Complete Algorithm

-- Prioritized Experience Replay (Schaul et al. 2016) Initialize replay buffer B with capacity N, sum tree T Initialize β ← β0 for each training step: -- Sample proportional to priority for j = 1 to batch_size: segment ← [(j−1) · ptotal/k,  j · ptotal/k] sample uniform s from segment retrieve transition i from tree T at cumulative priority s -- Compute IS weights wi ← ((1/N) · (1/P(i)))β normalize: ŵi ← wi / maxj wj -- Compute TD-error and update δi ← r + γ maxa' Q(s', a') − Q(s, a) Δθ ← ŵi · δi · ∇θQ(s, a) update θ -- Update priorities pi ← |δi| + ε update tree T with new piα -- Anneal β β ← min(1, β + Δβ)

Code Repositories

openai/baselines torchrl PrioritizedSampler Howuhh/prioritized_experience_replay
Application to RCWM

For RCWM, the TD-error concept generalizes naturally to SPIB per-fragment prediction error. Fragments (economic sub-regimes) whose latent-variable reconstruction loss is highest should be replayed more frequently. The α parameter lets you tune how aggressively rare-but-surprising regime transitions dominate the replay distribution. The IS correction ensures the S5 SSM's parameter updates remain unbiased despite the non-uniform sampling across temporal fragments. For multi-timescale operation, maintain separate priority queues per timescale and sample from each in proportion to its temporal bandwidth.

3. Deep Generative Replay

Citation

Primary Reference
Hanul Shin, Jung Kwon Lee, Jaehong Kim, Jiwon Kim. "Continual Learning with Deep Generative Replay." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS / NIPS), 30:2990–2999, 2017. arXiv: 1705.08690

Core Idea: Pseudo-Rehearsal via Generative Models

Instead of storing raw data in a replay buffer (which has privacy and memory concerns), train a generative model (GAN or VAE) to learn the distribution of previous tasks. When a new task arrives, generate pseudo-samples from the generator to interleave with new task data, preventing catastrophic forgetting without explicit data storage.

The Scholar Framework

A "scholar" is a dual-model system comprising:

  • Generator G: A deep generative model (GAN) that learns to produce samples resembling past data distributions
  • Solver S: A task-solving model (classifier) that learns to perform the target task

Both G and S are updated together at each stage; the scholar at stage t replaces the scholar at stage t−1.

Training Algorithm

-- Deep Generative Replay (Shin et al. 2017) -- Scholar = (Generator G, Solver S) Initialize Scholar0 = (G0, S0) for each new task t = 1, 2, ..., T: Receive new dataset Dt = {(xi, yi)} -- Step 1: Generate pseudo-samples from previous scholar for j = 1 to m: x'j ← Gt−1(zj) -- z ~ N(0, I), sample from prior generator y'j ← St−1(x'j) -- label via prior solver D't = {(x'j, y'j)} -- Step 2: Combine real and replayed data Dcombined = Dt ∪ D't -- mix ratio is a hyperparameter -- Step 3: Train new generator G_t Train Gt on Dcombined (adversarial loss for GAN) -- Step 4: Train new solver S_t Train St on Dcombined (task loss, e.g. cross-entropy) Scholart ← (Gt, St)

Loss Functions

Generator Loss (GAN objective)

Generator: LG = −Ez~p(z)[log D(G(z))] Discriminator: LD = −Ex~pdata[log D(x)] − Ez~p(z)[log(1 − D(G(z)))] The generator is trained on the combined data distribution: x ~ pcombined = mixture of real data from task t and pseudo-data from Gt−1

Solver Loss

LS = −(1/n) Σi [yi log S(xi) + (1−yi) log(1−S(xi))] computed over both real samples from task t and pseudo-samples from Gt−1.

Code Repositories

kuc2477/pytorch-deep-generative-replay GMvandeVen/continual-learning GMvandeVen/brain-inspired-replay hursung1/DeepGenerativeReplay

Key Follow-Up Work

  • Brain-Inspired Replay (BI-R): van de Ven et al. (NeurIPS 2020) — replaces the GAN with a VAE that shares its decoder with the classifier's internal representation, improving sample efficiency.
  • DDGR: Gao et al. (ICML 2023) — uses diffusion models instead of GANs for higher-fidelity generative replay.
  • DRAGO: Sun et al. (arXiv 2025) — generative replay for continual world models, using synthetic past experiences to retain dynamics knowledge across tasks.
Application to RCWM

For RCWM, the generative replay paradigm maps directly onto the structured latent-variable model's decoder. Rather than storing raw economic time series fragments, train a conditional VAE or normalizing flow in the RCWM's latent space to generate synthetic past-regime trajectories. The solver is the SPIB-trained encoder + S5 SSM. When a new economic regime arrives, replay synthetic trajectories from the latent generator to maintain the model's ability to recognize prior regimes. The GateL0RD update rules already provide a gating mechanism that can be co-trained with the generator's regime-conditioned outputs. This eliminates the need to store raw market data (addressing data-retention compliance) while maintaining regime memory.

4. Dark Experience Replay (DER / DER++)

Citation

Primary Reference
Pietro Buzzega, Matteo Boschini, Angelo Porrello, Davide Abati, Simone Calderara. "Dark Experience for General Continual Learning: a Strong, Simple Baseline." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 33, 2020. arXiv: 2004.07211

Key Insight: Store Logits, Not Just Labels

Standard experience replay stores input-label pairs (x, y) in the buffer. DER stores input-logit pairs (x, g) where g = fθ(x) is the full output logit vector at the time the example was stored. This captures the model's "dark knowledge" — its full predictive distribution over all classes, not just the hard label — analogous to Hinton et al.'s knowledge distillation (2015).

The buffer is managed via reservoir sampling (Section 1), storing tuples (x, g, y) where g is the logit snapshot and y is the ground-truth label.

DER Loss Function

LDER(θ) = (1/|B|) Σ(x,y)∈B l(fθ(x), y) + (α/|M|) Σ(xm, gm)∈M ‖fθ(xm) − gm‖22 where: B = current minibatch of new data M = minibatch sampled from replay buffer l = cross-entropy loss fθ(x) = model's current logit output for input x gm = stored logit vector (dark knowledge) from when xm was added α = weight for logit-matching regularization

DER++ Loss Function

DER++ extends DER by adding a supervised loss on the replay buffer's ground-truth labels:

LDER++(θ) = (1/|B|) Σ(x,y)∈B l(fθ(x), y) + (α/|M|) Σ(xm, gm)∈M ‖fθ(xm) − gm‖22 + (β/|M|) Σ(xm, ym)∈M l(fθ(xm), ym) where: Term 1: cross-entropy on current task data (learn new) Term 2: MSE logit-matching on buffered dark knowledge (functional regularization) Term 3: cross-entropy on buffered ground-truth labels (rehearsal) α, β = hyperparameters controlling the balance The three terms balance plasticity (term 1) against two forms of stability: - α-term: soft consistency with past model behavior (functional space) - β-term: hard consistency with past correct answers (label space)

Algorithm

-- DER++ (Buzzega et al. 2020) Initialize model fθ, reservoir buffer M of size m for each minibatch B = {(xi, yi)} from stream: -- Forward pass on new data logits ← fθ(xi) loss ← CrossEntropy(logits, yi) -- Sample from replay buffer {(xm, gm, ym)} ← sample from M -- Logit matching (dark knowledge distillation) buf_logits ← fθ(xm) loss += α · MSE(buf_logits, gm) -- Supervised replay (DER++ only) loss += β · CrossEntropy(buf_logits, ym) -- Backprop and update θ ← θ − η ∇θ loss -- Reservoir update: store new examples with current logits for each (xi, yi) in B: gi ← fθ(xi).detach() -- snapshot logits RESERVOIR_ADD(M, (xi, gi, yi)) -- Algorithm R

Code Repositories

aimagelab/mammoth (official) fostiropoulos/stream_benchmark

The Mammoth library (by the DER authors' lab at AImageLab, University of Modena) is the reference implementation and includes DER, DER++, ER, A-GEM, iCaRL, and many other CL methods under a unified framework.

Key Follow-Up

2025 Extension
Taisuke Kobayashi. "Improvements of Dark Experience Replay and Reservoir Sampling towards Better Balance between Consolidation and Plasticity." arXiv: 2504.20932, April 2025. Introduces automatic α/β adaptation, erroneous-replay filtering, and stratified reservoir buffers.
Application to RCWM

DER++ is the single most relevant method for RCWM. The insight of storing logits maps directly onto the RCWM architecture:

  • The "logits" to store are the S5 SSM's latent state predictions and the SPIB fragment-level sufficient statistics (μ, σ2) at the time each fragment was processed.
  • The α-term becomes an MSE loss between the current model's latent predictions on a replayed fragment and the stored sufficient statistics — enforcing functional consistency in the latent space.
  • The β-term becomes the SPIB reconstruction/prediction loss on replayed fragments with their ground-truth economic observables.
  • The GateL0RD update rules' sparsity provides a natural mechanism for which latent dimensions are regularized: only gates that were active when the fragment was stored need logit matching.

This yields a "dark economic experience" replay where the buffer stores (fragment, latent_snapshot, observables) tuples, and the three-term loss balances new-regime learning against both soft (latent-space) and hard (observable-space) consistency.

5. Replay for Time Series, Sequential Data & SSMs

This section surveys recent work (2023–2026) at the intersection of experience replay and sequential/temporal models, which is directly relevant to RCWM's S5 SSM backbone.

Key Papers

5.1   Attention-Based Experience Replay for Time Series Forecasting

Reference
Quentin Besnard, Nicolas Ragot. "Attention-based Experience Replay Framework for Continual Learning of Agnostic Time Series Forecasting Models." CAp & RFIAP 2026, Montpellier, France. arXiv: 2607.20493
Time Series Attention Experience Replay 2026

Method: Extends static forecasting models with an attention-guided experience replay strategy. The attention mechanism dynamically weights which stored time-series segments are most relevant for the current distribution, enabling selective replay that maintains temporal coherence. The framework is model-agnostic — it wraps around existing forecasting architectures.

5.2   Experience Replay Addresses Loss of Plasticity

Reference
Jiuqi Wang, Rohan Chandra, Shangtong Zhang. "Experience Replay Addresses Loss of Plasticity in Continual Learning." arXiv: 2503.20018, March 2025.
Plasticity Transformer Theoretical 2025

Key Finding: Experience replay combined with Transformers eliminates loss of plasticity in continual learning across regression, classification, and policy evaluation — without architectural modifications. The effect is attributed to in-context learning capabilities. This is significant for RCWM because it suggests that replay is not just a forgetting-prevention mechanism but actively maintains the network's ability to learn new regimes.

5.3   ODEStream: Buffer-Free Streaming Time Series

Reference
Futoon M. Abushaqra, Hao Xue, Yongli Ren, Flora D. Salim. "ODEStream: A Buffer-Free Online Learning Framework with ODE-based Adaptor for Streaming Time Series Forecasting." arXiv: 2411.07413, November 2024.
Neural ODE Buffer-Free Streaming 2024

Method: Uses neural ODEs as continuous-time adaptors that learn evolving dynamics without maintaining a replay buffer. Features a temporal isolation layer capturing temporal dependencies and handling irregularly-sampled data. Represents a complementary approach to replay — continuous adaptation via the ODE structure itself.

5.4   Class-Incremental Learning for Time Series: Benchmark

Reference
Zhongzheng Qiao, Quang Pham, Zhen Cao, Hoang H. Le, P.N. Suganthan, Xudong Jiang, Ramasamy Savitha. "Class-incremental Learning for Time Series: Benchmark and Evaluation." Proceedings of ACM SIGKDD, ADS track, 2024. arXiv: 2402.12035
Benchmark Time Series CIL KDD 2024

Key Finding: In time series class-incremental learning, experience replay proves to be the most effective approach when storage is not constrained, outperforming regularization and architecture-based methods. This validates replay as the primary anti-forgetting strategy for temporal data.

5.5   SuRe: Surprise-Driven Prioritised Replay for LLMs

Reference
Hugo Hazard, Zafeirios Fountas, Martin A. Benfeghoul, Adnan Oomerjee, Jun Wang, Haitham Bou-Ammar. "SuRe: Surprise-Driven Prioritised Replay for Continual LLM Learning." arXiv: 2511.22367, November 2025.
LLM Surprise Prioritized Replay 2025

Method: Ranks and stores the most surprising (high negative log-likelihood) sequences for replay. Introduces a dual-learner framework combining fast and slow LoRA adapters with exponential moving average (EMA) merging. Achieves +5 accuracy points over prior SOTA on continual LLM benchmarks. The surprise-based selection principle generalizes the PER concept (Section 2) from TD-error to NLL, applicable to any sequential model.

5.6   Abrupt Representation Change in Online CL

Reference
Lucas Caccia, Rahaf Aljundi, Nader Asadi, Tinne Tuytelaars, Joelle Pineau, Eugene Belilovsky. "New Insights on Reducing Abrupt Representation Change in Online Continual Learning." ICLR 2022. arXiv: 2104.05025
Representation Drift Asymmetric Update ICLR 2022

Key Insight: Experience Replay causes representations of new classes to overlap excessively with previous ones at task boundaries, triggering highly disruptive parameter updates. The solution is an asymmetric update rule that encourages new representations to adapt toward established ones rather than forcing older representations to shift. Directly relevant to RCWM's regime transitions, where new economic regimes should be represented in a way compatible with (not destructive to) existing regime encodings.

5.7   DRAGO: Continual World Models with Generative Replay

Reference
Yixiang Sun, Haotian Fu, Michael Littman, George Konidaris. "Knowledge Retention for Continual Model-Based Reinforcement Learning." arXiv: 2503.04256, March 2025.
World Model Generative Replay MBRL 2025

Method: DRAGO enables agents to develop world models progressively across multiple tasks. Combines: (1) synthetic past experiences via generative models to reinforce previously learned dynamics without data retention, and (2) intrinsic motivation for exploration of relevant prior states. This is the closest existing work to what RCWM needs — a continual world model with generative replay for dynamics retention.

Critical Gap: Replay for State Space Models

As of August 2026, there is no published work specifically addressing experience replay for S4/S5/Mamba-class state space models in continual learning settings. The existing CL-for-SSM literature focuses on:

  • Using SSMs (Mamba) as the backbone architecture for continual learning tasks (SS4Rec, Chen et al. 2025), without addressing the replay mechanism
  • Streaming/online learning for time series using ODEs (ODEStream) or simple fine-tuning, without structured replay

This represents a genuine invention surface for the RCWM program. The key technical challenge is that SSMs maintain continuous latent states that evolve through the sequence — naive replay of isolated fragments disrupts the state trajectory. Solutions must either:

  1. Store and restore the SSM's hidden state at fragment boundaries (analogous to storing LSTM hidden states)
  2. Use "warm-up" prefixes before replayed fragments to re-initialize the hidden state
  3. Develop a generative model over hidden-state trajectories (combining DGR with DER++ in state space)
Synthesis for RCWM

The recommended replay architecture for RCWM combines elements from all five methods:

  • Buffer management: Stratified reservoir sampling (Section 1) with per-timescale reservoirs
  • Sampling policy: SPIB-error-prioritized sampling (Section 2) with IS correction
  • Storage format: Dark experience tuples (Section 4) storing (fragment, S5_hidden_state, SPIB_sufficient_statistics, observables)
  • Generative augmentation: Latent-space generative replay (Section 3) for rare-regime synthesis when buffer capacity is exhausted
  • State continuity: Warm-up prefixes or stored S5 hidden states at fragment boundaries to maintain temporal coherence (Section 5 gap)

This "Dark Generative Prioritized Reservoir Replay" (DGPRR) would be novel in the literature and directly addresses the multi-timescale, non-stationary, regime-switching nature of economic state estimation.

6. Synthesis: Unified Replay Architecture for RCWM

Proposed Loss Function

LRCWM(θ) = LSPIB(B; θ) + α · (1/|M|) Σm∈M ŵm ‖ hθ(xm) − ĥm ‖22 + β · (1/|M|) Σm∈M ŵm LSPIB(xm, om; θ) + γ · Lgen(φ) where: B = current economic data fragment M = replay buffer sample (prioritized, IS-corrected) ŵm = normalized IS weight for sample m (PER, Section 2) hθ(xm) = S5 SSM latent state prediction on replayed fragment ĥm = stored dark latent state (DER++, Section 4) om = stored ground-truth observables Lgen = generative replay loss for rare-regime synthesis (DGR, Section 3) Term 1: Learn the current economic regime (plasticity) Term 2: Latent-space dark knowledge match (soft stability) Term 3: Observable-space supervised replay (hard stability) Term 4: Generative model for regime coverage (distributional stability)

Buffer Tuple Format

Each buffer entry stores: (xfrag, hdark, μSPIB, σ2SPIB, oobs, τscale, gmask) xfrag : raw economic fragment (time series window) hdark : S5 hidden state snapshot at fragment end (dark knowledge) μ, σ2 : SPIB sufficient statistics at storage time oobs : ground-truth economic observables τscale : timescale identifier (tick / daily / monthly / cycle) gmask : GateL0RD active-gate binary mask (for selective regularization)

A comprehensive survey of sequential change-detection methods: mathematical foundations, algorithmic detail, code availability, and applicability to multivariate continuous economic data streams.

Section 1

ADWIN: Adaptive Windowing

"Learning from Time-Changing Data with Adaptive Windowing" Albert Bifet and Ricard Gavalda
Proceedings of the 2007 SIAM International Conference on Data Mining (SDM 2007), pp. 443–448. SIAM, 2007.
DOI: 10.1137/1.9781611972771.42

A second, more detailed treatment appears in:

"Adaptive Learning from Evolving Data Streams" Albert Bifet and Ricard Gavalda
Advances in Intelligent Data Analysis VIII (IDA 2009), LNCS 5772, pp. 249–260. Springer, 2009.

Core Idea

ADWIN maintains a variable-length window W of the most recent elements from a data stream. At every step, it tests whether any partition of the current window into two contiguous sub-windows W_0 (older) and W_1 (newer) exhibits a statistically significant difference in their means. When such a difference is found, the older portion is discarded (the window shrinks). When no difference is found and a new element arrives, the window simply grows by one.

Algorithm Detail

The Naive Version (ADWIN0)

Given a confidence parameter δ, at each time step consider every possible cut of the window W into two sub-windows W_0 and W_1. For each cut, compute the means μ̂_0 and μ̂_1. If for any cut:

|μ̂_0 - μ̂_1| ≥ εcut

where εcut is a threshold derived from a Hoeffding-style bound, then drop the oldest elements (everything in W_0). The cut-specific threshold is:

εcut = sqrt( (1/2m) · ln(4/δ') ) where: m = harmonic mean: 1/m = 1/(2n_0) + 1/(2n_1) n_0 = |W_0|, n_1 = |W_1| δ' = δ / ln(n) (Bonferroni correction over ~ln(n) cuts) n = |W| = n_0 + n_1

This is O(n) per step because every possible partition must be tested. Unacceptable for streaming.

The Efficient Version (ADWIN2): Exponential Histograms

ADWIN uses an exponential histogram (Datar et al., 2002) to compress the window. The key data structure maintains a sequence of buckets of exponentially increasing sizes. Each bucket stores:

  • The count of elements in that bucket
  • The sum of element values in that bucket
  • The variance (sum of squares) for the bucket

Bucket sizes are powers of 2: the most recent buckets have size 1, then 2, then 4, etc. The constraint is that there are at most M buckets of each size (where M is a parameter, typically M = ceil(1/ε) + 1 for the memory precision parameter ε). When a new element arrives:

ADWIN2-UPDATE(new_element x_t): 1. Insert x_t as a new bucket of size 1 at the head 2. COMPRESS: merge adjacent same-size buckets if count exceeds M // Two size-k buckets merge into one size-2k bucket // Merging propagates: like carry in binary addition 3. CHECK-FOR-CHANGE: For each bucket boundary (representing a partition W_0 | W_1): Compute μ̂_0, μ̂_1 from bucket aggregates If |μ̂_0 - μ̂_1| ≥ εcut: Delete all buckets older than the cut point return CHANGE_DETECTED return NO_CHANGE

Because there are at most O(M log n) buckets, step 3 checks only O(log n) partitions rather than O(n). Total amortized cost per element: O(log(n/δ)) time and O(log n) memory.

Theoretical Guarantees

Theorem (Bifet & Gavalda 2007, Theorem 1)

ADWIN provides the following guarantees simultaneously, for a stream of values in [0, 1]:

(i) False positive bound: If the distribution generating the data in the window has not changed, the probability that ADWIN shrinks the window is at most δ.

(ii) False negative bound: Suppose at some point the distribution generating elements in W_0 has mean μ_0 and the distribution generating elements in W_1 has mean μ_1 with |μ_0 - μ_1| > 2εcut. Then with probability at least 1 - δ, ADWIN will shrink the window.

(iii) Window size: At every time step, the length of W is upper-bounded (in expectation and with high probability) by 4/μt2 · ln(2/δ') where μt is the mean-difference at the true change point.

In essence, the window length adapts: it is long during stationary periods (accumulating more data for statistical power) and short after a change (flushing stale data quickly). The parameter δ controls the confidence: smaller δ means fewer false alarms but slower detection.

Key Parameters

  • δ (delta): confidence parameter. Typical values: 0.002 (the default in MOA/river). Controls the probability of false alarms. Smaller δ → larger εcut → fewer false positives but slower to detect real drift.
  • M (max_buckets): controls the compression granularity of the exponential histogram. Higher M → more accurate mean estimates at the cost of more memory.

Relevance to Economic World Models

ADWIN monitors a single scalar stream. For economic world models, it can be applied to a derived univariate summary (e.g., prediction error, a rolling log-likelihood, or a single economic indicator). It cannot directly detect changes in the joint distribution of a multivariate system. However, it is the standard building block: many multivariate approaches run one ADWIN per feature or apply ADWIN to a projected scalar summary statistic.

Code Availability

river (Python) river.drift.ADWIN

scikit-multiflow skmultiflow.drift_detection.ADWIN

Also implemented in MOA (Java) — the original reference implementation by the authors.

Section 2

Page-Hinkley Test

"Continuous Inspection Schemes" E. S. Page
Biometrika, 41(1/2):100–115, 1954.
DOI: 10.2307/2333009

The Page-Hinkley (PH) test is a sequential analysis technique derived from the CUSUM (Cumulative Sum) framework. It is designed to detect a change in the mean of a Gaussian sequence. Unlike ADWIN, it does not maintain a window; it accumulates a statistic from the beginning of the stream (or from the last detected change point).

Mathematical Formulation

Given a sequence of observations x_1, x_2, ..., x_T, maintain the running mean and a cumulative deviation statistic:

Running mean: x̄T = (1/T) · ∑t=1..T x_t Cumulative sum statistic: mT = ∑t=1..T (x_t - x̄T - δ) Minimum of cumulative sum: MT = mint=1..T mt Detection rule (Page-Hinkley test): PHT = mT - MT Signal drift when PHT > λ

Parameters

  • δ (delta, also called the "magnitude threshold"): the minimum magnitude of change to detect. It controls sensitivity. Setting δ too small leads to many false alarms; too large and small changes are missed. Typical values: 0.005 to 0.05 depending on the scale of data.
  • λ (lambda, the detection threshold): controls the trade-off between detection delay and false alarm rate. Larger λ means fewer false alarms but longer detection delay.
  • α (forgetting factor): some implementations use an exponential weighting x̄T = α · x̄T-1 + (1-α) · x_T instead of the true running mean, to give more weight to recent observations.

Algorithm (Pseudocode)

PAGE-HINKLEY-TEST(stream): Initialize: T ← 0, m ← 0, M ← +∞, sum ← 0 for each x_t in stream: T ← T + 1 sum ← sum + x_t x_bar ← sum / T m ← m + (x_t - x_bar - δ) M ← min(M, m) if (m - M) > λ: signal CHANGE_DETECTED // Reset: T ← 0, m ← 0, M ← +∞, sum ← 0

Detection of Decrease

The formulation above detects an increase in the mean. To detect a decrease, replace (x_t - x̄T - δ) with (x̄T - x_t - δ), or equivalently, negate the input stream. The standard implementations in river/scikit-multiflow provide a mode parameter for this.

Theoretical Basis

Property (Page 1954)

Under H_0 (no change in mean), the statistic PH_T = m_T - M_T fluctuates near zero. Under H_1 (the mean increases by at least δ at some unknown time τ), the statistic m_T will trend upward for t > τ, eventually exceeding M_T + λ. The expected detection delay (the Average Run Length under H_1, or ARL_1) decreases as δ increases relative to the true change magnitude, and increases with λ.

The false alarm rate (1/ARL_0 under H_0) can be controlled by choosing λ via the relationship for Gaussian data: ARL_0 ≈ exp(λ · h(δ, σ)) where h is a function of the normalized change magnitude.

Relevance to Economic World Models

The Page-Hinkley test monitors a single scalar stream. It detects changes in the mean, making it suitable for monitoring prediction error, residuals, or a single economic indicator. For multivariate data, one must either (a) run parallel PH tests on each dimension (losing correlation information) or (b) apply it to a scalar summary. Its advantage over ADWIN is simplicity and well-understood statistical properties; its disadvantage is that it only detects mean shifts (not changes in variance or higher moments).

Section 3

DDM: Drift Detection Method

"Learning with Drift Detection" Joao Gama, Pedro Medas, Gladys Castillo, and Pedro Rodrigues
Advances in Artificial Intelligence — SBIA 2004. 17th Brazilian Symposium on Artificial Intelligence, LNAI 3171, pp. 286–295. Springer, 2004.
DOI: 10.1007/978-3-540-28645-5_29

Core Idea

DDM monitors the error rate of a learning algorithm on a stream of classification decisions. Under the assumption that the error rate of a learner on stationary data will decrease (or remain stable) as more examples are seen, a significant increase in the error rate signals concept drift.

The method models the stream of prediction results (0 = correct, 1 = error) as a Bernoulli process. At each time step i, it tracks:

pi = error rate up to time i = (number of errors) / i si = standard deviation = sqrt(pi · (1 - pi) / i)

Algorithm

DDM(stream of predictions): Initialize: p_min ← ∞, s_min ← ∞ n ← 0, error_count ← 0 for each prediction ŷ_t with true label y_t: n ← n + 1 if ŷ_t ≠ y_t: error_count ← error_count + 1 p_i ← error_count / n s_i ← sqrt(p_i * (1 - p_i) / n) if p_i + s_i < p_min + s_min: p_min ← p_i s_min ← s_i // Record minimum (best performance so far) // WARNING LEVEL: if p_i + s_i ≥ p_min + 2 · s_min: signal WARNING // Start storing examples for retraining // DRIFT LEVEL: if p_i + s_i ≥ p_min + 3 · s_min: signal DRIFT_DETECTED // Reset learner; retrain from warning-point examples // Reset: n ← 0, error_count ← 0, p_min ← ∞, s_min ← ∞

Theoretical Justification

Statistical Basis

For a Bernoulli random variable with parameter p, the Central Limit Theorem gives that p̂n is approximately Gaussian with mean p and standard deviation sqrt(p(1-p)/n) for large n. The "2σ" and "3σ" thresholds correspond to approximately 95% and 99.7% confidence bounds respectively. A stationary learner will have p_i + s_i decreasing (because s_i ∼ 1/sqrt(n)), so the minimum p_min + s_min tracks the best-case error rate. When drift occurs and errors increase, p_i + s_i departs upward from this minimum.

Strengths and Weaknesses

  • Strength: Simple, low memory, well-suited for classification streams.
  • Weakness: Only monitors binary error streams — it does not work directly with continuous-valued data. Requires a classifier in the loop.
  • Weakness: Insensitive to gradual drift. Because it tracks the cumulative error rate from the start, the accumulated mass of correct predictions dilutes the signal from recent errors.
  • Weakness: The 3σ threshold is derived from the CLT, which requires n to be reasonably large; for very small streams or rare classes, the Gaussian approximation is poor.

Code Availability

river (Python) river.drift.DDM

scikit-multiflow skmultiflow.drift_detection.DDM

Section 4

EDDM: Early Drift Detection Method

"Early Drift Detection Method" Manuel Baena-Garcia, Jose del Campo-Avila, Raul Fidalgo, Albert Bifet, Ricard Gavalda, and Rafael Morales-Bueno
Fourth International Workshop on Knowledge Discovery from Data Streams (IWKDDS 2006), held at ECML-PKDD 2006, Berlin, Germany, 2006.
Available from the authors' websites and in the MOA framework documentation.

Improvement Over DDM

EDDM's key insight is that monitoring the distance between consecutive classification errors is more sensitive to gradual drift than monitoring the error rate itself. Under a stationary distribution, as the learner improves, the distance between errors should increase (errors become rarer). When drift begins, errors cluster closer together before the overall rate visibly increases.

Algorithm

Let d_i be the number of examples between the (i-1)-th and i-th classification error. EDDM monitors the mean and standard deviation of these inter-error distances:

p'i = mean distance between errors up to the i-th error s'i = standard deviation of inter-error distances
EDDM(stream of predictions): Initialize: n_errors ← 0, last_error_pos ← 0 sum_distances ← 0, sum_sq_distances ← 0 p'_max + s'_max ← 0 // track maximum of (p' + 2s') for each prediction ŷ_t (at position t) with true label y_t: if ŷ_t ≠ y_t: // error occurred n_errors ← n_errors + 1 d ← t - last_error_pos // distance since last error last_error_pos ← t // Update running mean and std of distances sum_distances ← sum_distances + d sum_sq_distances ← sum_sq_distances + d² p'_i ← sum_distances / n_errors s'_i ← sqrt(sum_sq_distances/n_errors - p'_i²) if n_errors > 30: // need enough errors for statistics if p'_i + 2*s'_i > p'_max + 2*s'_max: p'_max ← p'_i s'_max ← s'_i // WARNING LEVEL: if (p'_i + 2*s'_i) / (p'_max + 2*s'_max) < α: signal WARNING // Typically α = 0.95 // DRIFT LEVEL: if (p'_i + 2*s'_i) / (p'_max + 2*s'_max) < β: signal DRIFT_DETECTED // Typically β = 0.90 // Reset everything

Intuition

Key Property

Under stationary data, the distance between errors increases over time (the learner improves), so p' + 2s' is increasing. When drift sets in, errors begin to cluster — the inter-error distance shrinks — and p' + 2s' drops below its historical maximum. A drop to 95% of the maximum triggers a warning; a drop to 90% triggers a drift signal. This detects gradual drift earlier than DDM because the inter-error distance is a leading indicator of increasing error rate.

Relevance to Economic World Models

Same fundamental limitation as DDM: requires a binary error stream from a classifier. Not directly applicable to continuous multivariate data. Could potentially be adapted by thresholding a continuous loss into "acceptable" vs. "anomalous" predictions, but this introduces an arbitrary binarization step.

Code Availability

river (Python) river.drift.EDDM

scikit-multiflow skmultiflow.drift_detection.EDDM

Section 5

KSWIN: Kolmogorov-Smirnov Windowing

"Reactive Soft Prototype Computing for Concept Drift Streams" Christoph Raab, Moritz Heusinger, and Frank-Michael Schleif
Neurocomputing, 416:340–351, 2020.
DOI: 10.1016/j.neucom.2019.11.111

Note: The KSWIN method is also described in the context of the scikit-multiflow library. A related treatment appears in:

"KSWIN — Kolmogorov-Smirnov Windowing" Christoph Raab, Moritz Heusinger, and Frank-Michael Schleif
Described in the scikit-multiflow documentation and related workshop presentations, 2019–2020.

Core Idea

Unlike DDM/EDDM (which require binary error streams) and unlike ADWIN/Page-Hinkley (which test for mean shifts), KSWIN uses the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to compare the distributions of data in two sliding windows. This makes it capable of detecting any change in the marginal distribution of a continuous-valued stream, not just changes in the mean.

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test

The two-sample KS test compares the empirical CDFs of two samples. Given samples X = {x_1, ..., x_n} and Y = {y_1, ..., y_m}, the KS statistic is:

Dn,m = supz |F̂X(z) - F̂Y(z)| where F̂X(z) = (1/n) · #{x_i ≤ z} is the empirical CDF of X.

The null hypothesis (both samples come from the same distribution) is rejected at significance level α when:

Dn,m > c(α) · sqrt((n + m) / (n · m)) where c(α) = sqrt(-ln(α/2) / 2) (from the Kolmogorov distribution)

KSWIN Algorithm

KSWIN(stream, window_size=W, stat_size=S, α): // W: total reference window size (e.g., 100) // S: recent "test" sub-window size (e.g., 30), S < W // α: significance level for the KS test (e.g., 0.005) Initialize: window ← first W elements from stream for each new element x_t: Append x_t to window; remove oldest element (sliding) // Split window into reference and test R ← window[0 : W-S] // older reference portion T ← window[W-S : W] // newer test portion // Two-sample KS test (D, p_value) ← KS_2sample_test(R, T) if p_value < α: signal DRIFT_DETECTED // Reset window to contain only the test portion T window ← T

Strengths for Continuous Data

Key Advantage

The KS test is a nonparametric, distribution-free test. It detects any change in the underlying distribution — shifts in mean, variance, skewness, or any other distributional property. This makes KSWIN fundamentally more powerful than ADWIN or Page-Hinkley for continuous data streams where changes may not be limited to mean shifts.

Limitation: Univariate Only

The classical KS test is defined for univariate distributions only. While multivariate generalizations exist (Fasano & Franceschini 1987; Peacock 1983), they are computationally expensive (O(n^2) or worse) and do not have clean distribution-free critical values. KSWIN as implemented in river/scikit-multiflow handles a single scalar stream.

Code Availability

river (Python) river.drift.KSWIN

scikit-multiflow skmultiflow.drift_detection.KSWIN
