2.3 Constraint Fields (Φ)

Definition 2.3 (Constraint Field)

The constraint field Φ(t) = (Φ_reg(t), Φ_liq(t), Φ_phy(t), Φ_acc(t)) is a 4-layer structure:

  • Φ_reg — Regulatory constraints: capital requirements (Basel III/IV), position limits, short-sale bans, circuit breakers. Formalized via IG 2.0 / ADICO grammar (Crawford & Ostrom 1995).
  • Φ_liq — Liquidity constraints: margin requirements, funding availability, collateral haircuts, market depth. These are endogenous—they tighten under stress.
  • Φ_phy — Physical constraints: settlement cycles (T+1/T+2), network latency, computational limits, storage capacity for commodities.
  • Φ_acc — Accounting constraints: double-entry identities, balance sheet mechanics (assets = liabilities + equity), flow-of-funds consistency. These are inviolable—they hold by definition.

Constraint fields interact with the construction operator C by projection: any proposed next state W'(t+1) is projected onto the feasible set F(Φ(t)) = {W : Φ_reg(W) ≤ 0 ∧ Φ_liq(W) ≤ 0 ∧ Φ_phy(W) ≤ 0 ∧ Φ_acc(W) = 0}. The projection is not optional—it is load-bearing. Violations of accounting identities are not “small errors”; they are incoherent states.

2.4 Reflexive Loops (RL)

Definition 2.4 (Reflexive Loop)

A reflexive loop is the cyclic dependency B → A → ΔW → ΔB where beliefs drive actions, actions change the world, and the changed world updates beliefs. The reflexivity coefficient ε measures the sensitivity:

ε = sup_(θ, θ') || D(θ) - D(θ') ||_W / || θ - θ' ||

where D(θ) is the data distribution induced when agents act on model parameters θ, and ||·||_W is the Wasserstein-1 distance. This is exactly the “ε-sensitivity” of Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020, Def. 3.1). When ε is large, the model strongly affects the data it learns from—the hallmark of financial markets where published forecasts, algorithmic strategies, and central bank guidance all reshape the very quantities they predict.

2.5 Composition Operators

Definition 2.5 (Fragment Composition)

The tensor product WF_a ⊗ WF_b → WF_{ab} composes two world fragments into a joint fragment, satisfying three axioms:

  1. Associativity: (WF_a ⊗ WF_b) ⊗ WF_c = WF_a ⊗ (WF_b ⊗ WF_c)
  2. Constraint preservation: Φ(WF_a ⊗ WF_b) ⊆ Φ(WF_a) ∩ Φ(WF_b) (composition cannot relax constraints)
  3. Scale consistency: τ_{ab} = min(τ_a, τ_b) (the composite updates at the faster timescale)

Composition operators enable hierarchical world construction. A “market microstructure” fragment composes tick-level and order-book fragments. A “credit conditions” fragment composes institutional-state and flow fragments. The composition is not concatenation—it creates genuine interaction terms through the coupling functions ρ.

3Belief Fields

Beliefs are not static parameters—they form a field over the space of constructive units, evolving through a combination of private updating and social contagion.

b_i(t+1) = (1 - α) · U(b_i(t), o_i(t)) + α · Σ_j w_{ij} · b_j(t)

where:

  • U(b, o) — private Bayesian update of belief b given observation o (or an approximate update via a learned recognition model)
  • α ∈ [0,1] — social influence weight (how much agent i is swayed by others’ beliefs)
  • w_{ij} — influence weight from agent j to agent i, typically sparse (most agents don’t directly observe each other)
  • o_i(t) — agent i’s observation at time t, which depends on W(t) and the agent’s observation function

Definition 3.1 (Belief Coherence)

The coherence measure χ(t) = 1 - (1/N(N-1)) Σ_{i≠j} D_KL(b_i(t) || b_j(t)) ranges from 0 (complete disagreement) to 1 (consensus). Low coherence signals fragile markets; high coherence signals herding risk.

The social influence term connects to Morris and Shin’s global games framework (AER 2002): when agents share a strong common signal, coherence spikes, and actions correlate—producing the coordination cascades observed in currency crises, bank runs, and liquidity spirals. The weight matrix w_{ij} can be learned from observed co-movement patterns using DCC-GARCH (Engle 2002) or network inference methods.

4Reflexive Fixed Points

A reflexive fixed point is a pair (B*, W*) satisfying:

B* = U(B*, W*)     and     W* = C(W*, A(B*), Φ)

This is the performative stable point (Perdomo et al. 2020, Def. 3.2): the model parameters at which retraining on the distribution they induce produces the same parameters. Existence requires the composed map F = U ˆ C ˆ A to be a contraction.

Stability Analysis

Linearize around the fixed point. Let δB = B - B* and δW = W - W*. The Jacobian of the coupled system is:

J = ∂(B(t+1), W(t+1)) / ∂(B(t), W(t)) =
[ (1-α) · ∂U/∂b + αW , (1-α) · ∂U/∂o · ∂o/∂W ]
[ ∂C/∂A · ∂A/∂B , ∂C/∂W ]

Stability requires ρ(J) < 1 where ρ denotes spectral radius. The off-diagonal blocks encode reflexivity: ∂C/∂A · ∂A/∂B is the “beliefs shape the world” channel; ∂U/∂o · ∂o/∂W is the “world shapes beliefs” channel. Their product controls stability.

Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner & Hardt (ICML 2020). “Performative Prediction.” Theorem 3.5: Repeated Risk Minimization converges to a performative stable point if ε < γ/β, where ε is sensitivity, γ is strong convexity, and β is smoothness of the loss. Proposition 3.6 proves the bound is tight.
Attribution warning. The convergence condition ε < γ/β is Theorem 3.5 of Perdomo et al. ICML 2020, not the survey by Hardt & Mendler-Dünner (Statistical Science 2025). The survey cites this result but does not originate it. A referee would catch this.

5World Models: Theoretical Lineage

RecWM inherits ideas from four lines of research in deep learning-based world models, while extending each in fundamental ways.

Ha & Schmidhuber (2018) — “World Models”

Introduced the V-M-C architecture: a Vision model (VAE) compresses observations, a Memory model (MDN-RNN) predicts future latent states, and a Controller selects actions. Key insight: you can train the controller entirely inside the learned dream. Limitation: untyped latent space, no constraint enforcement, no reflexivity. (NeurIPS 2018)

Dreamer / DreamerV2 / DreamerV3 (Hafner et al. 2020–2023)

Replaced the MDN-RNN with a Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM): a deterministic path plus a stochastic branch, enabling long-horizon imagination. DreamerV3 introduced symlog predictions, free bits for KL balancing, and showed a single architecture could master 150+ tasks without tuning. Limitation: single homogeneous latent state; no multi-timescale fragments. (ICLR 2020, NeurIPS 2021, arXiv 2023)

JEPA — LeCun (2022)

Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture: instead of predicting raw observations (pixel-level), predict in latent space. Avoids the generative model’s curse of modelling irrelevant detail. Limitation: no notion of actions or interventions; static architecture. (Position paper, Meta AI)

State Space Models: S4, S5, Mamba

Gu et al. (2022) S4 showed structured state spaces can model long-range dependencies with O(N log N) complexity. S5 (Smith et al. 2023) simplified to parallel scan over diagonal A, enabling O(N) training. Mamba (Gu & Dao 2024) added input-dependent selection. Limitation: untyped, single timescale, no constraint awareness. (ICLR 2022, ICLR 2023, arXiv 2024)

How RecWM extends these. (1) Typed fragments replace the homogeneous latent state, each with its own timescale and schema. (2) Constraint fields are first-class objects, not post-hoc projections. (3) Reflexivity is modelled explicitly: the loop B → A → ΔW → ΔB is the architecture, not a nuisance. (4) Continual learning is native: financial regimes change, so the model must update without catastrophic forgetting.

6State Space Models: S5 Typed-Delta Backbone

RecWM uses S5 (Smith et al. 2023) as the backbone dynamics model, but with a critical extension: typed discretization step sizes matched to fragment timescales.

Continuous Form

dh/dt = A · h(t) + B · u(t)
y(t) = Re(C · h(t)) + D · u(t)

where h(t) ∈ C^N is the hidden state, u(t) is the input, y(t) is the output, and A is diagonal (the key S5 simplification from S4’s DPLR parameterization).

ZOH Discretization with Typed Step Sizes

The standard zero-order hold (ZOH) discretization uses a uniform step size Δ. RecWM replaces this with fragment-typed step sizes:

A_k = exp(A · Δ_k),    B_k = A^{-1}(A_k - I) · B

where Δ_k = τ_k / τ_max is the normalized timescale for fragment type k. This means tick-level fragments update with fine temporal resolution while narrative fragments use coarse steps—matching the natural dynamics of each.

Fragment Typeτ (seconds)Δ_k (normalized)Effective Horizon
Tick0.001–1~10^{-8}Next milliseconds
Microstructure1–300~10^{-5}Next minutes
Price60–86400~10^{-3}Next hours–day
Flow3600–604800~10^{-2}Next days–week
Macro604800–7.9×10^6~10^{-1}Next weeks–quarter
Institutional2.6×10^6–3.15×10^7~0.5Next months–year
Narrative604800–3.15×10^71.0Next weeks–years
Why diagonal A enables O(N) RTRL. With diagonal A, the Jacobian ∂h(t)/∂h(t-1) = diag(A_k) is diagonal, so real-time recurrent learning (RTRL) requires only O(N) per step instead of O(N^3). This is critical for continual learning (Section 11): the model can update online without ever unrolling through time.

7GateL0RD Fragment Updates

Not every fragment should update at every timestep. The GateL0RD mechanism (Gumbsch, Butz & Martius, NeurIPS 2021) provides a principled way to learn when to update each fragment, using hard-concrete gates with L0 regularization.

Hard-Concrete Sampling

The gate variable g(t) ∈ {0, 1} is sampled from a stretched hard-concrete distribution:

u ~ Uniform(0, 1)
s = sigmoid((log(u/(1-u)) + log(α)) / β)
s_bar = s · (ζ - γ) + γ
g = min(1, max(0, s_bar))

where α is a learned location parameter (per fragment), β is a temperature, and γ < 0, ζ > 1 are the stretch parameters ensuring exact zeros and ones.

State Update Rule

z(t) = g(t) · z̃(t) + (1 - g(t)) · z(t-1)

When g(t) = 0, the fragment is perfectly preserved (not approximately—exactly copied). When g(t) = 1, the fragment updates to the new candidate z̃(t). The L0 penalty encourages sparsity:

L_gate = Σ_k λ_k · P(g_k ≠ 0)

where λ_k ∝ τ_k / τ_max: slow fragments (narrative, institutional) are penalized more heavily for updating, naturally encoding the prior that slow things should change rarely.

Gumbsch, Butz & Martius (NeurIPS 2021). “Sparsely Changing Latent States for Prediction and Planning in Partially Observable Domains.” Introduced GateL0RD: L0-gated RNNs that naturally segment temporal sequences into events, with the gate providing interpretable “event boundaries.”

The connection to continual learning is immediate: when a gate is closed, the effective learning rate for that fragment is zero, providing natural protection against catastrophic forgetting without any explicit memory mechanism.

8Information-Theoretic Foundations

Stochastic Predictive Information Bottleneck (SPIB)

The representation for each fragment is trained via the SPIB objective (Wang et al. 2021):

max I(z; state_{t+Δ}) - β · I(z; X_t)

This is a stochastic extension of the Information Bottleneck (Tishby et al. 1999): compress the input X_t into a latent z that is maximally predictive of the future state at horizon Δ, while discarding information about the present that is not predictive. The trade-off parameter β controls compression.

Rate-Distortion Theory

SPIB is a special case of rate-distortion theory (Shannon 1948, Berger 1971). The rate-distortion function R(D) = min_{p(z|x): E[d(x,z)] ≤ D} I(X; Z) gives the minimum number of bits needed to represent the source at distortion level D. In RecWM, “distortion” is prediction error at the fragment’s characteristic horizon.

Why Δ_k = τ_k

A critical design choice: the prediction horizon for each fragment equals its characteristic timescale. This ensures that:

  • Tick fragments predict the next milliseconds (where they have signal)
  • Macro fragments predict the next quarter (where they have signal)
  • No fragment is asked to predict faster or slower than its natural dynamics

VampPrior for the Marginal

The marginal p(z) = (1/K) Σ_k q(z | x_k) is approximated via the Variational Mixture of Posteriors (VampPrior, Tomczak & Welling, AISTATS 2018). This avoids the over-regularization that a standard Gaussian prior causes in VAEs, and naturally clusters the latent space by regime.

9Identifiability and Causal Structure

A world model is only useful if its latent variables correspond to real quantities. RecWM achieves identifiability through four complementary mechanisms.

9.1 Independent Decoders with Sparse Jacobians

Each fragment type k has its own decoder g_k : z_k → x_k. The Jacobian ∂g_k / ∂z is constrained to be sparse: fragment k’s reconstruction depends only on its own latents and a small set of coupling terms. This is the multi-decoder approach of Locatello et al. (ICML 2020), extended with typing.

9.2 SlowVAE Laplace Prior

The SlowVAE (Klindt et al., ICML 2021) imposes a Laplace prior on temporal differences: p(z_t | z_{t-1}) ∝ exp(-|z_t - z_{t-1}| / λ). This biases latent variables toward slow features (Wiskott & Sejnowski 2002), which are identifiable up to component-wise transformations under mild conditions.

Klindt, Schott, Sharma, Ustyuzhaninov, Brendel, Bethge & Paiton (ICML 2021). “Towards Nonlinear Disentanglement in Natural Data with Temporal Sparse Coding.” Proved that slow features in nonlinear ICA are identifiable with Laplace transition priors.

9.3 Structural Sparsity

The causal structure among latent fragments is recovered via structural sparsity constraints. Zheng, Ng & Zhang (NeurIPS 2022) showed that with sparse mixing functions and sufficient diversity in the data, latent causal variables are identifiable from observational data alone. RecWM applies this at the fragment level: the coupling functions ρ_j are regularized toward sparsity.

9.4 Mechanism Sparsity and Causal Emergence

Lachapelle et al. (CLeaR 2022) formalized mechanism sparsity: each causal mechanism depends on few parents. Combined with the independent mechanism principle (Schölkopf et al. 2012), this gives identification of the causal graph from distribution shifts—exactly what regime changes provide in financial data.

Causal emergence is detected via SVD of the fragment interaction matrix: when a set of micro-level fragments can be compressed into a macro-fragment with higher effective information (Liu, Yuan & Zhang, Entropy 2024), the macro-fragment is “more causal” than its components. This provides a principled criterion for fragment hierarchy.

Liu, Yuan & Zhang (Entropy 26(8):618, 2024). “Exact Causal Emergence for Linear Stochastic Iteration Systems.” Closed-form optimal coarse-graining from principal eigenvectors of the transition matrix. Complexity O(n^3) in the number of variables. A “linear stochastic iteration system” is a VAR model.

10The Unified Loss Function

RecWM is trained end-to-end with a composite loss that balances reconstruction, prediction, sparsity, gating, martingale consistency, and cross-fragment coupling:

L = L_recon + Σ_k L_SPIB^{(k)} + α · L_sparsity + Σ_k L_gate^{(k)} + μ · L_MZ + ν · L_coupling

Each term:

TermDefinitionRole
L_recon Σ_k || x_k - g_k(z_k) ||^2 Reconstruction accuracy per fragment type
L_SPIB^{(k)} -I(z_k; state_{t+τ_k}) + β_k · I(z_k; X_t) Predictive compression at fragment timescale
L_sparsity Σ_{j≠k} |∂g_k / ∂z_j| Cross-fragment Jacobian sparsity (identifiability)
L_gate^{(k)} λ_k · P(g_k ≠ 0) GateL0RD L0 penalty, stronger for slow fragments
L_MZ E[(r_t - r_f) · z_t]^2 Martingale / no-arbitrage consistency
L_coupling Σ_{j,k} |ρ_{jk} - ρ̂_{jk}(z)|^2 Cross-fragment coupling accuracy
The martingale term L_MZ is unique to RecWM. It enforces the no-arbitrage principle directly in the loss: under the risk-neutral measure, discounted price processes must be martingales. This is not a soft preference—violations indicate the model has learned a spurious arbitrage that cannot exist in liquid markets.

11Continual Learning Theory

Financial markets are non-stationary by nature. Regimes change, regulations evolve, new instruments appear. RecWM addresses this through a five-layer continual learning stack, each layer providing progressively stronger protection against catastrophic forgetting.

Figure 7. Five-layer continual learning stack. Each layer adds progressively stronger forgetting protection at increasing computational cost. All layers are active simultaneously.

CL-0: GateL0RD Natural Continual Learning

The simplest and cheapest layer. When a gate g_k(t) = 0, the state z_k(t) = z_k(t-1) exactly. Gradients with respect to the parameters of fragment k are multiplied by the gate opening probability p, giving an effective learning rate η_eff = p · η. For slow fragments (narrative, institutional), p is typically 0.01–0.05, providing ~20–100x natural forgetting protection.

CL-1: O(N) RTRL Streaming

Because the S5 backbone has diagonal A, the sensitivity matrix dh(t)/dθ can be maintained in O(N) per timestep via Real-Time Recurrent Learning (Williams & Zipser 1989). This enables true streaming: the model processes each timestep once, updates parameters, and discards the observation. No truncated BPTT, no replay buffer, no epoch.

CL-2: Per-Fragment EWC

Elastic Weight Consolidation (Kirkpatrick et al., PNAS 2017) penalizes movement away from previously important parameters. RecWM applies EWC per fragment, using the online Fisher approximation of Schwarz et al. (2018). The regularization strength λ_k scales with the fragment timescale: slow fragments resist change more.

CL-3: BOCPD + DER++

Bayesian Online Change Point Detection (Adams & MacKay, arXiv 2007) monitors the fragment prediction errors for structural breaks. When a change point is detected with posterior probability > 0.8, the system triggers Dark Experience Replay++ (Buzzega et al. 2020): stored logits from the previous regime are replayed alongside new data, enabling graceful transition without destroying old knowledge.

CL-4: Slow-Fast Weights

A Polyak-averaged “slow” copy of the parameters tracks the long-term structure. The averaging rate adapts: during stable regimes, η_slow → 0 (the slow copy barely moves); at regime transitions, η_slow → 0.01 (the slow copy absorbs the new regime quickly). Inference uses the slow weights for stability, with fast weights contributing residual corrections.

12Financial Mathematics

RecWM is grounded in five pillars of modern financial mathematics, each contributing specific structural constraints or modelling techniques.

12.1 Rough Volatility

Gatheral, Jaisson & Rosenbaum (Quantitative Finance 2018) showed that log-volatility behaves as fractional Brownian motion with Hurst exponent H ≈ 0.1, far rougher than the H = 0.5 of standard Brownian motion. This implies:

log σ(t) ~ fBM_H,    H ≈ 0.1

RecWM’s state-space backbone naturally captures rough dynamics because the diagonal A matrix can represent arbitrary spectral densities, including the power-law spectrum S(f) ∝ f^{-(2H+1)} characteristic of rough processes. The fragment type “microstructure” is specifically designed for this timescale.

Gatheral, Jaisson & Rosenbaum (Quantitative Finance 18(6):933–949, 2018). “Volatility is Rough.” Demonstrated that H ≈ 0.1 across virtually all equity option markets, rendering classical stochastic volatility models (Heston H=0.5) misspecified.

12.2 Regime-Switching Models

Hamilton (Econometrica 1989) introduced Markov-switching models where the economy transitions between discrete regimes (expansion/recession) with state-dependent dynamics. RecWM generalizes this in two ways: (1) regimes are continuous (the narrative fragment, not a discrete label); (2) regime transitions are endogenous (driven by belief field dynamics, not an exogenous Markov chain).

12.3 BOCPD

Adams & MacKay (arXiv 0710.3742, 2007) provided a Bayesian framework for online change point detection with O(E[r]) amortised per-timestep updates, where r is the run length (with pruning to cap worst-case cost; without pruning the naive algorithm is O(t) per step). RecWM uses BOCPD at CL-3 to detect regime transitions in fragment prediction errors, triggering replay and adaptation.

12.4 Online Convex Optimization

Hazan (Foundations and Trends in Optimization 2016) provides the regret framework for online learning. RecWM’s streaming updates achieve sublinear regret R_T = O(sqrt(T)) under the assumption that the loss sequence has bounded variation. The constraint field Φ ensures the decision set is convex at each step.

12.5 Adaptive Kalman Filtering

The S5 backbone can be interpreted as a nonlinear Kalman filter with learned dynamics. The fragment-typed step sizes correspond to different process noise covariances per fragment, and the GateL0RD gates implement an adaptive measurement selection (only incorporating observations when the gate opens).

12.6 Cross-Asset Contagion

RecWM models contagion through the coupling functions ρ_{jk}. Three classical frameworks inform this:

  • DCC-GARCH (Engle 2002): dynamic conditional correlations as time-varying coupling strengths
  • Copulas (Joe 1997, Nelsen 2006): tail dependence beyond linear correlation, especially Clayton/Gumbel for asymmetric crash dependence
  • Network models (Acemoglu et al. 2015): contagion through interconnected balance sheets, where the adjacency matrix is learned from the fragment coupling structure

13Reflexivity and Performativity

Reflexivity is the central intellectual contribution of RecWM. We synthesize three traditions.

13.1 Soros Reflexivity Theory

George Soros (1987, 2013) argued that financial markets are fundamentally reflexive: participants’ biased views influence events, and events influence views, creating a two-way feedback. This was a philosophical claim, not a formal theory. RecWM provides the formalization.

13.2 MacKenzie: An Engine, Not a Camera

Donald MacKenzie (2006) documented how the Black-Scholes model did not merely describe options markets—it created them. Option prices converged toward Black-Scholes predictions as traders adopted the formula, a phenomenon MacKenzie called “Barnesian performativity.” RecWM generalizes this: every model deployed in a market is potentially performative; the reflexivity coefficient ε quantifies how strongly.

MacKenzie (2006). An Engine, Not a Camera: How Financial Models Shape Markets. MIT Press. The foundational sociological account of financial model performativity, documenting how Black-Scholes changed the very markets it claimed to describe.

13.3 Performative Prediction

Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020) formalized performativity in machine learning: when predictions influence the data-generating process, standard ERM assumptions break. Their framework defines:

  • ε-sensitivity (Def. 3.1): the distribution shift per unit parameter change
  • Performative stability (Def. 3.2): the fixed point where retraining reproduces the same model
  • Performative optimality (Def. 3.3): the parameters minimizing true performative risk

13.4 The ε < γ/β Condition

ε < γ / β

This is Theorem 3.5 of Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020): Repeated Risk Minimization converges to a performative stable point if the sensitivity ε is less than the ratio of strong convexity γ to smoothness β. Proposition 3.6 shows the bound is tight. Three distinct thresholds emerge:

ConditionGuaranteeSource
ε < γ/β RRM converges to performative stable point Perdomo et al. 2020, Thm 3.5
ε < γ/[(β+γ)(1+1.5ηβ)] Repeated Gradient Descent converges Perdomo et al. 2020, Thm 3.8
ε ≤ γ/(2β) Performative risk is convex (optimum findable) Miller, Perdomo & Zrnic, ICML 2021, Thm 3.1
The unnamed gap. The region γ/(2β) < ε < γ/β is stable but not optimizable: the system converges to a fixed point, but that fixed point may not minimize performative risk. This gap is unnamed in the literature. We conjecture that real financial markets live in this gap: stable enough to trade, but not optimizable enough for convergence to a social optimum.

13.5 How EWC Reduces Effective Reflexivity

EWC (CL-2) has an unexpected benefit for reflexivity. By penalizing large parameter changes, EWC reduces ||θ_{t+1} - θ_t||, which in turn reduces the distribution shift ||D(θ_{t+1}) - D(θ_t)||_W. The effective reflexivity becomes:

ε_eff = ε / (1 + λ_EWC · F_max)

where F_max is the largest Fisher diagonal entry. Strong EWC regularization can push ε_eff below γ/β even when bare ε exceeds it, stabilizing a system that would otherwise oscillate.

14Active Inference and Free Energy

14.1 Friston’s Free Energy Principle

The Free Energy Principle (Friston 2010) states that any system that persists in a changing environment must minimize a free energy functional:

F = E_q [log q(θ) - log p(o, θ)] = D_KL(q(θ) || p(θ | o)) + const

where q(θ) is the agent’s approximate posterior over world parameters, and p(o, θ) is the generative model. Minimizing F is equivalent to maximizing model evidence log p(o) while keeping the posterior close to the prior.

14.2 Active Inference for Decision-Making

Active inference (Friston et al. 2017) extends this to action selection: agents select actions that minimize expected free energy (EFE):

G(π) = E_{p(o,s|π)} [log q(s|π) - log p(o, s)] = -I(o; s | π) + D_KL(p(o|π) || p̃(o))

The first term drives epistemic behavior (explore to reduce uncertainty); the second drives pragmatic behavior (act to achieve preferred outcomes p̃(o)). In financial markets, this naturally decomposes into information-gathering (research, monitoring) and position-taking (trading).

14.3 Connection to Portfolio Optimization

The niche construction formulation (Constant & Friston): the environment (“niche”) infers the agent back, via dη/dt = -∇F(η | a). In financial markets, this is literal: a large fund’s trades move prices, changing the environment, which changes the optimal portfolio, which changes the trades. The dual flow dμ/dt = -∇F(μ | s) and dη/dt = -∇F(η | a) is the active inference formulation of reflexivity.

Planning as inference. Under active inference, planning reduces to inference over policies (sequences of actions). Combined with the S5 backbone for fast imagined rollouts, this provides a principled framework for multi-step portfolio planning that naturally trades off exploration and exploitation.

15Convergence Guarantees

RecWM’s convergence theory rests on showing that the master equation defines a contraction mapping.

Theorem 15.1 (Contraction)

Define F(W) = C(W, A(B(W)), Φ). If:

  1. C is L_C-Lipschitz in its first argument
  2. The composed map A ˆ B is ε-sensitive (Perdomo Def. 3.1)
  3. L_C · (1 + ε) < 1

then F is a contraction mapping with rate r = L_C · (1 + ε) < 1, and by the Banach fixed-point theorem, iteration W_{n+1} = F(W_n) converges to a unique fixed point W*.

Exponential Convergence Rate

|| W_n - W* || ≤ r^n · || W_0 - W* ||,     r = L_C(1 + ε)

The convergence is exponential with rate -log(r) = -log(L_C(1+ε)). Faster convergence requires either reducing L_C (tighter constraint fields, smoother construction) or reducing ε (less reflexive markets, stronger EWC regularization).

Role of Constraint Field Tightness

Constraint fields reduce L_C by projecting the construction operator onto a smaller feasible set. Tighter constraints (higher capital requirements, position limits, circuit breakers) directly shrink the Lipschitz constant of C, making convergence easier. This formalizes the intuition that regulation stabilizes markets—not by eliminating reflexivity, but by reducing the amplification of the reflexive loop.

Conversely, relaxing constraints (deregulation, shadow banking, regulatory arbitrage) increases L_C. If L_C(1+ε) exceeds 1, the system loses its contraction property and can enter unstable oscillations—a formal description of financial crises as loss of contractivity.

The crisis condition: L_C(1+ε) ≥ 1. This is our formal criterion for systemic instability. RecWM monitors both L_C (estimated from the Jacobian of the construction operator) and ε (estimated from the sensitivity of predictions to parameter perturbation) in real time. A rising product signals approaching instability before it manifests in prices.

Greif & Laitin (APSR 98(4), 2004). “A Theory of Endogenous Institutional Change.” Quasi-parameters as endogenous crisis mechanisms.

Ergodicity & Growth Optimality

Baumann, Noorani, Price, Peters, Connaughton & Schön (TMLR 2025). “Reinforcement Learning with Non-Ergodic Reward Increments.” Peer-reviewed treatment of ergodicity economics with code. Lead with this, not the 2019 Nature Physics perspective.
Kelly (Bell System Technical Journal 35(4), 1956). “A New Interpretation of Information Rate.” The Kelly criterion for growth-optimal allocation.

1 Executive Summary

RecWM has a strong theoretical core—the typed fragment architecture (S5 backbone + GateL0RD + SPIB), the constraint field formalism, and the five-layer continual learning stack are genuine differentiators. But comparing against a well-specified competitor and an exhaustive ideal-spec reveals significant gaps across 9 tiers that must be addressed before the product can compete in institutional markets.

The hard truth: RecWM currently exists as a theoretical architecture with zero production code. The competitor already has working implementations of HAR-RV volatility forecasting (11× better than GARCH), conformal prediction intervals, NOTEARS causal DAGs, differentiable portfolio optimization, sheaf neural networks for cross-asset contagion, and persistent homology for topological early warning. The ideal spec adds 14 full tiers of capability including fixed income, derivatives, compliance, execution analytics, and operational infrastructure. RecWM needs to close these gaps or it ships as an academic paper, not a product.
What RecWM has that others don’t:
• Constraint fields Φ — No competitor formalizes regulatory/liquidity/physical/accounting constraints as first-class mathematical objects that filter the action space. This is genuinely novel.
• Typed world fragments with characteristic timescales — The τk-driven discretization (different Δ for Liquidity vs Structure) is architecturally elegant and well-motivated.
• Reflexive loop formalism — The ε coefficient tracking Perdomo Thm 3.5 convergence is theoretically rigorous. No competitor has this level of performativity awareness.
• EWC reducing effective reflexivity — The result εeff ≤ ε/(1+Ω·λmin(F)) connecting continual learning to market stability is original theory.

Below: a tier-by-tier gap analysis with research-backed assessments of what to build, what papers to cite, what libraries to use, and what order to build in.

3 Tier 1: Market Understanding Gaps

3.1 Volatility Forecasting

Gap: RecWM has no explicit volatility forecasting module. The Risk fragment theoretically captures vol dynamics through the S5 backbone, but there is no HAR-RV implementation, no GARCH family, no realized semivariance decomposition, no implied volatility augmentation.

What to build:

  • HAR-RV cascade (Corsi, 2009): RVt+1 = β0 + βdRVt + βwRVt(w) + βmRVt(m). Three nested components at daily/weekly/monthly horizons. The competitor claims 11× better MSE than GARCH(1,1) and +4% QLIKE improvement vs vanilla HAR-RV.
  • Realized semivariance: RS+(t) = ∑ ri2 · 1(ri > 0) and RS−(t) = ∑ ri2 · 1(ri < 0). Separates “good vol” (upside) from “bad vol” (downside). Barndorff-Nielsen et al. (2010).
  • GARCH family: GJR-GARCH, EGARCH, TGARCH as baselines. Library: arch (Python, Kevin Sheppard).
  • Implied vol augmentation: Ingest free vol indices (VIX, VXN, RVX, OVX, GVZ). VIX term structure slope (VIX9D/VIX3M) as sentiment signal.
  • Variance risk premium: VRP = IV2 − RV2 as a forward-looking signal.

Implementation Path

Libraries: arch (GARCH), numpy (HAR-RV is just linear regression), Yahoo Finance API (VIX family).
Effort: 2–3 weeks for full vol forecasting module.
Integration: Feed HAR-RV forecasts as inputs to the Risk fragment’s S5 backbone. The S5 layer learns to combine realized and implied vol signals.

3.2 Regime Detection Enhancement

Gap: RecWM has BOCPD in CL-3 for changepoint detection, but is missing:

  • ADWIN (Bifet & Gavalda, 2007): Adaptive windowing for real-time distribution shift detection. Unlike BOCPD which detects changepoints, ADWIN monitors for any shift in mean/variance continuously. Library: river (Python).
  • HMM regime classification: 2/3/4-state Hidden Markov Models with BIC-selected state count. Hamilton (1989). Library: hmmlearn.
  • Posterior regime probabilities: Exposing P(regime | data) at each timestep, not just “changepoint detected yes/no.”
  • Hurst exponent H(t): Time-varying per-asset. H < 0.5 mean-reverting, H > 0.5 trending, H = 0.5 random walk. Library: nolds.
  • Critical slowing down: Variance amplification and autocorrelation increase 3–5 days before regime transitions. Scheffer et al. (2009).

3.3 Tail Risk Quantification

Gap: RecWM has zero tail risk computation. This is a critical gap for any institutional risk product.

What to build:

  • VaR & ES: 1-day and multi-horizon, at 99% and 95%. Parametric (normal, Student-t, Cornish-Fisher), historical simulation, filtered historical simulation (GARCH-FHS), Monte Carlo.
  • Conditional EVT: GPD tail fitting above threshold u. Automatic threshold selection via mean residual life plot. RecWM’s Risk fragment should estimate ξ (shape) and σ (scale) that vary with regime.
  • Conformal prediction intervals: Split conformal with conformalized quantile regression (Romano et al., NeurIPS 2019). Finite-sample 90% coverage guarantee without distributional assumptions.
  • Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI): Gibbs & Candès (NeurIPS 2021). Running miscoverage: αt+1 = αt + γ(α − errt). Coverage adapts online under distribution shift. This is the killer feature for non-stationary financial data.
  • Conformal risk control: Angelopoulos et al. (2022). Extend conformal from coverage to arbitrary monotone loss functions (CVaR exceedance, drawdown probability).
  • VaR backtesting: Kupiec unconditional coverage, Christoffersen conditional coverage, traffic light test.
Why conformal prediction matters: Traditional prediction intervals require distributional assumptions (normality, Student-t) that are violated in financial data. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free, finite-sample coverage guarantees. ACI adds online adaptivity—the intervals widen automatically during regime changes without explicit changepoint detection. This is orthogonal to RecWM’s BOCPD and should be layered on top.

3.4 Cross-Asset Contagion

Gap: RecWM has cross-fragment coupling functions ρij but these are generic learned functions. The competitor uses sheaf neural networks (Bodnar et al., NeurIPS 2022) with heterogeneous stalks per asset class and learned restriction maps.

Sheaf Laplacian: Lsheaf = B · WΦ · BT

where B is the signed incidence matrix, WΦ contains the restriction maps Φe per edge, and the diffusion respects heterogeneity: equity features (returns, vol, Greeks) transform differently than bond features (duration, spread, OAS) when propagating signals across asset classes.

Research finding: Sheaf NNs are pre-production (no confirmed finance deployment), but the architecture is a natural fit for cross-asset contagion where different asset classes have fundamentally different feature spaces. Open-source: twitter-research/neural-sheaf-diffusion. Computationally tractable at 500 assets with diagonal restriction maps.

4 Tier 2: Causal Reasoning & Scenarios

4.1 Causal DAG Discovery

Gap: RecWM has no causal discovery. The competitor uses NOTEARS (Zheng et al., NeurIPS 2018) with a differentiable acyclicity constraint: h(W) = tr(eW⊙W) − d = 0.

What to build:

  • NOTEARS/DAGMA: DAGMA (Bello et al., 2022) uses a log-det acyclicity constraint with better optimization landscape. Library: gCastle (Huawei, broadest coverage), causal-learn (CMU).
  • DYNOTEARS: Pamfil et al. (2020) extends NOTEARS to time series with contemporaneous + lagged edges. Natural fit for financial data.
  • Time-varying DAG: The causal structure shifts (USD/JPY becomes a driver during carry unwind, then stops). Windowed re-estimation or online DAG updates.
  • Transfer entropy: Non-linear Granger causality. Complements DAG discovery for bidirectional causality detection.
Caveat: NOTEARS assumes acyclicity, which is problematic for feedback-heavy financial systems. Research shows scale-invariance issues (Reisach et al., 2021). RecWM’s reflexive loops explicitly model feedback cycles—this is a tension between the DAG assumption and the reflexivity formalism that needs architectural resolution.

4.2 do(X) Interventions

Gap: Without a causal DAG, interventions are impossible. The competitor supports “what if the Fed hikes 50bp” by clamping the node in the DAG and propagating through the graph.

What to build: Once the DAG exists, implement Pearl’s do-calculus. Clamp any node, remove incoming edges (surgical intervention), propagate through the causal graph. Generate conditional distributions, not point estimates. Multi-node interventions for joint shocks.

Integration with RecWM: The do(X) operation maps to modifying the constraint field Φ or clamping a world fragment value. The constructive operator C then propagates the intervention through the remaining fragments. This is a natural extension of the existing formalism.

4.3 Scenario Engine

Gap: RecWM has no scenario generation capability.

What to build:

  • Monte Carlo engine: 10,000+ paths with antithetic variance reduction (halves variance for tail estimation). Student-t sampling with vol clustering for realistic kurtosis.
  • Conditional scenarios: Modify world model latent state, roll forward using the S5 backbone’s prior (imagination without observations—exactly what world models do).
  • 5 built-in stress templates: GFC 2008 (equity −40%, credit +500bp, vol 3×), COVID 2020, rate shock 2022, SVB 2023, stagflation.
  • Reverse stress testing: “What scenario causes a 10% portfolio loss?” Search the shock space for the boundary. This is in the ideal spec but neither RecWM nor the competitor has it—a genuine differentiator opportunity.
  • Scenario validation: KS test on marginals, autocorrelation matching, VaR violation rate check.
  • CCAR/DFAST templates: GDP path, unemployment trajectory, equity drawdown, credit widening, rate paths. Required for regulatory submission.

5 Tier 3: Portfolio Construction & Risk

5.1 Differentiable Portfolio Optimization

Gap: RecWM has no portfolio construction at all. The competitor has end-to-end differentiable Markowitz with gradients flowing back through the world model.

What to build:

End-to-end differentiable: minw −wTμ + λwTΣw    s.t.   w ≥ 0, ∑ w = 1

Using cvxpylayers (Agrawal et al., NeurIPS 2019): canonicalize the convex program, differentiate through KKT conditions via implicit differentiation: dw*/dθ = −(dK/dz)−1(dK/dθ). Gradients flow from portfolio loss back through the covariance estimator back through the S5 backbone.

Full strategy suite:

  • Minimum variance: No return forecast needed. Pure risk minimization.
  • Maximum Sharpe: With return forecasts from world model.
  • Risk parity: Equalize risk contribution across assets.
  • HRP (De Prado, 2016): Cluster-based allocation via hierarchical clustering + recursive bisection. Never inverts covariance matrix—robust when N > T. Weight formula: wleft = 1 − varleft/(varleft + varright).
  • Black-Litterman: Blend world model views with equilibrium returns.
  • CVaR optimization (Rockafellar & Uryasev, 2000): min η + (1/((1−α)T)) ∑ ui subject to ui ≥ −wTri − η. Reduces to an LP. Captures tail risk asymmetrically.

5.2 Transaction Cost Modeling

Gap: No market impact or execution cost modeling.

Almgren-Chriss (2001): Optimal execution trajectory xk = X · sinh(κ(T−k)) / sinh(κT) where κ depends on risk aversion and impact ratio. Decomposes cost into permanent impact g(v) (linear, shifts fundamental) and temporary impact h(v) (linear + spread, per-trade). Implementation shortfall (Perold, 1988): paper return minus actual return, decomposed into delay, impact, and opportunity cost.

5.3 Risk Decomposition

Gap: No component VaR, no marginal risk contribution, no factor attribution.

Competitor claims tropical algebra for risk decomposition:

Research finding: Tropical algebra for VaR/CVaR is unproven. No published paper connects the min-plus semiring to Value-at-Risk computation. The sole confirmed finance deployment of tropical geometry is the Bank of England’s Product-Mix Auction (Baldwin & Klemperer, 2019). The competitor may be overclaiming. RecWM should use standard risk decomposition (component VaR, Euler decomposition) rather than pursuing an unvalidated tropical approach.

6 Tier 4: Geometry & Topology

6.1 Persistent Homology

Gap: RecWM has no topological analysis. The competitor uses Betti numbers (β0 fragmentation, β1 feedback loops, β2 voids) and topological velocity as crash early warning.

Research assessment:

  • Gidea & Katz (2018): Used persistence landscapes on S&P 500/DJIA/NASDAQ/Russell 2000. Detected rising spectral density 250 trading days before 2000 and 2008 crashes. Published in Physica A.
  • Computational feasibility: With sliding window of ~250 days over 500 assets, Ripser handles this in seconds per window on CPU. Bottleneck is Wasserstein distance computation.
  • Production status: No confirmed production deployment. Research-stage with growing academic interest. 92.9% of TDA portfolio strategies on QuantConnect produced lower beta than benchmarks.
  • Libraries: ripser (fastest CPU), giotto-tda (scikit-learn compatible), torch_topological (differentiable persistence for PyTorch).
Recommendation: Add TDA as a diagnostic layer on top of the correlation structure. Use persistence landscapes for crash early warning alongside BOCPD. Do not make TDA a core architectural dependency—it’s a signal, not a backbone.

6.2 Sheaf Neural Networks

Research assessment: Bodnar et al. (NeurIPS 2022) demonstrated sheaf diffusion solving heterophily/oversmoothing in GNNs. A 2026 paper applies sheaf theory to financial clearing/systemic risk (arXiv 2605.15778). The key advantage for RecWM: heterogeneous stalks enable different feature dimensions per asset class (equity features ≠ bond features ≠ commodity features), with learned restriction maps translating signals between them.

Gap assessment: RecWM’s cross-fragment coupling ρij is a simpler version of restriction maps. Upgrading to sheaf structure would be a natural extension but adds complexity. Recommended for Phase 2, not Phase 1.

6.3 Product Manifold Representations

Research assessment: Gu et al. (ICLR 2019) demonstrated Hn × Sk × ℝm product spaces for mixed-curvature data. Musmeci et al. (2021) embedded European banking networks in hyperbolic space where latent dimensions map to systemic importance. Libraries: geoopt (PyTorch), geomstats. Riemannian ops add ~2–5× overhead at 500 assets.

Recommendation: Research-stage. Consider for long-term roadmap. The Lorentz model (not Poincaré ball—numerically stable) for sector hierarchy + sphere for cyclical patterns (sector rotation) is theoretically appealing but adds significant implementation complexity.

6.4 Deep Equilibrium for Reflexivity

Gap: RecWM models reflexivity via the ε coefficient and belief field dynamics, but does not use DEQ (Bai et al., NeurIPS 2019) to solve for the reflexive fixed point iteratively.

Research assessment: DEQ’s fixed-point equation z* = f(z*, x) maps directly to Soros’s two functions. The spectral radius ρ of the Jacobian at z* measures instability. Jacobian regularization (Bai et al., ICML 2021) cuts convergence from 17 to ~6 iterations. 88% memory reduction vs explicit deep nets. Library: torchdeq.

Strong recommendation: Replace or augment RecWM’s current reflexive loop with a DEQ layer. The convergence speed ρ becomes a real-time instability signal—slow convergence = bubble/crash dynamics. This operationalizes Soros reflexivity in a way no current product does. The DEQ-reflexivity connection is an open gap in the literature—publishing this would be a research contribution.

6.5 Renormalization Group Multi-Scale Decomposition

Gap: RecWM uses typed timescales τk per fragment but has no explicit multi-scale decomposition engine.

Research assessment: Sornette’s LPPL (Log-Periodic Power Law) model captures discrete scale invariance near crashes. Peron et al. (2013) developed inverse RG decomposition reproducing volatility clustering and power-law autocorrelation. The competitor uses 5 learned scales with wavelet-like decomposition and anomalous dimension tracking.

Recommendation: RecWM’s fragment timescales (τ from minutes to years) already provide a form of multi-scale decomposition. Add variance amplification monitoring across scales (Sornette) as an early warning signal. Do not build a full RG engine—the fragment architecture already captures the essential physics.

7 Tier 5: Interpretability & Trust

7.1 Forecast Decomposition

Gap: RecWM produces forecasts from the unified world model but does not decompose them into interpretable components. The competitor decomposes every forecast into: trend + mean-reversion + momentum + carry + macro + residual, each separately inspectable.

What to build: Route each world fragment’s decoder output through a factor decomposition layer. The Momentum fragment contributes the momentum component, the Risk fragment contributes mean-reversion and vol signals, the Policy fragment contributes macro, etc. The fragment architecture already supports this—it just needs to be exposed at the output layer.

7.2 Uncertainty Quantification

Gap: RecWM has no uncertainty quantification. This is arguably the most important missing piece for institutional deployment.

What to build:

  • Conformal prediction intervals on every point forecast. CQR (Romano et al., 2019) for heteroscedastic intervals.
  • ACI (Gibbs & Candès, 2021): αt+1 = αt + γ(α − errt). Online coverage under distribution shift.
  • Aleatoric vs epistemic uncertainty: Aleatoric from predictive variance (irreducible noise), epistemic from ensemble disagreement or dropout (model uncertainty). “I’m uncertain because the data is noisy” vs “I’m uncertain because I haven’t seen this regime before.”
  • Abstention: When uncertainty exceeds threshold, say “I don’t have a reliable estimate” instead of guessing.
  • Calibration monitoring: Are 90% intervals covering 90%? Continuous monitoring.

7.3 Natural Language Explanations

What to build: Template-based explanation engine (not LLM-generated text). Inputs: Hurst exponent, reflexivity ρ, regime probabilities, factor decomposition, causal DAG position. Output: structured analyst note where every claim traces to a module output. Confidence calibration: “likely” = >70% posterior, “elevated” = >1σ above mean, “extreme” = >2σ.

7.4 Temporal Attribution

What to build: Integrated gradients (Sundararajan et al., 2017) over the time axis: which timesteps in the lookback window drove this prediction. 20-step Riemann integration for stable attribution. Library: captum (PyTorch).

7.5 Audit Trail

What to build: Every prediction logs: input data hash, module versions, intermediate outputs, final prediction, confidence interval, explanation. Reproducibility: same input + same checkpoint = same output. Required for SR 11-7 compliance (Fed, 2011).

8 Tier 6: Continuous Learning Enhancement

RecWM’s CL stack (CL-0 through CL-4) is its strongest area. Gaps are incremental:

8.1 ADWIN Drift Detection

Gap: CL-3 uses BOCPD for changepoint detection but lacks ADWIN for continuous distribution monitoring. ADWIN detects mean/variance shifts without fixed windows—complementary to BOCPD’s changepoint posterior. Library: river.drift.ADWIN.

8.2 Test-Time Training

Gap: No inference-time adaptation. TTT-Linear (Sun et al., 2024) replaces RNN hidden state updates with gradient steps on a linear self-supervised objective. The hidden state is a weight matrix updated via a learning rule at each token. This enables online adaptation without explicit retraining—the model adjusts to regime changes at inference time.

Integration: TTT could be added as CL-0.5 between natural gates and RTRL. It provides faster adaptation than RTRL (simpler auxiliary objective) while being complementary to EWC (TTT adapts fast weights, EWC protects slow weights).

8.3 Regime-Tagged Replay

Gap: DER++ in CL-3 stores experiences but doesn’t tag by regime or provide per-regime capacity control. Add regime labels from BOCPD + HMM, configurable per-regime buffer size, and weighted sampling that over-samples rare regimes (crises).

8.4 Usage Pattern Learning

Gap: No personalization. The competitor learns which assets each client queries, which metrics they check, which explanations they act on. Build: query embedding layer + response head fine-tuning + proactive alert learning.

9 Tier 7: Data, Infrastructure & Operations

9.1 Data Ingestion

Gap: RecWM has no data pipeline. Need:

  • Yahoo Finance: global OHLCV (yfinance)
  • FRED: VIX, yields, credit spreads, USD index, NFCI (fredapi)
  • Fama-French: daily factor returns (pandas_datareader)
  • Oxford-Man Realized Library: 5-min realized vol for 17 indices (validation)
  • Client CSV/DataFrame upload
  • Live entity resolution: “Apple” → AAPL, “the DAX” → ^GDAXI

9.2 Query Interface

Gap: No user-facing interface. Need: plain language input, structured output with provenance, five query modes (analyze, compare, scenario, world, portfolio).

9.3 API & Integration

Gap: No API. Need REST endpoints, WebSocket for streaming, Python SDK. Ideal spec adds Bloomberg BPIPE/SAPI, OMS/PMS, FIX protocol—these are enterprise requirements for later phases.

9.4 Observability

Gap: No monitoring. Need per-module diagnostics on every forward pass: Hurst range, reflexivity ρ, regime probabilities, KL divergence, portfolio VaR/CVaR. Rolling checkpoint with auto-rollback if validation loss spikes.

9.5 Compliance & Regulatory

Gap: No regulatory reporting. For institutional deployment:

  • FRTB IMA: Expected shortfall at 97.5% over a 250-day stressed calibration window. Liquidity horizons: 10-day (large-cap equity), 20-day (small-cap, IG credit), 40-day (exotic credit), 60-day (securitized), 120-day (correlation). P&L attribution test required.
  • CCAR/DFAST: 9-quarter projections under baseline/adverse/severely-adverse scenarios. Stress capital buffer (SCB) since 2020.
  • Basel III/IV: CVA risk charge, revised market risk, 72.5% output floor on internal-model RWA.
  • SR 11-7: Model risk management—inventory, independent validation, ongoing monitoring, board-level governance.

10 Tier 8: Fixed Income, Derivatives & Advanced Analytics

The ideal spec includes comprehensive fixed income and derivatives capabilities that neither RecWM nor the competitor addresses. These are required for full-service institutional deployment.

10.1 Fixed Income

  • Yield curve construction: Nelson-Siegel (1987): f(τ) = β0 + β1e−τ/λ + β2(τ/λ)e−τ/λ. Svensson (1994) adds a second hump. Both used by central banks globally.
  • Key rate durations (Ho, 1992): DV01 decomposed across 2y/5y/10y/30y buckets for targeted hedging.
  • OAS decomposition: Credit + liquidity + tax + model risk, via backward induction on calibrated rate tree.
  • Credit transition matrices: CreditMetrics (JP Morgan, 1997). Rating migration probabilities + forward curves per rating → full P&L distribution for credit VaR.

10.2 Options & Derivatives

  • Vol surface fitting: SVI (Gatheral, 2004): w(k) = a + b(ρ(k−m) + √((k−m)2 + σ2)). SSVI (Gatheral & Jacquier, 2014): explicit no-arbitrage conditions across strikes and maturities.
  • Greeks: Delta, gamma, vega, theta, rho, vanna (∂2V/∂S∂σ), volga (∂2V/∂σ2).
  • Variance swap replication: Static strip of OTM puts/calls weighted by 1/K2. Underpins VIX methodology.
  • Dispersion trading: Sell index vol, buy single-stock vol. Requires consistent SVI/SSVI fitting across all constituents.

10.3 Macro Regime Modeling

  • GDP/inflation/employment nowcasting from high-frequency indicators
  • Taylor rule gap: where “should” rates be vs where they are
  • Custom financial conditions index
  • Yield curve shape classification (steep/flat/inverted) with historical sequencing

10.4 Alternative Data Integration

  • Satellite imagery (parking lots, crop yields)
  • Shipping data (AIS vessel tracking)
  • Social sentiment (aggregated NLP scores)
  • Patent filings, job postings, web traffic
  • Geopolitical risk indices (GPR, EPU)

11 Tier 9: Architecture Backbone Gaps

11.1 DreamerV3 RSSM vs RecWM S5

The competitor uses a DreamerV3-style RSSM with GRU deterministic path + 32×32 categorical stochastic latents. RecWM uses S5 with diagonal state matrices. Comparison:

DimensionRecWM (S5)Competitor (RSSM)Assessment
Training parallelismParallel via associative scanSequential (GRU)S5 is ~10× faster training (S5WM, 2025)
Long-range memoryHiPPO initialization, unboundedGRU limited to ~500 stepsS5 advantage for long lookback
Posterior collapse preventionContinuous latents32×32 categoricals + KL balancingRSSM’s categorical latents are more robust
Imagination (prior rollout)Possible but not designed for itNative (p(z|h) prior)RSSM designed for imagination
Heavy-tailed valuesNo special handlingSymlog predictionsFinancial data spans orders of magnitude
O(N) RTRLDiagonal A enables O(N)O(N3) for GRUS5 advantage for online learning
Recommendation: RecWM’s S5 backbone is the right choice for a CL-focused architecture (O(N) RTRL, parallel training). But add: (1) symlog predictions for handling financial value magnitudes, (2) categorical latent augmentation to prevent posterior collapse, (3) prior rollout mechanism for scenario generation / imagination.

11.2 Mamba as Alternative Backbone

Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2023) extends S4/S5 with input-dependent selective scan: B, C, and Δ become functions of the input, enabling content-aware filtering. For financial data: Mamba’s input-dependent Δ (controlling how much history to retain vs forget) is a natural fit for regime-dependent relevant history lengths.

Recommendation: Make the backbone switchable (S5 or Mamba). Mamba trades O(N) RTRL compatibility for better content-aware filtering. The ideal spec suggests exactly this: “Switchable backbone: GRU or Mamba, configurable per deployment.”

A New Mathematical Discipline

Endogenous World Model Theory

Seven fundamental units, a new processing algebra, and three methodologies for modelling economic reality from within. The first complete theoretical framework for world models that are simultaneously participants in and observers of the systems they model.

August 2026 · New field · New fundamental units · New processing paradigm

I

Endogenous World Model Theory: A New Field

We propose Endogenous World Model Theory (EWM-T) as a new mathematical discipline at the intersection of world models, performative prediction, and constructive economics. EWM-T is not an extension of any existing framework—it is a new field defined by a single axiom that separates it from all prior work:

The Dual-Position Axiom

The model is simultaneously inside the system it models and outside it. This duality is not a contradiction—it is a fixed point.

Every existing world model—JEPA, RSSM, Genie, Dreamer, Sora—operates under the exogeneity assumption: the model observes a system from outside. Pure endogeneity (the model is only inside) is equally wrong—a business world model must also observe, predict, and provide actionable intelligence from an external vantage point. The real situation is dual: the model is a participant (inside—its predictions move markets, its risk assessments trigger margin calls) and an observer (outside—it must provide accurate forecasts, risk signals, and scenario analysis). Mathematically, this duality is motivated by Lawvere’s fixed-point theorem (1969): in a cartesian closed category, if there exists a point-surjective morphism φ: A → BA, then every endomorphism f: B → B has a fixed point s with f · s = s. Applied to economic self-reference: the economy’s capacity for models to represent their own effects (the point-surjection) guarantees fixed points where the model’s prediction and the system’s reality coincide. The model is “inside” when it perturbs the system (Soros’s manipulative function), “outside” when it observes (Soros’s cognitive function), and the fixed point is where both perspectives collapse into identity.

The system is also inside a larger environment (pandemics, geopolitics, natural disasters) that the model cannot fully control. Filimonov & Sornette (2012) measure the endogenous fraction of price moves at ~30% (late 1990s) to ~70%+ (post-2007) for E-mini S&P 500 futures—the remainder is genuinely exogenous. A complete world model must handle both channels simultaneously.

From this dual-position axiom, EWM-T derives an entirely new theoretical apparatus: new fundamental units of economic reality, new processing paradigms, new mathematical objects, and new methodologies for building and evaluating world models that are simultaneously participants in and observers of the systems they model. RecWM is the first architecture built on EWM-T.

Mathematical foundation: Lawvere’s Fixed-Point Theorem

The dual-position axiom has a precise categorical formalization. Lawvere (1969) proved that in any cartesian closed category, if there exists a point-surjective morphism φ: A → BA (from an object A to the exponential object BA), then every endomorphism f: B → B has a fixed point—a global element s: 1 → B satisfying f · s = s. For EWM-T: the economy is modelled as a cartesian closed category; the model M and the economic state space C are objects within it; and the model’s capacity to represent its own effect constitutes a point-surjective morphism into the internal hom-object. The guaranteed fixed point is the state where prediction and reality coincide. Caveat: Verifying that a given economic category satisfies the cartesian closed and point-surjection conditions requires formal construction beyond what is given here; the theorem motivates the dual-position axiom but does not yet prove it for a specific economic model. The Yoneda lemma complements this: an object’s external relational embedding is naturally isomorphic to its internal structure. References: Lawvere, “Diagonal Arguments and Cartesian Closed Categories” (Springer LNM 92, 1969); Yanofsky, “A Universal Approach to Self-Referential Paradoxes, Incompleteness and Fixed Points” (Bull. Symbolic Logic 9(3), 2003); Barreto, “A Survey on Lawvere’s Fixed-Point Theorem” (arXiv:2503.13536, 2025).

II

The Seven Fundamental Units of Endogenous Economics

Just as physics has its fundamental units (metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela), EWM-T defines seven fundamental units that span the space of endogenous economic reality. These are not derived quantities or engineering choices—they are the irreducible primitives from which all economic phenomena are constructed.

Unit 1: The Constructon (𝒞)

Definition: The fundamental modelling primitive of economic construction. A constructon is a triple 𝒞 = (a, φ, w) where a is an action, φ is a constraint, and w is the resulting world-state change. It is the smallest unit that retains economic meaning within the EWM-T framework.

Analogy: The constructon is to EWM-T what the transaction is to accounting—the primitive unit of record. Unlike accounting transactions, constructons carry constraint and reflexive-feedback information. They are always observed in bound states (transactions, contracts, policy actions). Caveat: Emergent phenomena (network effects, institutional trust, culture) resist clean decomposition into discrete triples. The constructon is a useful modelling primitive, not a proven ontological atom—economic reality can be usefully approximated by constructon compositions, but residual phenomena that resist this decomposition exist.

What makes it new: Standard economics has no structured unit of economic change that captures action, constraint, and outcome simultaneously. The constructon provides this. Its composition rules (see Constructon Algebra below) formalise how atomic economic actions combine under constraints.

Formal specification:

  • Action space: a ∈ A(B(t)), where B(t) is the agent’s belief state
  • Constraint function: φ: A × W → {0, 1}, the hard feasibility gate
  • World update: w = δW(a, φ) ∈ ΔW, the minimal state change
  • Reflexive charge: q(𝒞) ∈ [0, 1], the degree to which this constructon feeds back into the system’s beliefs (see Reflexive Charge below)

Unit 2: Reflexive Charge (q)

Definition: A vector q ∈ ℝk attached to every constructon, measuring the degree to which the constructon’s execution feeds back into each of k impact channels: price (immediate), narrative (delayed), policy expectations (second-order), cross-asset correlations (structural), and liquidity (catalytic). The scalar summary |q| ∈ [0, ∞) recovers a single reflexive magnitude when a coarser view suffices.

What makes it new: Performative prediction (Perdomo 2020) has a single global sensitivity parameter ε. But in real markets, different actions have wildly different reflexive impact across different channels. A central bank rate announcement has high qprice and qpolicy but low qliquidity; a large dark-pool execution has high qliquidity but near-zero qnarrative. No existing framework parameterises reflexivity at the atomic level or distinguishes impact channels.

Formal specification:

  • q(𝒞) = (∂Dprice/∂𝒞, ∂Dnarrative/∂𝒞, ∂Dpolicy/∂𝒞, ∂Dcorrelation/∂𝒞, ∂Dliquidity/∂𝒞), the per-channel sensitivity vector
  • Aggregate reflexivity: εt = Σ𝒞 ∈ active ||q(𝒞)|| · ||𝒞||, recovering Theorem 5’s endogenous ε as an emergent quantity from atomic charge magnitudes
  • Concentration property: total reflexive charge magnitude is approximately conserved during calm markets (Σ||q|| ≈ const), but concentrates during crises (few actors carry most of the reflexive load). Filimonov & Sornette (2012) measure this concentration empirically via Hawkes branching ratio

Unit 3: Constraint Quantum (φ)

Definition: The indivisible unit of economic constraint. A constraint quantum is a typed, immutable rule-object that gates feasibility. Examples: a single regulatory clause (“leverage ratio ≥ 3%”), a single accounting identity (“assets = liabilities + equity”), a single physical bound (“delivery takes ≥ 1 day”).

What makes it new: Existing constraint optimisation treats constraints as continuous functions. EWM-T treats constraints as discrete, typed, and composable objects. The constraint quantum is the atom; the constraint field Φ (Theorem 4) is the emergent field formed by the interaction of all active constraint quanta.

Types:

TypeSymbolExamplesTimescale
PhysicalφPSettlement time, storage capacityFixed
RegulatoryφRCapital ratios, position limitsYears
ContractualφCMargin calls, covenants, ISDA termsMonths
InstitutionalφIMarket hours, clearing rules, nettingDecades
CognitiveφKMental models, heuristics, biasesVariable

Unit 4: Belief Field (B)

Definition: A spatiotemporal field B(x, t) over the space of economic agents x ∈ X and time t, encoding each agent’s probability distribution over future world states. Unlike a scalar or vector, the belief field has field dynamics: beliefs propagate, interfere, and resonate.

What makes it new: Standard economics treats beliefs as individual agent attributes (prior distributions, expectations). EWM-T treats beliefs as a field—a continuous distribution over agent-space with its own dynamics, analogous to how physics treats the electromagnetic field rather than individual charges. The field formulation enables:

  • Belief propagation: Expectations diffuse through the agent network with measurable speed and amplitude, governed by network topology (DeGroot dynamics, Hegselmann-Krause models)
  • Belief interaction: When multiple belief currents meet, they compete nonlinearly—producing amplification (herding, narrative dominance) or polarisation (bounded-confidence clustering). Unlike physical waves, belief dynamics are fundamentally nonlinear: superposition does not hold in general
  • Belief resonance: When the characteristic frequency of belief updating matches the system’s reflexive feedback cycle, producing amplification (bubbles, panics). This is a genuine dynamical-systems resonance, not a wave-physics metaphor
  • Belief damping: EWC regularisation (Theorem 3) reinterpreted as viscous damping of belief update rates

Unit 5: Liquidity Potential (Λ)

Definition: A scalar field Λ(t) ∈ [0, ∞) measuring the instantaneous capacity of the system to instantiate constructons. Not a fragment type but a catalyst potential—required for compositions to proceed, redistributed but not consumed.

What makes it new: Liquidity has been treated as a derived quantity (bid-ask spreads, market depth, volume) or an exogenous variable. EWM-T treats it as a fundamental potential field whose gradient drives the flow of economic activity. High Λ means constructions are easy to instantiate; low Λ means even simple constructions (selling a bond, rolling a loan) require extraordinary effort. The key insight: Λ is reflexive—the act of consuming liquidity changes the potential field, which changes what constructions are feasible, which changes liquidity consumption.

Dynamics:

  • Liquidity equation: dΛ/dt = Σ(source terms) − Σ(sink terms) − η · εt · Λ
  • The final term (−ηεΛ) captures the liquidity-reflexivity spiral: higher reflexivity drains liquidity, lower liquidity amplifies reflexivity
  • Steady-state: Λ* = sources / (ηε + sinks), which decreases monotonically with ε

Unit 6: Temporal Grain (τ)

Definition: The characteristic timescale at which a constructon or world fragment operates. Not a parameter but a fundamental unit—economic reality operates at multiple simultaneous timescales that cannot be reduced to a single clock.

What makes it new: Multi-scale models exist in physics (renormalisation group) and signal processing (wavelets). But in those domains, the timescales are nested (fine-grained causes coarse-grained). In economics, timescales interact bidirectionally: a microsecond flash crash (τ ≈ ms) can trigger a years-long regulatory response (τ ≈ years), which reshapes the microsecond dynamics. EWM-T formalises this as:

  • Temporal coupling tensor: Tij measures the causal influence of timescale τi on timescale τj. In physics, T is approximately lower-triangular (fast drives slow). In economics, T has significant off-diagonal entries in both directions.
  • Scale-dependent causality: The causal graph changes with the temporal grain. At τ ≈ seconds, order flow causes price. At τ ≈ quarters, policy causes investment. At τ ≈ years, institutions cause everything. The causal structure is not fixed—it is a function of τ.
  • Temporal arbitrage: When the same information propagates at different speeds across timescales, the discrepancy creates opportunities and instabilities. The temporal coupling tensor detects this.

Unit 7: Construction Entropy (SC)

Definition: The logarithm of the number of distinct constructon sequences that produce the same macroscopic world-state change: SC(W → W′) = log |{(𝒞1, ..., 𝒞n) : 𝒞1 ⊗ ... ⊗ 𝒞n maps W to W′}|.

What makes it new: Thermodynamic entropy counts microstates consistent with a macrostate. Construction entropy counts constructon sequences consistent with a macro-level economic outcome. This is the first entropy measure native to endogenous economic dynamics. High SC means many paths to the same outcome (robust, reversible). Low SC means few paths (fragile, path-dependent, potentially irreversible).

Key properties:

  • Crisis signature: SC drops sharply before crises as viable construction paths narrow. This is the entropic precursor—a new crisis signal distinct from all others. Empirical validation is needed to confirm this signature on historical data.
  • Irreversibility connection: SC(W → W′) ≠ SC(W′ → W) in general. The asymmetry quantifies the cost differential between destruction and reconstruction.
  • Path-narrowing conjecture: Under reflexive dynamics with no external input, SC tends to decrease (the system loses constructive degrees of freedom) as path dependence and constraint tightening reduce the feasible set. Status: conjecture requiring formal proof under stated dynamics. Unlike thermodynamic entropy (which increases in isolated systems), construction entropy measures accessible paths, not microstates. The analogy to thermodynamics is structural, not literal—no “economic second law” is claimed without rigorous derivation.
III

The Constructon Algebra: New Processing Paradigm (a compositional calculus; not yet a formal algebra in the ring/group-theoretic sense)

EWM-T processes economic reality not through time series, not through agent-based simulation, not through equilibrium computation, but through constructon algebra—a new computational paradigm for composing atomic economic actions under constraints with reflexive feedback.

The Four Operations

1. Composition (⊗)

Combine two constructons into a compound construction. 𝒞1 ⊗ 𝒞2 is defined only when φ1 and φ2 are compatible and Λ ≥ L12 (sufficient liquidity). The reflexive charge of the composite is q(𝒞1 ⊗ 𝒞2) ≥ max(q1, q2)—composition can only increase reflexive charge.

Example: (buy bond, margin rule, price impact) ⊗ (hedge with CDS, ISDA terms, spread change)

2. Reflection (ρ)

The reflexive feedback operator. ρ(𝒞) maps a constructon to the belief-field change it induces: ρ: 𝒞 → ΔB. This is the mechanism of performativity at the atomic level. ρ is not a separate step—it fires whenever a constructon with q > 0 is executed.

Example: Fed rate hike constructon → instantaneous belief-field reconfiguration across all agents

3. Filtration (Φ)

The constraint filter. Φ(𝒞) → {feasible, infeasible} gates each constructon against the active constraint field. The filter itself evolves: when enough constructons of type φR (regulatory) accumulate, the constraint field changes, altering which future constructons pass the filter.

Example: Basel IV adoption filters out previously-feasible high-leverage constructons

4. Dissolution (δ)

The irreversible destruction operator. δ(𝒞) removes a constructon from the active set permanently. Unlike composition (which is reversible through decomposition), dissolution has no inverse. The dissolved constructon’s reflexive charge redistributes across remaining constructons.

Example: Firm bankruptcy — the constructons constituting the firm’s operations are dissolved, not decomposed

IV

Three New Methodologies

Methodology 1: Reflexive Rollout (R-Rollout)

Standard world model rollouts (Dreamer, JEPA, diffusion models) simulate forward by repeatedly applying a learned transition function: st+1 = f(st, at). This assumes the transition function does not change during the rollout. In an endogenous system, each step of the rollout changes the system being modeled, which changes the transition function for the next step.

R-Rollout Algorithm

For each rollout step t → t+1:

  1. State prediction: st+1 = fθ(st, at) — standard forward pass
  2. Reflexive correction: θ′ = θ − α · ∇θ L(st+1, D(θ)) — update the model within the rollout to account for performative shift
  3. Constraint re-evaluation: Φ(t+1) = evolve(Φ(t), st+1) — the constraint field may have changed
  4. Feasibility re-check: if st+1 ∉ K(Φ(t+1)), flag as infeasible and branch
  5. Charge redistribution: qt+1 = redistribute(qt, δ(t)) — account for dissolutions and new entries

Key difference from standard rollout: Steps 2–5 are absent in all existing world model rollouts. The model updates itself during the rollout, the constraints evolve, and the feasibility set changes. This makes R-Rollout non-Markovian even when the underlying dynamics are Markov, because the transition function at step t+1 depends on the entire rollout history through the cumulative reflexive corrections.

Methodology 2: Performative Backtesting (P-Backtest)

Standard backtesting evaluates a model by replaying historical data: “if we had used this model in 2020, would it have predicted the crash?” This is fundamentally flawed for endogenous models: if the model had been deployed in 2020, its predictions would have changed the market, changing the data the backtest uses. Every backtest of a performative model is a counterfactual fiction.

P-Backtest Protocol

Instead of replaying historical data against the model, P-Backtest simulates the counterfactual history that would have existed had the model been deployed:

  1. Historical anchoring: Start from actual historical state W(t0)
  2. Model insertion: Deploy RecWM at t0 with estimated reflexive charge qmodel
  3. Distribution shift simulation: For each t > t0, compute D′(t) = Dhistorical(t) + ε · ΔD(θt), the counterfactual distribution
  4. Counterfactual evaluation: Compare RecWM’s predictions against D′(t), not against Dhistorical(t)
  5. Sensitivity analysis: Vary qmodel from 0 (no market impact) to 1 (dominant market force) and report performance as a function of reflexive charge

Key output: A performative backtest curve—model accuracy as a function of reflexive charge. A model that performs well only at q = 0 is a standard forecaster. A model that maintains performance across q values is genuinely reflexivity-aware. This curve is the proper evaluation metric for endogenous world models, replacing Sharpe ratio, RMSE, and other exogenous metrics.

Methodology 3: Constructive Stress Testing (C-Stress)

Standard stress tests (Fed DFAST/CCAR, EBA) apply predetermined adverse scenarios to bank balance sheets. The scenarios are exogenous (“assume GDP drops 10%”) and static (the same scenario is applied regardless of the bank’s response). EWM-T proposes constructive stress testing: the stress scenario is endogenously generated by the model ecology’s own dynamics.

C-Stress Protocol

  1. Viability kernel computation: Estimate Viab(t) for the current state
  2. Boundary identification: Find the states on the viability kernel boundary—the closest points to non-viability
  3. Constructon path enumeration: For each boundary state, enumerate the constructon sequences that lead there from the current state
  4. Reflexive amplification: For each path, compute the reflexive amplification: how does the path change if market participants observe the stress test results and react?
  5. Worst-case construction: The stress scenario is the constructon sequence with the highest reflexive amplification—the self-fulfilling worst case

Key difference from standard stress testing: The scenario is not predetermined—it is discovered by the model as the worst-case path through the constructon algebra. And the scenario accounts for reflexivity: the stress test’s own publication can amplify the stress (if market participants learn the worst-case path, they may front-run it). C-Stress is the first stress testing methodology that accounts for this feedback.

The segment-defining question

Every existing world model answers: “What will happen?” EWM answers a fundamentally different question: “What can be constructed, by whom, under what constraints, and how does the act of answering this question change the answer?” This is not a better answer to the same question. It is a different question entirely. That is what makes it a new segment.

The Reflexive Constructive World Model

RecWM: Five Theorems for Economic Reality

Economics has no world model because the mathematics does not exist. Reflexivity, evolving constraints, non-ergodicity, and performative forgetting are not engineering problems—they are unsolved mathematical problems. We address all five with novel theorems—three provable, one conditional, one conjectural.
