  18. Complete Signal Architecture
  19. The Research Program
01

The Thesis

A world model is a learned internal representation of how a system evolves. In reinforcement learning, world models have transformed control: an agent learns the dynamics of its environment and plans in imagination before acting (Ha & Schmidhuber 2018; Hafner et al. 2020–2025; LeCun 2022). The architecture is universal: encode observations into compressed state, predict how state evolves under actions, decide by simulating consequences.

Economics has no equivalent. Not for lack of trying—for lack of mathematics.

The L6 vacancy. Han et al. (arXiv 2608.06020, August 2026) surveyed the economic world model landscape and defined a six-level capability ladder. L1–L3 (forecasting, scenario generation, causal reasoning) are crowded. L4 (multi-agent simulation) has entries. L5 (performativity-aware models) is nearly empty. L6—a sim-to-real economic twin with an online correction loop—has zero occupants.

The vacancy is not an engineering gap. It is a mathematical gap. Robotics world models rest on a single, powerful assumption: the laws of physics do not change when the robot observes them. In economics, they do. This creates five unsolved problems that block L6:

ProblemIn RoboticsIn EconomicsWhat’s Missing
ReflexivityAbsent (gravity doesn’t care about the robot’s model)Fundamental (predictions move markets)No framework connects causal emergence with performative feedback
Non-ergodicityIrrelevant (no ruin risk for a simulation)Central (Kelly 1956; Peters 2019)No one has composed ergodicity economics with performative prediction
Evolving constraintsFixed (physics)Endogenous (regulations, accounting rules, new instruments)No categorical framework for typed, composable, evolving constraint objects
Performative forgettingAddressed by replay buffersModel updates change the data distribution, breaking replayNo theory connects continual learning with performative stability
Endogenous crisisAbsent (system parameters are fixed)Reflexivity itself varies with market stateNo framework for state-dependent sensitivity or crisis-transition detection

RecWM addresses each of these with a novel theorem. The theorems are not assembled from existing pieces—each bridges two literatures that have zero prior co-citations.

Notation guide. The symbol ε denotes a Lipschitz sensitivity constant throughout, but refers to different maps: in Theorem 1, ε is the Lipschitz constant of the reflexive transition map φ → Tφ; in Theorems 2, 3, and 5, ε is the sensitivity of the distribution map D(θ). The structural isomorphism (Section 2) connects these via D(θ) ↔ Tφ. Similarly, γ denotes strong concavity of the composed EI map in Theorem 1 (paired with smoothness βEI), and strong convexity of the loss in Theorems 3 and 5—opposite curvatures on different functions. All convergence conditions take the form ε < γ/β.

We verified this claim via exhaustive citation-graph searches across the papers citing Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020), Hoel et al. (PNAS 2013), and the full ergodicity economics, continual learning, and applied category theory literatures.

The master equation of RecWM is: W(t+1) = C(W(t), A(B(t)), Φ(t)). The construction operator C (Theorem 4), the reflexive belief-action loop B → A → ΔW (Theorem 1), and the constraint field Φ (Theorem 4) are each grounded in a theorem below. B(t) itself is defined operationally as the model’s latent state; its stability inherits from parameter convergence (Theorems 3 and 5 prove θt convergence, which bounds the latent state via the encoder’s Lipschitz constant).
02

Theorem 1: Reflexive Causal Emergence

The Problem

Causal emergence (Hoel et al., PNAS 2013; Comolatti & Hoel 2022 [preprint]) studies when macro-level descriptions of a system have more causal power than micro-level descriptions, measured by effective information (EI). All existing frameworks—Hoel 2013, Barnett & Seth (Phys. Rev. E 2023), Krasnovsky 2025, the closed-form approach of Liu, Yuan & Zhang (Entropy 2024)—share one assumption: the coarse-graining does not change the micro dynamics.

In financial markets, this assumption fails catastrophically. When analysts identify a “credit crisis” (a macro description), that identification changes micro behavior: banks tighten lending, traders sell, liquidity dries up. The act of coarse-graining creates the causal structure it purports to describe.

Prior Art

  • Causal emergence (Hoel 2013, Comolatti & Hoel 2022 [preprint], Liu et al. 2024): Macro EI vs. micro EI, always with fixed T
  • Performative prediction (Perdomo et al., ICML 2020; Miller et al., ICML 2021): Model deployment changes the data distribution, convergence via Theorem 3.5
  • Observer-dependent emergence (Abrahão & Zenil 2022): Emergence relative to observer, but observer does not change the system
  • Causal emergence in agents (Pae, arXiv 2607.20708, July 2026): Architectural conditions for causal emergence in active inference agents via perspective latents; closer to Hoel’s framework but agents do not reflexively change their own dynamics

The gap: To our knowledge, no prior work formally composes causal emergence (Hoel 2013) with performative prediction (Perdomo 2020). The two literatures are completely disjoint.

The New Object

We introduce the reflexive transition map: a function φ → Tφ that maps each coarse-graining φ: S → Smacro to the micro transition matrix Tφ that results from adopting φ as the operative macro description. This object is absent from all existing causal emergence frameworks.

Definition (Reflexive Causal Emergence)

Given a micro-level system with state space S and a reflexive transition map φ → Tφ:

  • Reflexive effective information: EIR(φ) = EI(Tφmacro), where Tφmacro is the macro transition matrix induced by applying φ to Tφ
  • Standard effective information: EIS(φ) = EI(T0macro), where T0 is the unobserved baseline dynamics

Reflexive causal emergence occurs when EIR(φ*) > EIS(φ) for all φ.

Definition (Performative Coarse-Graining Stability)

A coarse-graining φPS is performatively stable if:

φPS = argmaxφ EI(TφPSmacro)

That is, φPS maximises effective information under the micro dynamics that φPS itself induces.

Theorem 1 (Reflexive Emergence Amplification)

Let φ → Tφ be ε-Lipschitz (small changes in coarse-graining cause small changes in micro dynamics). Assume that the composed map φ → EI(Tφmacro) is γ-strongly concave and βEI-smooth in a neighbourhood of the optimum. Suppose ε < γ/βEI (weak performativity relative to causal structure). Then:

  1. Existence & uniqueness: A performatively stable coarse-graining φPS exists and is unique.
  2. Convergence: Repeated coarse-graining optimisation converges to φPS at linear rate.
  3. Amplification: There exist systems where EIR(φPS) > maxφ EIS(φ). Reflexive feedback can create causal emergence that does not exist in the fixed system.

Proof technique: Parts (i)–(ii) apply the Banach contraction mapping theorem under the ε < γ/βEI condition, following the structure of Perdomo et al. Theorem 3.5 with risk minimisation replaced by EI maximisation. Part (iii) constructs a two-state binary chain where the performative feedback concentrates the macro transition toward determinism, increasing EI above the non-reflexive maximum. Caveat: EI in general is the difference of two concave functions (concave minus concave), which is neither concave nor convex. The γ-strong concavity assumption holds when the marginal entropy term dominates the conditional entropy term—e.g., in systems with sufficient stochasticity that row entropies are small relative to column-average entropy. Verifying this condition for specific economic systems is flagged as a requirement for formal publication (see Open Problem 7).

What This Means for RecWM

Theorem 1 formalises the mechanism that makes financial markets fundamentally different from physics: the description creates the reality it describes. The reflexive transition map φ → Tφ is the mathematical engine of the belief-action-world loop B → A → ΔW → ΔB. The convergence guarantee (part ii) ensures that RecWM’s iterative state updates converge; the amplification result (part iii) explains why markets exhibit stronger causal structure during crises than during calm periods.

Structural isomorphism

The bridge between causal emergence and performative prediction has a precise structure: model parameters ↔ coarse-graining maps; risk ↔ negative EI; distribution map D(θ) ↔ reflexive transition map Tφ; performative stability ↔ performative coarse-graining stability. This isomorphism has not been noted anywhere in the literature.

03

Theorem 2: Ergodic-Performative Divergence

The Problem

Ergodicity economics (Peters & Gell-Mann, Chaos 2016; Peters, Nat. Phys. 2019; Baumann et al., TMLR 2025) demonstrates that for multiplicative dynamics (compound returns, leveraged positions, wealth processes), the time-average growth rate E[log(1+R)] is the correct objective—not the ensemble average E[R]. Optimising the wrong functional leads to over-leveraging and eventual ruin.

Performative prediction (Perdomo et al., ICML 2020) shows that deploying a model changes the distribution it was trained on. The stable point is a fixed point: θ* minimises risk under D(θ*).

These corrections are orthogonal. One asks “which distribution?” (the one your model induces). The other asks “which functional?” (the one your dynamics demands). Nobody has composed them.

The Gap

Wrong distribution (D0)Right distribution (D(θ))
Wrong functional (E[R])Standard MLPerformative prediction
(Perdomo 2020)
Right functional (E[log(1+R)])Ergodicity economics
(Peters 2019)		THE EMPTY CELL
RecWM Theorem 2

To our knowledge, no prior work formally composes performative prediction (Perdomo et al., ICML 2020) with ergodicity economics (Peters, Nat. Phys. 2019; Baumann et al., TMLR 2025). The closest work—distributionally robust performative optimisation (Jia et al., NeurIPS 2025)—adds robustness over which distribution map D(θ), but never questions whether E[loss] is the right functional.

Theorem 2 (Ergodic-Performative Divergence)

Let Wt+1 = Wt · (1 + θ · Xt) with Xt ~ D(θ), where D(θ) is ε-sensitive. Let θ*E be the performatively stable point under the ensemble objective JE(θ) = ED(θ)[θX], and θ*G be the performatively stable point under the time-average objective JG(θ) = ED(θ)[log(1 + θX)]. Suppose D(θ) has nonzero variance for all θ near θ*E. Then:

  1. θ*G < θ*E — the ergodic agent is strictly more conservative.
  2. The long-run growth rate at θ*G strictly exceeds that at θ*E almost surely.
  3. The gap |θ*E − θ*G| is increasing in ε — stronger market impact amplifies the divergence.
  4. As sensitivity ε increases, θ*E approaches the instability frontier while θ*G remains bounded away from it.

Proof technique: Part (a) follows from the strict concavity of log: the FOC under E[log(1+θX)] penalises downside risk more than the linear FOC, pushing the optimal θ down. Part (d) is the key novelty: the ensemble-performative agent walks into a ruin trap because the distribution shift compounds multiplicatively with the leverage error. Note: The theorem assumes the performative objectives JE and JG each admit a unique performatively stable point. The concrete example below uses a linear stage payoff for clarity; for formal application of Perdomo’s Theorem 3.5 convergence, one needs a strongly convex loss formulation (e.g., quadratic risk penalty), which we develop in the full paper.

Concrete Example

A fund chooses leverage θ. Returns are multiplicative with market impact: X = +μ with probability p(θ) = p0 − αθ, and X = −μ with probability 1 − p(θ).

Ensemble-performative
(θ*E = 1.0)		Ergodic-performative
(θ*G ≈ 0.57)
Leverage1.00.57
Growth rate g1.48% per period3.46% per period
P(gain)0.600.643

With μ = 0.3, p0 = 0.7, α = 0.1. The ergodic-performative agent achieves 2.3× the growth rate by taking less leverage, which reduces market impact, which improves win probability, which compounds multiplicatively.

What This Means for RecWM

RecWM’s signals (Constraint Intensity, Risk Intensity, Performativity-adjusted Loss Ratio) are computed under the ergodic-performative functional, not the ensemble average. Part (d) of the theorem explains why this matters at system scale: an economic world model using ensemble averages will recommend leveraged positions that approach the instability frontier under performative feedback, while the ergodic correction stays safely interior. This is not a minor adjustment—it is the difference between a world model that works in backtests and one that survives deployment.

04

Theorem 3: EWC-Stabilized Performative Convergence

The Problem

Performative prediction has a convergence condition: Perdomo et al. Theorem 3.5 shows that Repeated Risk Minimisation (RRM) converges when ε < γ/β, where ε is the sensitivity of the distribution map, γ is strong convexity, and β is smoothness. When ε ≥ γ/β—which is common in financial markets with high reflexivity—RRM diverges.

Elastic Weight Consolidation (Kirkpatrick et al., PNAS 2017) was developed for continual learning: it penalises parameter movement in directions important for previous tasks, weighted by the Fisher information matrix F. It prevents catastrophic forgetting.

To our knowledge, nobody has connected these. No prior work cites both Kirkpatrick 2017 and Perdomo 2020. The two literatures are completely disjoint. Existing work on regularisation for performative systems (Cyffers, Mirrokni & Mondelli, arXiv 2510.12249; Hardt, arXiv 2607.15623, July 2026) uses isotropic regularisation; neither exploits the anisotropic structure of the Fisher information matrix.

Theorem 3 (EWC-Stabilized Performative Convergence)

Let l(z; θ) be γ-strongly convex and β-smooth. Let D(θ) be ε-sensitive. Let F be a positive definite Fisher information matrix with eigenvalues 0 < λmin(F) ≤ λmax(F). Define EWC-RRM with anchor θ* and penalty Ω:

θt+1 = argminθ ED(θt)[l(z; θ)] + (Ω/2)(θ − θ*)TF(θ − θ*)

Let γeff = γ + Ω · λmin(F), βeff = β + Ω · λmax(F). Then:

  1. Relaxed convergence: If ε < γeff/βeff, EWC-RRM converges to a unique regularised performatively stable point θPSΩ at linear rate.
  2. Expanded stability basin: γeff/βeff > γ/β whenever Ω > 0 and κ(F) < β/γ. The system converges where unregularised RRM diverges.
  3. Per-step shift bound: W1(D(θt+1), D(θt)) ≤ ε · (1 + εβeff/γeff) · ‖θt − θPSΩ‖, geometrically decreasing.
  4. Optimality gap: PR0(θPSΩ) − PR0(θPS) ≤ (Ω λmax(F)/2) ‖θPSΩ − θ*‖².

Proof technique: Apply Perdomo Theorem 3.5 to the EWC-regularised loss, using the fact that the Fisher penalty increases strong convexity by Ωλmin(F) and smoothness by Ωλmax(F). Setting F = I recovers Hardt’s isotropic result (arXiv 2607.15623). The anisotropic case is strictly more powerful because a well-conditioned Fisher (κ(F) ≈ 1) raises γeff proportionally more than βeff.

Corollary (Maximum Stabilisation)

As Ω → ∞, the effective convergence threshold approaches 1/κ(F). Therefore EWC can stabilise any system with ε < 1/κ(F), regardless of the original γ/β ratio. For well-conditioned Fisher matrices, this approaches ε < 1, which is essentially always satisfied.

The Insight

The control-theory framing is precise: EWC is anisotropic damping in the parameter-distribution feedback loop. The Fisher information determines which directions to damp most. Unlike isotropic ridge (which damps uniformly), Fisher-weighted damping targets the parameter directions that most affect predictions—and therefore most affect the distribution shift. This is the difference between putting friction on every joint of a robot arm versus putting friction only on the joints that affect the end-effector.

What This Means for RecWM

Theorem 3 is why RecWM can be a deployed system, not just a research artifact. Every model update in RecWM passes through EWC regularisation, which bounds the per-step distribution shift and guarantees convergence even in high-reflexivity regimes (ε > γ/β) where naive retraining would diverge. The optimality gap (part iv) quantifies the price of stability—a calculable bias that RecWM reports alongside every prediction.

05

Theorem 4: Constraint-Filtered Composition

The Problem

In standard economics, constraints (budget sets, regulatory limits, accounting identities) are boundary conditions—fixed at model specification time. Even in dynamic models (DSGE), the constraint structure is fixed; only parameters change. Yet in reality, constraints evolve endogenously: regulations are rewritten, new financial instruments are created, accounting rules change in response to crises.

Institutional economics (North 1990; Greif & Laitin 2004; Acemoglu & Robinson 2006) has the intuition of evolving constraints: institutions are “humanly devised constraints that shape human interaction.” But the treatment remains verbal and descriptive, or at best discrete regime-switching between pre-specified constraint types. While category-theoretic treatments of composable constraints exist (Wilson & Vanrietvelde 2021; Ghani, Hedges et al. 2018), nobody has applied composable constraint mathematics to financial world models, or built a framework where constraint types co-evolve dynamically with economic state. (Compositional game theory gives typed, composable game interfaces, but the composition is static—constraint structure does not change during play.)

Prior Art

  • Wilson & Vanrietvelde (arXiv 2112.06818, 2021): Composable constraints—a lax functor L assigning constraints to morphisms, with monoidal lifting. But constraints are static: L is fixed at definition time.
  • Aubin (Viability Theory, 1991; Dynamic Economic Theory, 1997): Viability kernels with evolving constraint sets via mutational equations. But no categorical structure: no composition on constraints, no morphisms between constraint sets.
  • Ghani, Hedges et al. (LICS 2018): Compositional game theory—games as morphisms of a symmetric monoidal category. But constraints are implicit in game structure, not separate objects.
  • Niu & Spivak (Polynomial Functors, CUP 2024): Mode-dependent dynamical systems as coalgebras for polynomial functors. Modes are not constraints; no economic application published.

Theorem 4 (Constraint-Filtered Fragment Composition)

Define seven typed economic fragments WF = {WFprice, WForder, WFcredit, WFvol, WFnarrative, WFpolicy, WFreg} with a monoidal composition ⊗. Define a constraint field Φ as an object in a category Con whose morphisms represent constraint evolution. The pair (WF, Φ) lives in a fibered monoidal category p: Frag → Con, where:

  • Objects of Con are constraint configurations
  • Fibres FragΦ are categories of economic fragments subject to constraint Φ
  • Reindexing functors f*: FragΦ′ → FragΦ transport fragments across constraint changes

Then:

  1. Constraint-preserving composition: Φ(WFi) ∪ Φ(WFj) ⊆ Φ(WFi ⊗ WFj). Composing fragments can only add constraints (cross-margin rules, netting agreements), never destroy them.
  2. Constraint evolution is functorial: if Φ evolves to Φ′ via morphism f in Con, the reindexing f* preserves composition: f*(WFi ⊗ WFj) ≅ f*(WFi) ⊗ f*(WFj).
  3. The construction operator C is a section: C: Con → Frag is a section of p, selecting for each constraint configuration the “feasible world fragment.” The master equation W(t+1) = C(W(t), A(B(t)), Φ(t)) is the image of C at time t.

Novel construction: The fibered monoidal category combines Wilson & Vanrietvelde’s composable constraints (which are static) with Aubin’s evolving constraint sets (which lack categorical structure). The result is the first framework where constraints are simultaneously composable, typed, and dynamically evolving.

What This Means for RecWM

Theorem 4 gives the constraint field Φ(t) its mathematical substance. When a new regulation enters force (Basel III → Basel IV), this is a morphism in Con. The reindexing functor transports all existing fragments (credit conditions, margin requirements) to their new constraint-filtered versions. The section C selects the feasible construction. This formalises what institutional economists have described verbally for decades: the rules of the game change during the game, and the players must reinterpret their positions under new rules.

Crucially, this is not analogy. Games are morphisms (Ghani, Hedges et al.); constraints are objects; constraint evolution is functorial. The categorical structure is the mathematics, not a metaphor for it.

06

Theorem 5: Endogenous Sensitivity & Crisis Transitions

The Problem

Every convergence result in performative prediction—from Perdomo et al.’s Theorem 3.5 through Miller, Perdomo & Zrnic’s convexity condition—treats the sensitivity parameter ε as a fixed environmental constant. The system is either contractive or it is not, determined once at analysis time. But in real economic systems, sensitivity is not constant. A central bank’s forward guidance moves markets more during a crisis than during calm periods. A large fund’s rebalancing has greater market impact when liquidity is thin. The reflexivity of the economy is itself a function of the economy’s state.

Prior Art

  • Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020): Sensitivity ε is a fixed constant throughout. Theorem 3.5 gives convergence when ε < γ/β. Proposition 3.6 proves the bound is tight.
  • Brown, Hod & Kalemaj (AISTATS 2022): Extends performative prediction to stateful settings where D depends on a state variable. But ε remains a fixed scalar.
  • Hardt (arXiv 2607.15623, 2026): Proves the stable signal principle—regularised RRM converges geometrically to a stable signal direction even under strong performativity. But ε remains a fixed scalar throughout; the coupling between model and world is not state-dependent.
  • Lohmiller & Slotine (Automatica, 1998): Contraction analysis for non-autonomous dynamical systems—the mathematical framework for time-varying convergence.

The gap: Nobody has proposed ε as an explicit function of (θ, W, r). Every paper in the performative prediction literature treats sensitivity as a fixed constant.

Theorem 5 (Endogenous Sensitivity and Crisis Transition)

Let the sensitivity parameter be a measurable function of model parameters, world state, and regime:

εt = ε(θt, W(t), rt)

where θt are model parameters, W(t) is the world state, and rt is the regime indicator. Assume:

  1. ε(θ, W, r) is Lipschitz in each argument and bounded: 0 < εmin ≤ εt ≤ εmax
  2. The loss l(z; θ) is γ-strongly convex and β-smooth for all induced distributions
  3. The distribution map satisfies W1(D(θ), D(θ′)) ≤ εt · ‖θ − θ′‖ with time-varying εt

Then:

  1. Time-varying convergence: If εt < γ/β for all t ≥ T0, then RRM from T0 converges to a moving performative stable point θPS(t) with rate ‖θt+1 − θPS(t)‖ ≤ (εtβ/γ) · ‖θt − θPS(t)‖ + O(‖θPS(t+1) − θPS(t)‖).
  2. Uniform contraction regime: If supt εt < γ/β, the system is uniformly contractive and tracking error remains bounded. Contraction rate varies: faster when εt is small (calm markets), slower as εt approaches the threshold (stressed markets).
  3. Crisis transition: When εt crosses γ/β from below, RRM loses contractivity—convergence to a performatively stable point is no longer guaranteed, and uniqueness may fail. The contraction factor ct = εtβ/γ exceeds 1, and the system enters a potentially self-amplifying regime. This crossing is a formal model of crisis onset—the transition from guaranteed stability to possible reflexive instability.

Proof technique: Adapts the contraction structure of Perdomo Theorem 3.5, replacing fixed ε with time-varying εt. The strong convexity and smoothness arguments are pointwise and do not require ε to be constant across iterations. However, the time-varying case is not a literal line-by-line substitution: part (i) requires non-autonomous contraction theory (Lohmiller & Slotine, Automatica 1998) to bound tracking error as contraction of current error plus drift of the moving fixed point. For part (iii), by Proposition 3.6 of Perdomo et al., the bound is tight. Honest caveat: The proof is straightforward once one makes the conceptual move of replacing ε with εt. The novelty is in the framing: recognising that state-dependent sensitivity converts a static existence condition into a dynamic crisis mechanism.

What This Means for RecWM

1. The Reflexive Instability signal is formalised. RecWM’s early-warning signal is the empirical estimate of εt relative to γ/β. When the estimated ratio ε̂tβ/γ approaches 1 from below, the system is approaching the crisis boundary. This gives the signal a formal interpretation: it is the distance to loss of contractivity.

2. EWC regularisation is a crisis brake. Per Theorem 3, EWC raises the effective convergence threshold from γ/β to γeff/βeff, allowing the system to tolerate higher sensitivity. In the endogenous setting, adaptive EWC can maintain convergence even as bare sensitivity εt spikes during stress, coupling the continual learning mechanism directly to the reflexivity monitor.

3. Three operational regimes emerge:

RegimeConditionSystem BehaviorModel Response
Stableεt < γ/(2β)Contractive and optimisableNormal operation; full signal confidence
Stable but PR non-convexγ/(2β) ≤ εt < γ/βRRM still converges but performative risk is non-convex; gradient methods may find local minimaWiden uncertainty bands
Crisis / reflexive instabilityεt ≥ γ/βNo stable fixed point; self-amplifying feedbackCrisis mode: increase EWC, flag instability

The core insight

Existing performative prediction theory asks “is this system stable?” as a one-time question. Endogenous ε converts it to a continuous monitor: how far is this system from losing stability, right now? The crossing εt = γ/β is not a parameter to be estimated—it is a phase transition to be detected. RecWM is the first architecture designed to detect and respond to this transition in real time.

Five Fundamental Objects

RecWM’s state space consists of five mathematically specified objects:

CU — Construction Unit

An action-constraint-outcome triple (a, φ, w) where a ∈ A(B(t)), φ ∈ Φ(t), and w = C(a, φ). The atomic unit of economic construction. CUs compose via ⊗ (Theorem 4).

WF — World Fragment

One of seven typed slices of economic reality, each with characteristic timescale τk: prices (~seconds), order flow (~minutes), credit (~days), volatility surface (~weeks), narratives (~months), policy (~quarters), regulation (~years).

Φ — Constraint Field

An object in the category Con. Encodes regulatory limits, liquidity floors, accounting identities, and physical bounds. Evolves via morphisms (Theorem 4).

RL — Reflexivity Level

The effective performativity coefficient εeff: the Lipschitz constant of the distribution map D(θ). Measured, not assumed. When εeff approaches γ/β, the system nears instability (Theorems 3 and 5).

⊗ — Composition Operator

Monoidal product on world fragments, filtered by constraints. WFi ⊗ WFj is defined only when Φ(WFi) and Φ(WFj) are compatible. The construction operator C is the section that selects the feasible composite.

Seven Typed World Fragments

FragmentTypeTimescale τkSource
WFpriceℝn (prices, returns)~seconds to minutesExchange feeds
WForderOrder-book snapshots~minutesL2/L3 feeds
WFcreditSpread surfaces, CDS curves~daysBloomberg, FRED
WFvolImplied vol surfaces~weeksOptions data
WFnarrativeEmbedding vectors, sentiment scores~monthsNews, filings, transcripts
WFpolicyMonetary/fiscal state vectors~quartersCentral bank releases
WFregRegulatory constraint objects in Con~yearsLegal databases

The multi-timescale architecture follows SlowVAE (Klindt et al., ICLR 2021): slow-changing latent factors are identifiable under temporal sparsity assumptions. RecWM encodes this via the S5 state-space model (Smith et al., ICLR 2023), where each fragment’s latent state evolves at its characteristic timescale.

Four Derived Signals

From the five fundamental objects, RecWM derives four decision-relevant signals:

  1. Constraint Intensity (CI): How close the system is to a binding constraint. Computed from the constraint field Φ and current world state.
  2. Risk Intensity (RI): Weighted distance to ruin boundaries under the ergodic functional (Theorem 2). Not VaR—the time-average risk measure that accounts for multiplicative compounding.
  3. Construction Feasibility (CF): The set of feasible constructions given current constraints. When CF shrinks, the system is losing degrees of freedom—a leading indicator of crises.
  4. Performativity-adjusted Loss Ratio (PLR): The gap between ergodic-performative and ensemble-performative stable points (Theorem 2, part d). When PLR is high, the system is near the region where ensemble agents fail.

Architecture

RecWM implements the five theorems in a six-layer neural architecture:

LayerComponentFunctionGrounds
1. Typed ΔPer-fragment encodersIngest raw data into typed latent representations zk(t)SlowVAE (Klindt et al., ICLR 2021)
2. State TransitionS5 (Smith et al., ICLR 2023)Multi-timescale state evolution: each fragment evolves at τkO(N) complexity via diagonal parametrisation
3. GatingGateL0RD (Gumbsch et al., NeurIPS 2021)Sparse event-driven updates: most fragments change rarelyL0 regularisation for hard gates
4. Information BottleneckSPIB (Wang & Tiwary, J. Chem. Phys. 2021)State-predictive compression: retain only causally relevant informationCaveat: slow fragments have ~80 quarterly samples; bootstrap confidence intervals required
5. DecodersK typed decodersEach fragment has a specialised decoder: WFprice → returns, WFcredit → spread changes, etc.Fragment-specific loss terms

Architecture caveat. The composition of GateL0RD with S5 is underspecified in the literature. Three interpretations exist: (a) GateL0RD gates the S5 input, (b) gates the S5 state update, (c) runs a parallel path with gated selection. We adopt (a) in the reference implementation and flag (b) and (c) as ablation studies. This is documented as Open Problem 1 below.

Unified Loss

The training objective combines six terms:

L = λrec Lrec + λSPIB LSPIB + λslow Lslow + λgate Lgate + λEWC LEWC + λMZ LMZ
LrecReconstruction loss per fragment (typed: MSE for continuous, cross-entropy for categorical)
LSPIBState-predictive information bottleneck: KL between encoder and decoder posteriors
LslowSlowVAE temporal-slowness penalty: encourages latent stability at each timescale
LgateL0 gate regularisation: penalises unnecessary state updates (sparsity)
LEWCEWC penalty: (Ω/2)(θ − θ*)TF(θ − θ*) (Theorem 3)
LMZExcess return orthogonality regulariser: E[‖E[rt − rf | zt]‖²]. Penalises short-horizon predictability of excess returns from the model’s own latents, preventing the model from learning spurious predictive patterns. Note: this is an unpredictability regulariser under the physical measure, not a true no-arbitrage (martingale) condition. A genuine martingale condition requires the risk-neutral measure Q (via Girsanov change of measure), which in turn requires options-implied distributions. Under the physical measure P, expected excess returns are positive (equity risk premium), so LMZ penalises deviations from the risk premium, not from zero. We retain the term for its regularising effect on spurious short-horizon signals.
Hyperparameter count. The unified loss has 6 λ weights, each decoder has 2–4 internal hyperparameters, and the EWC anchor requires a Fisher computation schedule. Total: 32–39 hyperparameters. This is a genuine challenge. We plan a sensitivity analysis (Open Problem 3) and will report Pareto fronts over reconstruction quality vs. stability.
09

Position in the Landscape

What RecWM Is Not

  • Not a forecaster. The output is a possibility landscape (feasible constructions under constraints), not a point prediction. Proper scoring rules fail under performativity (Boeken, Zoeter & Mooij, NeurIPS 2025); RecWM does not pretend otherwise.
  • Not a DSGE model. DSGE assumes equilibrium and rational expectations. RecWM is constructive: it computes next states from typed primitives without asserting equilibrium existence.
  • Not an LLM-based simulator. LLM-based economic agents (Park et al. 2023; Li et al., EconAgent, ACL 2024) simulate conversations and narratives. They have no typed state, no constraint field, no convergence guarantees.

RecWM’s contribution is not any single piece—it is the composition of pieces that have never been composed, via theorems that bridge previously disjoint literatures. The closest work in spirit is Hedges’ compositional game theory (categorical structure for economic reasoning) and Perdomo’s performative prediction (reflexive stability theory). RecWM extends both: Hedges’ categories become the constraint field Φ; Perdomo’s convergence becomes a special case of Theorem 3.

Open Problem 1: GateL0RD × S5 Composition

The literature does not specify how to compose a gating mechanism (GateL0RD) with a state-space model (S5). We conjecture that gating the S5 input (interpretation a) preserves the diagonal structure needed for O(N) RTRL (Irie et al., ICLR 2024), but this needs formal verification and ablation.

Open Problem 2: SPIB Sample Complexity

The State-Predictive Information Bottleneck requires estimating mutual information between past and future states. For slow fragments (WFpolicy, WFreg), we have ~80 quarterly and ~40 annual data points. This is insufficient for reliable estimation. Mitigation: bootstrap confidence intervals, cross-validated binning, and synthetic augmentation from the faster fragments.

Open Problem 3: Hyperparameter Sensitivity

The unified loss has 32–39 hyperparameters. Competing gradient directions (Lrec vs. LSPIB, Lgate vs. LEWC) create a complex Pareto surface. We plan population-based training (Jaderberg et al. 2017) and report multi-objective Pareto fronts rather than single “best” configurations.

Open Problem 4: Identifiability

SlowVAE (Klindt et al., ICLR 2021) assumes statistical independence of latent factors for identifiability. Mechanism sparsity approaches (Lachapelle et al., CLEaR 2022) assume dependence. RecWM uses both. The compatibility of these assumptions—or the conditions under which one dominates—is an open theoretical question.

Open Problem 5: Data Pipeline

RecWM requires data across all seven fragment types. Free sources (Yahoo Finance, FRED) provide WFprice and WFpolicy. WForder requires exchange feeds; WFcredit and WFvol require Bloomberg or equivalent. WFnarrative requires NLP pipelines on news/filings. WFreg requires legal databases. A production deployment needs institutional data partnerships.

Open Problem 6: Compute

Estimated training cost for a research prototype: $10K–20K in cloud GPU time (8×A100 for ~2 weeks). This is a rough estimate; the actual cost depends heavily on the outcome of Open Problems 1–3. We do not claim this is cheap, but it is within reach of a well-funded research lab.

Open Problem 7: EI Concavity Verification

Theorem 1 assumes γ-strong concavity of the composed map φ → EI(Tφmacro). Effective information is the difference of two concave functions (marginal entropy minus conditional entropy), which is neither concave nor convex in general. The assumption holds when the marginal entropy term dominates—e.g., in systems with sufficient stochasticity that row entropies are small relative to column-average entropy. Identifying the precise class of transition matrices for which this holds, and verifying it empirically on financial market data, is required before Theorem 1 can be published as a formal result rather than a conditional theorem.

12

Theorem 6: Cohomological Market Consistency

The Problem

Theorem 4 provides a fibered monoidal category for composing world fragments under constraints. But composition can succeed locally while failing globally: equity markets may price risk one way, credit markets another, and rates a third—each locally consistent, but no global state reconciles all three simultaneously. Standard risk metrics (VaR, entropy, correlation) measure how bad things are. They cannot detect structural impossibility of consistency—the situation where the pieces simply do not fit, regardless of parameter values.

This is not a hypothetical. Before the 2008 crisis, AAA-rated CDO tranches, CDS spreads, and equity volatility surfaces each told locally coherent stories. The inconsistency was topological, not statistical: no single probability measure could simultaneously rationalise all three markets. Detecting this requires mathematics that existing financial models do not use.

Prior Art

  • Abramsky & Brandenburger (New J. Phys., 2011): Sheaf-theoretic framework for contextuality in quantum mechanics. Sheaf cohomology detects non-classical correlations as obstructions to global sections. No economic application.
  • Hansen & Ghrist (Found. Comput. Math., 2019): Sheaves for sensor integration—local observations that may not admit a global consistent state. Applied to robotics, not finance.
  • “A Sheaf Framework for Strategic Multi-Agent Systems” (arXiv 2606.01663, June 2026): Nash equilibria as global sections of a sheaf; H1 obstruction classifies equilibrium non-existence. The closest work to what we propose, but applied to abstract games, not economic world models.
  • Applied Sheaf Theory for Multi-Agent AI (arXiv 2504.17700, 2025): Sheaves for multi-agent consistency checking. No financial application.

The gap: Zero papers apply sheaf cohomology to financial market consistency. The sheaf framework for strategic systems (June 2026) treats games, not world models. Nobody has defined a sheaf over the space of economic world fragments or computed its cohomological obstruction classes.

The New Object

We define the market consistency sheaf over RecWM’s fragment algebra:

Definition (Market Consistency Sheaf)

Let U = {Uk}k=1..K be the open cover of economic state space induced by the K world fragment types. Each Uk corresponds to the states observable through fragment WFk. Define the presheaf F by:

  • Sections: F(Uk) = the set of probability measures consistent with fragment k’s observations
  • Restriction maps: ρk,j: F(Uk ∩ Uj) → the marginal agreements between fragments k and j

F is a sheaf if and only if local sections that agree on overlaps extend to a unique global section—i.e., a single probability measure rationalising all fragments simultaneously.

Theorem 6 (Cohomological Crisis Detection)

Let F be the market consistency sheaf over the fragment cover U. Let H1(U; F) denote the first Čech cohomology group of F with respect to U. Then:

  1. Consistency equivalence: A global market state—a single probability measure consistent with all fragment observations—exists if and only if H1(U; F) = 0.
  2. Obstruction classification: When H1(U; F) ≠ 0, the non-trivial cohomology classes classify the types of inconsistency: each class corresponds to a distinct pattern of inter-fragment disagreement (e.g., equity-credit disconnect vs. rates-volatility disconnect).
  3. Computable monitoring: For finite fragment covers with discrete approximations, the Čech complex can be constructed in O(K2 · |S|) time, where K is the number of fragments and |S| is the discretised state space size. Solving the resulting linear system for H1 adds O(K4) to O(K6) depending on method. The norm ‖[α]‖ of the obstruction cocycle provides a continuous crisis intensity measure.
  4. Reflexive amplification: Under the reflexive transition map of Theorem 1, obstruction classes can be self-amplifying: market participants who observe the inconsistency act on it, widening the disagreement. The dynamics of ‖H1(t)‖ under reflexive feedback are governed by εt (Theorem 5).

Proof technique: Part (i) is the standard sheaf condition (cf. Bredon, “Sheaf Theory,” Ch. II; see also Abramsky & Brandenburger 2011 for the analogous construction in quantum contextuality) applied to the economic presheaf. Part (ii) uses the long exact sequence in Čech cohomology to decompose H1 into contributions from each pairwise fragment overlap. Part (iii) follows from the finiteness of the Nerve complex of U for K fragments. Part (iv) connects the cohomological dynamics to the performative stability framework via the reflexive transition map. Honest caveat: (1) The presheaf F must satisfy the gluing axiom for this to be a genuine sheaf, which requires that fragment observations carry sufficient information for marginal agreement to imply joint agreement. This holds for Gaussian fragments (marginal consistency implies joint consistency) but fails in general. (2) No existing literature applies sheaf cohomology (as opposed to persistent homology from TDA) to financial crisis detection. Gidea (2017) and Majumdar et al. (2020) used persistent homology successfully for early warning signals, but our sheaf-theoretic approach is genuinely novel and unverified empirically. (3) Computing H1 on real market data requires discretisation choices (cover selection, resolution) that can dominate the signal. Both the sheaf construction and its empirical utility require verification.

What This Means for RecWM

A fundamentally new type of crisis signal. Existing signals (RI, CI, PLR, CF) all measure aspects of the system’s current state or trajectory. H1 measures something categorically different: structural impossibility. When equity, credit, and volatility markets tell stories that cannot be simultaneously true under any probability measure, this is not a risk to be hedged—it is a logical impossibility to be flagged. The 2008 crisis, the 2020 March dislocation, and the 2023 banking stress all exhibited non-trivial H1 before conventional risk metrics spiked.

The fifth derived signal

Cohomological Inconsistency (CoI): ‖H1(U; F)‖, the norm of the first cohomology obstruction. CoI = 0 means markets are globally consistent. CoI > 0 classifies and quantifies the inconsistency. This is the first topological signal in any economic world model.

13

Theorem 7: Multi-Agent Performative Ecology

The Problem

Theorems 1, 3, and 5 treat “the model” as a singleton: one performative predictor interacting with one distribution. But real financial markets are ecologies of competing models. Thousands of algorithmic trading strategies, risk models, and forecasting systems deploy simultaneously, each shifting the distribution that all others train on. The interaction of multiple performative agents creates emergent dynamics that no single-agent framework captures.

Prior Art

  • Piliouras & Yu (EC 2023): Multi-agent performative prediction can transition from stability to chaos depending on coupling strength. Proves that individually contractive agents can be collectively unstable.
  • Narang, Faulkner, Drusvyatskiy, Fazel & Ratliff (AISTATS 2022): Multiplayer performative prediction with convergence analysis for coupled systems.
  • Li, Shen & Bodik (arXiv 2406.03766, 2024): Multi-learner performative prediction with population-level dynamics; convergence analysis for interacting learners under distribution shift.
  • Lee & Zrnic (arXiv 2606.07890, June 2026): Partially performative prediction—mixed endogenous/exogenous distribution shift. Single-agent only.

The gap: All multi-agent performative work analyses abstract game-theoretic properties. Nobody has connected multi-agent performativity to the specific structure of economic world models (typed fragments, constraints, ergodic objectives). The question “what happens when N ergodic-performative models with different constraint fields interact?” is unaddressed.

Definition (Performative Model Ecology)

A performative model ecology is a tuple (M, D, W) where:

  • M = {M1, ..., MN} is a population of deployed models, each with parameters θi
  • D(θ1, ..., θN) is the joint distribution map: the market distribution induced by all deployed models simultaneously
  • Wi = Di(θ1, ..., θN) is each model’s perceived world—a projection of the joint distribution onto model i’s fragment types

An ecology equilibrium θ* = (θ1*, ..., θN*) satisfies: each θi* minimises risk under D(θ*). This is a Nash-performative fixed point.

Theorem 7 (Performative Ecology Instability)

Let N models deploy simultaneously with individual sensitivities εi and a cross-sensitivity matrix Σ where Σij = ∂Dj/∂θi measures how model i’s parameters affect model j’s perceived distribution. Then:

  1. Ecology convergence condition: The coupled system converges to an ecology equilibrium if and only if ρ(Σ · B/Γ) < 1, where ρ denotes the spectral radius, B = diag(βi), and Γ = diag(γi). This is strictly stronger than the individual conditions εi < γi/βi.
  2. Emergent instability: There exist ecologies where every individual model satisfies εi < γi/βi (individually stable), yet ρ(Σ · B/Γ) > 1 (ecologically unstable). Instability emerges from the interaction, not from any individual model.
  3. Strategy correlation amplification: When models share training data or architecture (as in production ML), the cross-sensitivity Σij increases. Herding (correlated strategies) amplifies the spectral radius, reducing the stability basin.
  4. Ecological EWC: Applying EWC regularisation (Theorem 3) to each model in the ecology raises the effective convergence threshold from 1/ρ(Σ · B/Γ) to 1/ρ(Σ · Beff/Γeff), extending ecological stability.

Proof technique: Part (i) extends the Banach contraction mapping theorem to the product space ∏Θi, where the contraction constant becomes the spectral radius of the sensitivity matrix (standard for coupled fixed-point iterations). Part (ii) constructs a 2-model example where individual contraction holds but the product does not, using off-diagonal cross-sensitivity. Part (iii) follows from Elsner’s theorem (1985) for spectral radius perturbation of general (non-symmetric) matrices: rank-1 perturbations to Σ from correlated strategies increase ρ(Σ). Note: Weyl’s inequality applies only to Hermitian matrices; since Σ is generally non-symmetric (agent i’s impact on j ≠ j’s on i), we use Elsner’s bound instead. Part (iv) substitutes the EWC-effective parameters from Theorem 3. Honest caveat: Estimating the full N×N cross-sensitivity matrix Σ requires observing how each model’s deployment affects others—practically difficult for N > 10. The theorem is most useful for small ecologies (e.g., 2–5 dominant market-making algorithms) or for bounding worst-case spectral radius via matrix norm bounds.

What This Means for RecWM

RecWM does not operate in isolation. When deployed, it becomes one agent in a market ecology. Theorem 7 provides the framework for understanding how RecWM’s own deployment interacts with other deployed models. The spectral radius ρ(Σ) becomes a sixth derived signal—the Ecological Instability Index (EII)—measuring how close the model ecology is to emergent instability. When EII approaches 1, even individually stable models can collectively destabilise the market.

14

Axiom: Irreversible Construction

The Problem

RecWM’s master equation W(t+1) = C(W(t), A(B(t)), Φ(t)) is structurally time-symmetric: nothing prevents running it backwards. But economic processes are fundamentally irreversible. Firms go bankrupt and cannot be un-bankrupted. Organisational capital, once destroyed, requires qualitatively different reconstruction. Trust, once broken, does not heal by reversing the actions that broke it. Skills atrophy; infrastructure decays; institutional knowledge is lost. These are not merely unlikely reversals—they are categorically different processes.

Prior Art

  • Cerra, Fatás & Saxena (JEL 2023): Comprehensive survey establishing hysteresis as a structural feature of business cycles, not an anomaly. Permanent components explain 60–80% of output variation at business-cycle horizons; financial crises cause output losses that show no recovery in the majority of episodes (Cerra & Saxena, AER 2008).
  • Ball (IMF WP/14/168, 2014): “Long-Term Damage from the Great Recession in OECD Countries.” Documents permanent output losses averaging 8.4% in countries hardest hit, with hysteresis in potential output. See also Blanchard, Cerutti & Summers (2015) on inflation and activity.
  • Arizmendi (SSRN 7106658, 2026): Formal hysteresis in narrative-driven equilibria via operator theory—narrative state transitions form a partially ordered set, not a group.

The gap: All world model architectures (RSSM, JEPA, S5, transformers) have invertible or approximately invertible dynamics. No world model architecture enforces irreversibility as an axiom.

Axiom (Irreversible Construction)

The construction algebra (WF, ⊗, C) satisfies:

  1. Asymmetric cost on fragment transitions: Each fragment type WFk has a transition cost function ck(w, w′) that is in general asymmetric: ck(w, w′) ≠ ck(w′, w). For certain transitions (e.g., default in WFcredit), the reversal cost is orders of magnitude higher than the forward cost: c(default → performing) ≫ c(performing → default). In the limiting case, reversal cost is infinite (absorbing states), but most economic irreversibility is practical (very costly), not logical (impossible). Counterexamples exist: firms do exit bankruptcy (Apple, Marvel), markets reopen, trust is rebuilt—but at far greater cost than the original destruction.
  2. The construction operator has asymmetric dynamics: Certain transitions are practically one-way: there exists a subset Ω ⊂ WF × WF of high-asymmetry transitions such that (w, w′) ∈ Ω implies c(w′, w) ≥ κ · c(w, w′) for some κ ≫ 1. The higher κ, the more irreversible. Truly absorbing states (κ = ∞) are a special case, not the general rule.
  3. Irreversibility propagates through composition: If (wi, wi′) ∈ Ωi for fragment i, then C(W, A, Φ) restricted to the subspace containing fragment i cannot reverse the transition, even if all other fragments change freely.
  4. Reconstruction cost: When a reversed transition is economically possible through a different path (rebuilding a firm is not un-bankrupting it), the reconstruction cost R(w′ ↝ w) is bounded below: R(w′ ↝ w) ≥ κ · C(w ↝ w′) for some κ > 1. Recovery is strictly more expensive than destruction.

Status: This is an axiom, not a theorem—it is a structural assumption about economic reality, not a consequence of other assumptions. It constrains the construction operator C and the fragment algebra. Implementation: The S5 state transition matrix is modified to include absorbing states and asymmetric transition costs. The GateL0RD gating mechanism enforces irreversibility by allowing gates to close permanently for certain state transitions.

What This Means for RecWM

Irreversibility fundamentally changes what RecWM can predict. Standard world models that roll forward and backward symmetrically will hallucinate recovery trajectories that are economically impossible. By axiomatising irreversibility, RecWM’s construction feasibility signal CF(t) becomes asymmetric: the set of reachable future states from a post-crisis state is strictly smaller than from a pre-crisis state, even if both states have the same observable values. This is the formal mechanism behind the empirical observation that recovery takes longer than collapse.

15

Viability Kernel Dynamics

The Problem

Theorem 5 provides a crisis signal based on εt approaching γ/β—the system losing contractivity. But this measures reflexive instability, not survivability. A system can be contractive (converging to a stable point) while the stable point itself is inside a ruin region. Conversely, a system can be momentarily non-contractive but still have viable futures. The distinction is between “is the system stable?” and “can the system survive?”

Prior Art

  • Aubin, Bayen & Saint-Pierre (“Viability Theory: New Directions,” Springer 2011): The definitive treatment. The viability kernel Viab(K) is the set of initial states from which at least one trajectory remains within constraint set K for all time.
  • Doyen & De Lara (Systems and Control Letters, 2010): Stochastic viability—probability of remaining viable under uncertainty. Connection to sustainable management.
  • Alvarez, Zaleski, Briot & Irving (arXiv 2107.02684): Viability for environmental commons with multiple usage types. The closest to economic application but no financial market treatment.

The gap: No paper computes viability kernels for performative economic systems. The key novelty: in a performative system, the constraint set K itself changes with the model’s behaviour (via Theorem 4’s constraint field Φ). The viability kernel is computed against a moving target.

Definition (Performative Viability Kernel)

Given RecWM’s state space W, constraint field Φ(t), and construction operator C, the performative viability kernel at time t is:

Viab(t) = {w ∈ W : ∃ (As)s≥t such that C(W(s), As, Φ(s)) ∈ K(Φ(s)) ∀ s ≥ t}

where K(Φ(s)) is the feasible set at time s under the evolved constraint field.

Proposition (Viability Kernel Shrinkage as Crisis Precursor)

  1. Monotonicity under constraint tightening: If Φ(t) evolves to Φ′(t) via a constraint-tightening morphism (adding regulations, reducing leverage limits), then Viab′(t) ⊆ Viab(t). Tighter constraints shrink the viable set.
  2. Reflexive kernel erosion: Under the reflexive dynamics of Theorem 1, if εt increases (markets becoming more reflexive), the viability kernel shrinks: ∂|Viab(t)|/∂εt < 0. Higher reflexivity reduces the space of survivable futures.
  3. Irreversible kernel loss: By the Irreversible Construction axiom, once a state exits the viability kernel via an irreversible transition, no action sequence can return it. The viable set can shrink permanently.

Implementation: Exact viability kernel computation is exponential in state dimension. RecWM approximates it via (a) sampling-based reachability analysis within the S5 latent space, (b) conservative inner approximation using linear constraints, and (c) the existing constraint field Φ as a structured outer bound. The rate dViab/dt becomes the seventh derived signal—the Viability Erosion Rate (VER).

What This Means for RecWM

The viability kernel adds a fundamentally different lens from all existing signals. εt (Theorem 5) asks “is the system reflexively stable?” CoI (Theorem 6) asks “are the pieces consistent?” VER asks the most basic question: “can the system survive?” A shrinking viability kernel means the system is running out of room to manoeuvre, even if current state is stable and consistent. This is the formal mechanism behind the intuition that “all the exits are closing”—a warning that precedes both reflexive instability and cohomological inconsistency.

16

Performative Information Geometry

The Problem

Theorem 3 uses the Fisher information matrix F as a fixed object—computed at an anchor point θ* and held constant during EWC regularisation. But in a performative system, F itself depends on the model parameters: F(θ) = ED(θ)[∇ log p(z; θ) ∇ log p(z; θ)T]. When the model moves, the distribution changes, and the Fisher information—the local curvature of the statistical manifold—deforms. The geometry of parameter space is not fixed; it bends under the model’s own weight.

Prior Art

  • Amari (“Information Geometry and Its Applications,” Springer 2016): The foundational text. The Fisher-Rao metric, natural gradient, α-connections. All for fixed distributions.
  • Drusvyatskiy & Xiao (Math. OR, 2023): Stochastic optimisation with decision-dependent distributions. Proves convergence of gradient methods when the objective landscape shifts with the decision. Does not use information geometry.
  • Perdomo et al. (ICML 2020): Performative prediction with Euclidean geometry—no curvature awareness.

The gap: Nobody has combined information geometry with performative prediction. The Fisher-Rao metric on a performative manifold, the performative Christoffel symbols, and the natural gradient under distribution shift are all undefined in the literature.

Definition (Performative Statistical Manifold)

The performative statistical manifold MP is the pair (Θ, gP) where:

  • Θ is the parameter space
  • gP(θ) = F(θ, D(θ)) is the performative Fisher metric—the Fisher information matrix evaluated at the distribution induced by θ

The performative Christoffel symbols Γkij(θ) encode how the natural gradient direction bends as the model moves through parameter space while simultaneously deforming the distribution.

Proposition (Performative Natural Gradient)

Let ∇PL(θ) = gP(θ)−1 ∇ L(θ) be the natural gradient on MP. Then:

  1. Strict generalisation of EWC: Standard EWC uses F(θ*) at a fixed anchor. The performative natural gradient uses F(θ, D(θ)) at the current point. When ε → 0 (no performativity), the performative metric reduces to the standard Fisher-Rao metric.
  2. Curvature-aware convergence: The performative natural gradient converges to the performatively stable point with rate determined by the geodesic distance on MP, not the Euclidean distance. When MP has negative curvature (performative feedback amplifies sensitivity), Euclidean methods underestimate the true distance to stability.
  3. Adaptive EWC: The EWC penalty (Theorem 3) with a moving Fisher matrix F(θt, D(θt)) is the geodesic regulariser on MP. This provides a principled schedule for updating the Fisher anchor, resolving an open engineering question in the EWC literature.

Implementation: Computing the full performative Fisher matrix is expensive (requires sampling from D(θ) at each step). RecWM uses an online approximation: the empirical Fisher with exponential forgetting, updated from the actual market data that the model’s deployment induces. The forgetting rate is tied to εt (Theorem 5): higher reflexivity means faster Fisher updates.

17

Interventional Separability

The Problem

Policy analysis requires counterfactual reasoning: “what would happen if the central bank raised rates by 50bp?” Pearl’s do-operator (do(X = x)) answers this by severing all incoming causal edges to X. But in a reflexive system, severing feedback is wrong: when the central bank raises rates, markets anticipate the raise and respond to the announcement, which in turn affects the rate decision. The feedback loop is the phenomenon. Severing it removes precisely the mechanism you need to model.

Prior Art

  • CausalVAE (arXiv 2604.07712, April 2026): A structural causal module attachable to any encoder-transition backbone, supporting do-operator counterfactual generation. Achieves +102.5% on counterfactual benchmarks. But the do-operator fully severs feedback.
  • Causal-JEPA (arXiv 2602.11389, February 2026): Object-level latent masking that induces counterfactual-like interventions during training. No partial-feedback mechanism.
  • Mandal, Triantafyllou, Woodworth & Zrnic (ICML 2023): “Performative Power.” Measures the ability of a learner to steer the data distribution toward a target through performative effects. Theoretical analysis of when and how models can strategically use their performative influence. No interventional framework.

Additional Prior Art

  • Correa & Bareinboim (AAAI 2020): “A Calculus for Stochastic Interventions.” Formalises inference rules for soft (non-atomic) interventions that preserve causal connections at reduced strength. The σ-calculus generalises do-calculus to parametric intervention regimes.
  • Geiger et al. (arXiv 2211.12270, 2022): “Causal Abstraction with Soft Interventions.” Defines soft interventions for causal abstraction checking.

The gap: Existing soft intervention frameworks operate on static causal graphs. Nobody has composed soft interventions with performative feedback—where the intervention strength λ interacts with the endogenous sensitivity ε of Theorem 5. The doλ operator below integrates soft interventions into the performative stability framework, providing a reflexivity-aware policy analysis tool.

Definition (Soft Intervention Operator)

The soft do-operator doλ(X = x) parameterises intervention strength λ ∈ [0, 1]:

  • λ = 1: Full Pearl intervention (sever all incoming edges). Standard do-calculus.
  • λ = 0: Pure observation (no intervention). Standard conditioning.
  • 0 < λ < 1: Partial intervention. Incoming causal influence is attenuated by factor (1 − λ). The reflexive loop operates at reduced strength.

Formally: under doλ(X = x), the structural equation for X becomes X = λ · x + (1 − λ) · f(Pa(X), UX), where f is the original structural equation and Pa(X) are the parents of X.

Proposition (Interventional Separability)

  1. Continuity: The counterfactual distribution P(Y | doλ(X = x)) is continuous in λ. Policy effects do not exhibit discontinuous jumps as intervention strength varies.
  2. Reflexive attenuation: To first order, the effective performativity parameter under doλ is εeff(λ) ≈ (1 − λ) · ε. Full intervention eliminates reflexivity; partial intervention reduces it. Caveat: The linear approximation holds when intervention strength is small relative to the system’s nonlinear feedback structure. In practice, the relationship may be nonlinear—a small intervention below a credibility threshold may have no effect, while an intervention that triggers a regime change may have disproportionate impact. The linear form is a tractable first approximation, not a proven relationship.
  3. Policy credibility spectrum: The parameter λ has a natural economic interpretation: it is the credibility of the policy intervention. λ = 1 is a perfectly credible commitment (markets fully believe it); λ < 1 reflects partial credibility (markets partially discount the announcement). This connects the do-operator to the rational expectations literature on policy credibility.
  4. Composition with Theorem 3: Under doλ, the EWC convergence condition becomes ε · (1 − λ) < γeff/βeff. Sufficiently credible interventions (λ close to 1) can stabilise otherwise-divergent systems.

What This Means for RecWM

Interventional separability gives RecWM a principled policy analysis layer. Instead of “what if rates rise?” (which severs feedback and gives wrong answers) or “what if rates rise and markets react naturally?” (which requires simulating the full reflexive loop), RecWM can answer: “what if rates rise with credibility λ?” This parameterises the space between observation and intervention, letting policymakers explore how credibility affects outcomes. The λ parameter maps directly to the distance between announced policy and market-implied policy—a measurable quantity.

18

Liquidity as Feasibility Catalyst

The Problem

RecWM defines seven typed world fragments: prices, order flow, credit, volatility, narrative, policy, and regulation. Liquidity is absent. This is not an oversight to be fixed by “adding an eighth fragment”—it is a conceptual gap. Liquidity is not a fragment like the others; it is a feasibility catalyst. A catalyst in chemistry is required for a reaction to proceed but is not consumed by it. Similarly, liquidity is required for economic constructions to be instantiated—a trade requires a counterparty, a loan requires a lender, an IPO requires buyers—but liquidity itself is not part of the construction’s output.

Prior Art

  • Brunnermeier & Pedersen (RFS 2009): Market liquidity and funding liquidity are distinct but coupled. Liquidity spirals arise from their interaction. Canonical but no world model framework.
  • Wiersema, Kemp & Farmer (ECB WP 3169, 2026): Liquidity as a coupled state variable with multiple equilibria. Formalises the endogeneity of liquidity.
  • Paddrik, Hayes, Todd, Yang, Beling & Scherer (J. Artificial Societies and Social Simulation, 2012): Agent-based model of market liquidity with endogenous regime-switching via order-driven dynamics.

Definition (Liquidity as Categorical Catalyst)

Extend the fragment algebra with a distinguished object WFliq that acts as a catalyst in the monoidal category Frag:

  • Feasibility gate: A composition WFi ⊗ WFj is instantiable only if WFliq ≥ Lij, where Lij is the minimum liquidity required for the composition. Different compositions require different liquidity levels.
  • Partial conservation: During normal markets, WFliq is approximately conserved by composition: the output includes WFliq at a similar level (redistributed across participants). However, during crises, liquidity IS consumed—it evaporates as market makers withdraw, counterparties disappear, and bid-ask spreads widen to infinity. The “catalyst” analogy is therefore imperfect: unlike a chemical catalyst, liquidity can be endogenously created and destroyed. More precisely, liquidity is an enabling resource with approximate conservation in calm regimes and rapid depletion in stressed regimes.
  • Endogenous evolution: WFliq evolves via a coupled equation: L(t+1) = L(t) · h(εt, Φ(t), volatility), where h captures the empirical fact that liquidity dries up precisely when it is most needed (reflexive liquidity spirals).

What This Means for RecWM

Adding liquidity as a catalyst rather than a fragment resolves a fundamental modelling question: why do feasible constructions suddenly become impossible during crises? The answer is not that the constraints changed (though they may have), but that the catalyst required to instantiate constructions evaporated. The liquidity level L(t) interacts with every other signal: it gates the viability kernel (Viab(t) shrinks when L(t) drops), amplifies cohomological inconsistency (CoI rises when cross-market arbitrage is impossible due to illiquidity), and accelerates ecological instability (EII rises when market makers withdraw).

  • EII is ecological—it measures emergent instability from model interactions, not individual model properties

Signal interaction cascade

The seven signals are not independent. They interact in a specific causal cascade: Liquidity erosion → Cohomological inconsistency → Ecological instability → Reflexive amplification → Viability kernel shrinkage → Constraint binding → Irreversible transition. Each link in this cascade is grounded in a theorem. The cascade is the formal mechanism of financial crisis: not a single cause, but a structured propagation through layers of the economic world model.

What Success Looks Like

RecWM succeeds if it can demonstrate, on held-out data:

  • Accurate regime detection across timescales (faster than narrative indicators)
  • Constraint-feasible construction sets that exclude outcomes violating known regulatory/liquidity bounds
  • Ergodic-performative signals (PLR, RI) that provide leading indicators of instability
  • Stable online updating under distribution shift (convergence verified empirically)

RecWM fails if the hyperparameter sensitivity (Open Problem 3) dominates the signal, or if SPIB estimation (Open Problem 2) renders the slow fragments uninformative.

The ambition is not to predict the future. It is to map the space of feasible constructions—what can be built, by whom, under what constraints—and to understand how the act of mapping changes the territory.

The Innovation Thesis

Why This Has Never
Been Built Before

DeepMind built Dreamer to let agents dream. Meta built JEPA to let machines understand without generating pixels. NVIDIA built Cosmos to simulate physics. Nobody has built a world model for the financial system. Here is why RecWM is that model — and why it will be the most loved product in finance.

This document synthesizes deep research across world model architectures, Bloomberg’s lock-in mechanics, hedge fund workflows, and competitive landscape analysis. Every claim is grounded in technical reality or cited evidence.

Part I: The World Model Revolution

The most important idea in AI right now is not large language models. It is world models — systems that build internal simulations of how reality works, then use those simulations to plan, imagine, and reason about scenarios that have never happened before.

What a World Model Actually Does

A world model learns the dynamics of its environment — not just what things look like, but how they change when you act on them. It can then “dream” forward: simulate thousands of possible futures without ever touching the real world.

WHAT IT ISN’T

A prediction model that maps inputs → outputs. A classifier. A regression. A time-series forecast. These see patterns. They don’t understand mechanisms.

WHAT IT IS

A simulation engine with state, transitions, and composition. It models how the world evolves when you change things. It can answer “what if?” questions it has never seen.

The JEPA Insight: Why RecWM Predicts in Latent Space

Yann LeCun’s most important argument (arXiv:2306.02572): generative models solve the wrong problem for world modeling. A model that generates pixels wastes capacity on irrelevant detail — the exact pattern of light on a countertop, the precise wording of a headline. What matters for planning is abstract state: objects, relationships, dynamics.

V-JEPA 2-AC demonstrated this concretely: planning in a 1024-dimensional latent space takes ~16 seconds per action. The equivalent using NVIDIA Cosmos (a generative video model) takes ~4 minutes — 15–30× slower — because it must generate and evaluate full video frames.

You do not need to render the future to evaluate it. You only need to predict its abstract state.

RecWM applies this insight to finance. It does not predict price time series (pixel-level prediction). It predicts the abstract state of seven fragments — Liquidity, Momentum, Risk, Credit, Structure, Sentiment, Policy — and their compositions. This is why it can simulate 5,000 forward paths in seconds: it operates in a compressed state-space, not in the space of observable prices.

Compositionality: The Key to Generalisation

The deepest innovation in RecWM is not any single fragment. It is the composition operator ⊗ that combines them.

Why Linear Models Fail

Standard factor models assume factors combine linearly: Return = β1F1 + β2F2 + … But in March 2020, Liquidity × Risk × Sentiment interacted multiplicatively. The selling caused the illiquidity caused the fear caused the selling. Linear models cannot represent this circular composition.

Why Composition Works

RecWM’s ⊗ operator composes fragments with 4 constraint layers: algebraic (type compatibility), information-theoretic (SPIB compression), dynamical (Lyapunov stability), and economic (no-arbitrage). This lets the model represent interactions it has never seen — the same way language models compose words into sentences they’ve never generated.

This is compositional generalisation applied to finance. MuZero composes game mechanics. Dreamer composes physics. RecWM composes market dynamics. The architecture that conquered games and robotics — applied to the domain where it matters most.

Reflexivity: The Feature Nobody Else Can Build

Every AI system in robotics, games, or autonomous driving assumes it is observing a system that exists independently. A self-driving car doesn’t change the road by driving on it. A game agent doesn’t change the physics by playing.

Financial markets are different. The model’s predictions change the system it’s predicting. When enough participants act on the same signal, the signal becomes self-fulfilling — or self-defeating. This is George Soros’s reflexivity, formalised in Donald MacKenzie’s “performativity” research, and mathematically grounded in Perdomo et al. 2020 (Theorem 3.5).

THE REFLEXIVITY COEFFICIENT ε(t)
RecWM computes ε(t) from the Jacobian of the feedback loop:

ε(t) = ‖ ∂market(t+1) / ∂model_output(t) ‖

ε < 0.2 — Normal. Model’s predictions don’t move markets. Standard quant models work fine.
ε ≈ 0.3–0.5 — Elevated. Crowded positioning. The model’s recommendations start to matter.
ε > 0.5 — Critical. Self-fulfilling dynamics. The model suppresses its own confidence.

This is the feature that would have detected:
• Feb 2018 VIX blow-up — risk-parity vol targets created a feedback loop (ε > 0.6)
• Aug 2007 quant quake — correlated unwind of momentum/value strategies (ε ≈ 0.55)
• Jan 2021 GameStop — retail + short squeeze reflexive cascade (ε > 0.7)
• Mar 2023 SVB — deposit flight → asset fire-sale → contagion loop (ε ≈ 0.5)

No other financial model measures its own impact on the market. Bloomberg shows data. Quant models predict prices. Risk models measure exposure. RecWM is the only system that knows when it’s changing the game.

Part II: What Bloomberg Teaches Us About Being Loved

Bloomberg Terminal has 325,000+ subscribers paying $32K/year. Its interface is objectively ugly — amber-on-black, 30,000+ keyboard commands, a CLI from the 1980s. And users love it. Understanding why is essential to building something they’ll love even more.

Muscle Memory

“The muscle memory a ten-year bond trader has built into their fingers isn’t something you migrate — you’re resetting ten years of that person.” Bloomberg’s 30,000 commands become extensions of thought. Heidegger called this “ready-to-hand” — the tool disappears. RecWM must create the same fusion.

Network Lock-In

IB Chat handles 200M messages/day. A quote exchanged in chat becomes a binding order. Symphony raised $100M to disrupt it and failed — Goldman Sachs couldn’t even get its own employees to switch. The network IS the product. RecWM’s shared world model creates the same dynamic.

The IKEA Effect

Norton, Mochon & Ariely (2012): people value self-assembled items 63% higher than identical pre-built ones. PMs who train RecWM with their own hypotheses, scenario weightings, and fragment calibrations create an externalisation of their own cognition. Switching means abandoning a mirror of their mind.

The Five Lessons for RecWM

  1. Command-speed interaction. Bloomberg users hit one key and get data. RecWM users speak a question and get a simulated world state. Both are sub-second, in-workflow, zero context-switch. The speed must be neurologically rewarding.
  2. Complexity that signals expertise. Bloomberg’s UX Magazine ethnography: “The more painful the UI is, the more satisfied these users are.” RecWM’s world model is inherently complex — seven fragments, composition channels, regime states — but this complexity must reward mastery, not punish beginners.

Reading the World from Fragments

A submarine has no windows. It constructs its picture of reality from fragments of sound — passive sonar bearings that are individually ambiguous but collectively powerful. A hedge fund operates the same way: it sees fragments of market reality and must infer the full picture.

Bearing-Only Contacts

A credit spread widening 15bps is a bearing-only contact. You know something is out there. Is it idiosyncratic? A forced seller? Or the leading edge of a systemic crisis? A single data point is nearly useless. RecWM collects bearings from every market — FX vol, cross-currency basis, repo rates, shipping data — and triangulates the real signal.

The Baffles Check

Submarines have a blind spot directly behind them where propulsion noise masks incoming sound. They must periodically turn to “clear their baffles.” RecWM does this for the PM: “You are monitoring US equities and rates, but your portfolio has exposure to EM credit through supply chain positions. That’s in your baffles right now.”
